ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Contrastive Loss for Unbiased Utilization Signal Estimation
PROPOSAL: We design a new contrastive loss function to estimate the utilization of external context and internal knowledge in response generation. The loss is minimized by training a discriminator to distinguish between responses generated with and without access to the relevant external context. In the "with context" branch, the generator receives the query, the context, and generates a response. In the "without context" branch, the generator receives only the query and generates a response relying only on its internal knowledge. The discriminator predicts the probability that each response was generated with context access. During training, the generator's goal is to produce responses that are predictable by the discriminator, when context access is available, and unpredictable otherwise. This setup encourages the generator to utilize external context in a meaningful way and to avoid over-reliance on internal knowledge.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: Training the generator with an epoch-based rehearsal curriculum, Baseline 2: Training the generator with a random masking of its input, Baseline 3: Training a simple heuristic-based discriminator that outputs 0.5 for all responses.
COST: 1080
PREDICTION: The proposed approach should lead to a more accurate estimation of external context utilization, while the heuristic-based discriminator might oversimplify the task, leading to a less effective model overall.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Module Attention-Masked Language Model
PROPOSAL: We introduce a novel multi-module attention-masked language model (MAML) architecture, where the model is divided into two parallel sub-networks: one that processes the external context and another that processes the query. The outputs of these sub-networks are then distilled into a single response. To discourage over-reliance on internal knowledge, we introduce attention masking: during training, the model randomly masks certain attention queries pointing towards the internal knowledge, and instead receives information from a learned embedding of the context. The embedding is conditioned on the context and the query, allowing the model to ground its response in the external context.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: A vanilla transformer-based retrieval-augmented generator, Baseline 2: A transformer-based generator with hand-selected attention heads and layers, Baseline 3: A competitive state-of-the-art retrieval-augmented generator.
COST: 1620
PREDICTION: The proposed MAML architecture should significantly reduce hallucinations by promoting external context usage and discouraging internal knowledge over-reliance, but might require more computational resources to train.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Data Conditioning for Protocol Semantic Entropy Estimates
PROPOSAL: We propose that data conditioning, where external context is manipulated to induce regimes of high or low semantic entropy, can facilitate more accurate protocol semantic entropy estimates. We develop a novel data conditioning framework where we selectively amplify or attenuate relevant external context tokens, taking into consideration the input query, thus modulating semantic entropy. We then use probes to estimate the internal semantic entropy; when external context semantic entropy increases, and internal responds with reduced semantic entropy, we consider this a strong indication that the model has utilized the new contextual information, improving the reliability of information provided.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: Basic probes that don't leverage conditioning, Baseline 2: State-of-the-art probes that only use semantic entropy, without any data conditioning, Baseline 3: A simulator to test for the sensitivity of the probes to data quality.
COST: 2070
PREDICTION: The proposed protocol should enable precise quantitative estimates of – internal knowledge dependency during – LLM work, even with manipulations ranging from – straightforward supervised methods to semi-supervised or unsupervised variants; the amount of conditioning might have a moderate-to-severe impact in its effects.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Data Conditioning for Protocol Semantic Entropy Estimates (improved version)
PROPOSAL: We refine the data conditioning framework to include both token-based conditioning and prototype-based conditioning. Token-based conditioning manipulates specific tokens in the external context to induce high or low semantic entropy, as previously proposed. Prototype-based conditioning, on the other hand, leverages the learned prototype representations of the external context to selectively amplify or attenuate the influence of relevant contextual signals. By combining both approaches, we aim to better capture the nuanced relationships between external context and internal semantic entropy, leading to more accurate protocol semantic entropy estimates.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: Basic probes that don't leverage conditioning, Baseline 2: State-of-the-art probes that only use semantic entropy, without any data conditioning, Baseline 3: A simulator to test for the sensitivity of the probes to data quality.
COST: 2160 (minor update from original proposal)
PREDICTION: This revised approach should offer a more robust and accurate way to estimate internal knowledge dependency during LLM work, but might require careful tuning of the trade-off between token-based and prototype-based conditioning.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Prior Knowledge Graph Embeddings for Context Grounding
PROPOSAL: We propose to incorporate prior knowledge graph embeddings into the retrieval-augmented generation model to better capture the contextual relationships and grounding aspects of the external context. Specifically, we augment the input context with learned graph embeddings that represent the keyword relationships and their associated semantic constraints. This allows the model to reason explicitly about the context, incorporate relevant background knowledge, and adapt the generated response accordingly. By leveraging the structure and semantics of the context, we enable more effective utilization of external context and more accurate detection of hallucinations.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: A vanilla retrieval-augmented generator, Baseline 2: A retrieval-augmented generator with a simple context embeddings, Baseline 3: A knowledge-augmented retrieval-augmented generator that uses weakly-supervised learning.
COST: 2700
PREDICTION: The proposed use of prior knowledge graph embeddings should lead to a more contextually-grounded retrieval-augmented generator, but their integration might require careful calibration to avoid over❆️reliance on the graph embeddings.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Per-Contextualized Auditing of Internal Knowledge Utilization
PROPOSAL: We introduce a novel auditing methodology to evaluate the utilization of internal knowledge on a per-contextual basis. By probing the model's responses with context-specific queries, we can assess the extent to which the model relies on internal knowledge versus external context for each specific context. This allows us to identify contexts where the model tends to over-rely on internal knowledge and hallucinate, and to develop targeted fine-tuning strategies to mitigate these issues. To facilitate this auditing process, we propose to allocate a dedicated perturbation space for per-contextualized audits, allowing the model to adapt to the specific contextual requirements.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: A simple context-aware probing mechanism, Baseline 2: A context-agnostic auditing approach, Baseline 3: A state-of-the-art auditing model specifically designed for generic knowledge testing.
COST: 3150
PREDICTION: The proposed per-contextualized auditing approach should offer a more nuanced understanding of internal knowledge utilization and hallucination, allowing for targeted interventions to improve model performance, however, it may add computational overhead during the auditing process.

TITLE: Joint Training for Interleaved Interpretable Retrieval and Generation
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel approach to jointly training the retrieval model and the generation model in an interleaved manner, where the retrieval model learns to retrieve relevant context given the query, and the generation model learns to generate responses based on the retrieved context. This approach allows for iterative refinement of both the retrieval and generation processes, promoting a more informed and contextually-grounded generation of responses. We implement an attention-sharing mechanism to encourage the generation model to focus on key aspects of the retrieved context and detect hallucinations based on the attention allocation of the generation model.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: A vanilla retrieval-augmented generator, Baseline 2: A retrieval-augmented generator with pre-trained retrieval model, Baseline 3: A competitive state-of-the-art retrieval-augmented generator with joint training.
COST: 4020
PREDICTION: The proposed joint training approach should lead to a more effective combination of retrieval and generation, reducing hallucinations and improving context grounding, but the added complexity may make model training and inference more computationally expensive.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Joint Training for Interleaved Interpretable Retrieval and Generation (improved version)
PROPOSAL: We refine the approach to jointly train the retrieval model and the generation model in an interleaved manner, introducing a novel attention-weighted retrieval mechanism. This mechanism allows the generation model to focus on specific aspects of the retrieved context, and the retrieval model to adapt to the generation model's needs, leading to a more informed and contextually-grounded generation of responses. Additionally, we incorporate a failure prediction module that monitors the generation model's reliance on internal knowledge, allowing for early detection of potential hallucinations.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: A vanilla retrieval-augmented generator, Baseline 2: A retrieval-augmented generator with pre-trained retrieval model, Baseline 3: A competitive state-of-the-art retrieval-augmented generator with joint training and failure prediction.
COST: 4200 (minor update from original proposal)
PREDICTION: The revised approach should lead to a more effective combination of retrieval and generation, with improved context grounding and early detection of potential hallucinations, but the added complexity may require careful tuning to achieve optimal performance.

TITLE: Weakly-Supervised Syntactic Analysis for Identifying Hallucinated Parts
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel approach to weakly-supervised syntactic analysis that identifies potential hallucinated parts in generated responses. By using a syntactic parser and a graph-based representation of the generated text, we can detect inconsistencies between the context and the generated text, providing clear indications of potential hallucinations. This approach can be used in conjunction with the other methods proposed here to improve hallucination detection and mitigation.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: A simple syntactic parser-based approach, Baseline 2: A state-of-the-art hallucination detection model without syntactic analysis, Baseline 3: A competitive state-of-the-art hallucination detection model with weakly-supervised learning.
COST: 4825
PREDICTION: The proposed approach should offer a complementary method for detecting hallucinations, but may require careful tuning to achieve optimal performance and could add computational overhead during parsing.

TITLE: Robust Ensemble Learning Framework for Hallucination Detection
PROPOSAL: We propose a robust ensemble learning framework that combines the strengths of the previous methods to improve hallucination detection. By leveraging multiplelearners and weighing their predictions, we can produce more accurate and robust predictions of hallucination. Additionally, we introduce a novel consensus-driven approach to handle disagreements between ensemble members, reducing the likelihood of hallucination.

COST: 6000
PREDICTION: The proposed ensemble learning framework should offer a robust and accurate method for detecting hallucinations, but may require careful tuning to achieve optimal performance and could be computationally expensive to train and deploy.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Quantifying External and Internal Knowledge Utilization via Transfer Learning
PROPOSAL: We propose training a separate "dual-context" transformer model to transfer learn from the RAG system's language understanding and knowledge retrieval abilities by fine-tuning it on a large-scale external knowledge base, while simultaneously training a masked language modeling objective on the same data to capture internal knowledge patterns. This dually-trained transformer can produce robust signals of external (E) and internal (I) knowledge utilization. We hypothesize that the ratio E/I can distinguish well between genuine and hallucinated responses in RAG systems, and evaluate the performance across various experimental domains. The model will be trained on the Wikidata knowledge base and fine-tuned on a diverse set of real-world datasets in retrieval-augmented generation, retrieval-augmented question answering, news summarization, and data-to-text generation.
CONTROLS: We compare our approach with the state-of-the-art hallucination detection methods ReDeEP and others, using Cocktail and a set of real-world common sense reasoning benchmarks as ablation studies.
COST: 2700
PREDICTION: We anticipate a 3% relative improvement in hallucination detection F1-score over existing methods, but potentially underperform on datasets requiring very specialized domain-specific knowledge.

TITLE: Analyzing Local Consistency of RAG Responses
PROPOSAL: We propose analyzing the internal consistency of RAG responses by evaluating the sentiment, a local property, at every possible segment of text from the start to the end of the response. By computing a consistency score for each segment, we can quantify how consistent the predicted facts and narrative flow within the response are, providing an indication of whether or not the response is a coherent "thought" in itself.
CONTROLS: We compare with and without the inclusion of external context documents and with/without internal knowledge-based hallucination metrics in the analysis.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: REVISED Quantifying External and Internal Knowledge Utilization via Transfer Learning
PROPOSAL: We refine our proposal on transfer learning by modifying the dual-context transformer model to focus specifically on combining semantic representations of the query and retrieved documents with the internal knowledge patterns of the RAG system. Instead of training on a large-scale external knowledge base, we propose to fine-tune the model on a smaller dataset of diverse few-shot learning tasks that require significant external context utilization and internal knowledge retrieval. This setup can highlight nuanced patterns in knowledge utilization and hallucination behaviors.
CONTROLS: We retain the comparison with state-of-the-art hallucination detection methods and our original ablation study on a range of real-world RAG applications. Additionally, we propose a strong baseline where we pre-train the dual-context model on general knowledge bases and evaluate its transfer learning performance on both low and high few-shot learning tasks.
COST: 2400
PREDICTION: By focusing on few-shot learning tasks, we anticipate being more robust to domain-specific knowledge distribution and achieving at least a 10% relative improvement in hallucination detection performance, potentially at the cost of more computational overhead. However, we are concerned about overfitting to few-shot tasks and require a strong baseline to evaluate the transfer learning performance across a variety of scenarios.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Contrastive Knowledge Retrieval with Adversarial Insertion
PROPOSAL: We propose an adversarial approach that aims at distinguishing between meaningful and hallucinated incorporation of external context. We create pairs of input queries and their corresponding transformed queries where the original information from the external context is replaced with irrelevant or misleading information. Then, we train a Siamese network with the real external context and the transformed (adversarial) external context. The model learns to distinguish the difference between the two types of context utilization.
CONTROLS: We train and compare our approach to models trained with pre-finetuned external context (common knowledge-bases), contrastive learning on retrieved contexts with removal of redundant or highly-relevant information, and closure learning on knowledge graphs.
COST: 5400
PREDICTION: The proposed model can potentially pinpoint whether the incorporation of external context contributes to the hallucinated response or supports the generated content with verifiable facts and indicates issues in models utilizing them. We anticipate a significant improvement in capturing and preventing knowledge hallucination.

TITLE: Adversarial Knowledge Retrieval Optimization
PROPOSAL: We propose incorporating an adversarial knowledge retrieval module that trains to maximize the knowledge overlap between the retrieved context and the internal knowledge representation. Simultaneously, we optimize the ranking function of the retrieval module to minimize the overlap. This trade-off helps in identifying the balance between the retrieval quality and the divergence between the retrieved context and the internal knowledge.
CONTROLS: We compare against standard and adversarial-normalized retrieval optimization methods and study the impact on hallucination detection and knowledge grounding.
COST: 18900
PREDICTION: By balancing the trade-off between knowledge overlap and divergence, we anticipate improving hallucination detection and knowledge grounding performance. However, this may come at the expense of decreased retrieval effectiveness for certain task sets and potentially interacts negatively with the precision/ accuracy required in handling uncommon situations.

TITLE: Adversarial Knowledge Retrieval Optimization

PROPOSAL: We design an experiment to validate the effectiveness of using statistical methods (such as hypothesis testing, confidence intervals, and regression analysis) to quantify the utilization of external context and internal knowledge in LLMs. Specifically, we will use a diverse range of tasks (e.g., news summarization, question answering) and will measure the reliance on internal vs. external knowledge by comparing the correlation between model predictions and retrieved context. However, we may see some limitations in tasks with complex or ambiguous context, where statistical methods may fail to capture the nuances of LLM behavior.

TITLE: Self-Supervised Learning of Hallucination Detection
PROPOSAL: We explore self-supervised learning for hallucination detection, where the model is trained on its own outputs without relying on human labels or ground truth. Specifically, we will train a discriminator on the internal knowledge utilization scores generated by the model itself, using a dataset with mixed LLM outputs and apply mechanisms like hard negative sampling to essentially learn the models's hallucinogenic biases. This approach may learn to detect hallucinations without relying on external data or human judgement.
CONTROLS: We will compare our self-supervised approach with a supervised baseline trained on human-labeled data and an unsupervised baseline that uses only the data's intrinsic properties.
COST: 1600
PREDICTION: We expect our self-supervised approach to show competitive results to the supervised baseline, but may struggle with tasks that require domain-specific knowledge, where the model's hallucinations may be highly contextual and dependent on the specific task.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Domain-Agnostic Utilization Scores through Graph Analysis
PROPOSAL: We propose a graph-based approach to compute utilization scores that are agnostic to the model's architecture and the task domain. Specifically, we use graph convolutional networks to analyze the directed graph of interactions between tokens in the model's output, retrieved context, and internal knowledge representations. Our goal is to identify patterns in the graph that distinguish between tangible and hallucinated context. We assume that hallucinated text tends to be densely connected with internal knowledge nodes, whereas using externally-retrieved context results in more sparse connections with internal knowledge.
CONTROLS: We will compare our graph-based approach with ablations using different graph representation methods (e.g., spatial graphs, temporal graphs) and a baseline that relies on common attention mechanisms.
COST: 2400
PREDICTION: We expect our graph-based approach to generalize well across domains and models, but may be computationally expensive to train due to the need to compute the graph convolution.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Domain-Agnostic Utilization Scores through Graph Analysis (Revision 1)
PROPOSAL: In this revised proposal, we extend the graph-based approach by incorporating a " hallucination-aware" edge weighting scheme. Specifically, we modify the weights assigned to the edges in the graph to reflect the likelihood that a given interaction between tokens is indicative of a hallucination. This revised weighting scheme can be learned in conjunction with the graph convolutional network, thereby adaptively pruning the importance of potentially misleading relationships. The intuition is that hallucinations often involve a particular "cognitive pattern," which would be suppressed or diminishing in the hallucination-aware weighted graph.
CONTROLS: We will evaluate this revised weighting scheme against various baselines, including the graph-based approach without hallucination-aware weighting and a standard attention-based approach.
COST: 2400
PREDICTION: We expect this revised graph-based approach to improve performance on hallucination detection, by reducing false positives and false negatives, but the effectiveness might degrade if the weighting scheme becomes overly sensitive or captures similar patterns unrelated to hallucinations.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multimodal Retrieval-Augmented Counterfactuals
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel approach to hallucination detection by generating and evaluating multimodal counterfactuals that represent possible alternative generations conditioned on both the input, external context, and internal knowledge. Our generation process is paired with a contrastive learning framework, in which the model learns to evaluate the differences between the generated text and the provided information. The proposed method will serve as a source of evidence for the joint maximization signal and perform counterfactually aware hallucination detection. Our goal is to improve detection accuracy while also providing insights into how hallucinations originate and are expressed.
CONTROLS: We will compare our multimodal method with baselines that focus on comparing attention distributions and gradient differences to identify „hallucinations".
COST: 3600
PREDICTION: We expect the proposed counterfactually aware approach to achieve state-of-the-art performance on hallucination detection, and significantly valuable for diagnosing unrealistic text but we might struggle to balance the complexity of evaluation in counts that also guarantee supporting plausible responses.

TITLE: Meta-Learning for Hallucination-Aware Retrieval
PROPOSAL: We propose a meta-learning approach to advance hallucination-aware retrieval by improving the model's ability to adapt to diverse retrieval settings and task domains. Our approach involves training a model to learn a task-agnostic hallucination detection strategy that can be fine-tuned for specific retrieval tasks. This is achieved by designing a meta-training objective that encourages the model to seek hallucination-aware representations that can generalize across different domains and tasks. We evaluate our approach on a variety of retrieval tasks and datasets, and predict that it will outperform state-of-the-art hallucination detection methods on tasks involving structured and unstructured data.
CONTROLS: We will compare our meta-learning approach against a fine-tuned version of the baseline methods, including the self-supervised learning and graph-based approaches.
COST: 5200
PREDICTION: We expect our meta-learning approach to achieve significant performance improvements on hallucination detection, and demonstrate its adaptability to a wide range of retrieval tasks. However, we may encounter high computational costs associated with the meta-training process, which could limit its scalability.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Unified Framework for Hallucination-Aware Retrieval and Generation
PROPOSAL: We present a unified framework that integrates the key insights and components from our previous proposals, providing a novel combination of self-supervised learning, graph-based analysis, and meta-learning to tackle the challenges of hallucination-aware retrieval and generation. Our framework, called HALLUCINATOR, aims to capture the subtleties of human-like behavior and improve the robustness of retrieval-augmented generation systems. By employing a novel attention mechanism that synergizes internal knowledge and external context, HALLUCINATOR will be capable of reducing hallucinations and producing high-quality, context-aware responses.
CONTROLS: To validate our framework, we will compare HALLUCINATOR against state-of-the-art hallucination detection methods and perform an ablation study to assess the contribution of each component.
COST: 11520
PREDICTION: We expect HALLUCINATOR to significantly outperform existing approaches in terms of hallucination detection and generation quality, while also providing a unified framework for tackling the complex challenges of retrieval-augmented generation. However, we anticipate that the level of computational complexity will be substantial due to the integration of numerous components and the need to train an attention mechanism that combines internal knowledge and external context in a unified framework.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE:  Dual-Path Transformer for Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We propose an experiment that designs a dual-path transformer for multivariate time-series forecasting, consisting of two paths: (i) a channel-independent encoder, which captures temporal dependencies within each variable, and (ii) a cross-channel attention mechanism, which models interactions among variables. The dual-path architecture leverages the strengths of both paths by selectively incorporating the cross-channel information into the prediction process based on variable-specific importance scores learned during training. We compare the proposed dual-path transformer with existing single-path architectures, including a baseline with no cross-channel interaction, a state-of-the-art channel-independent encoder, and a previous channel-dependent encoder.
We evaluate our dual-path transformer on a set of multivariate time-series forecasting tasks from real-world domains, such as electricity consumption forecasting, traffic flow forecasting, and solar power generation forecasting. We also explore the model's ability to handle variable importance scores by controlling the amount of cross-channel interaction included in predictions.
CONTROLS: 
- Baseline with no cross-channel interaction
- State-of-the-art channel-independent encoder (e.g., LSTM)
- Previous channel-dependent encoder 
- Simple linear projection as a baseline decoding method
COST: 600
PREDICTION: We expect the dual-path transformer to outperform existing single-path architectures, offering improved forecasting accuracy, and variable importance discovery, especially for tasks with high dimensional channels. However, its performance might decrease when the importance score's reliability is challenged.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE:  Hybrid Forecasting Super-Resolution for Multivariate Time-Series Data
PROPOSAL: We propose an experiment that employs a hybrid forecasting super-resolution approach for multivariate time-series data, combining the strengths of traditional forecasting models with a super-resolution transformation (SRT) method. The traditional forecasting model serves as a domain-invariant prior, while the SRT method refines the predictions by amplifying fine-grained patterns in the data. We evaluate the proposed hybrid approach on real-world multivariate time-series datasets from diverse domains, including traffic flow, electricity consumption, and solar power generation forecasting.
We compare the performance of the hybrid SRT-based forecasting method with state-of-the-art deep learning models specifically designed for time-series forecasting, and assess its potential to improve forecasting performance in scenarios with limited training data or high variability.
CONTROLS: 
- State-of-the-art deep learning models (e.g., transformer-based)
- Traditional forecasting models (e.g., ARIMA, SARIMA)
- Baseline with no super-resolution transformation
COST: 840
PREDICTION: The hybrid SRT-based approach is expected to achieve higher forecasting accuracy than traditional methods, particularly in scenarios with limited data or high variability, due to its ability to amplify fine-grained patterns. However, it may be sensitive to the hyperparameters used for the traditional forecasting model and the SRT method.

PROPOSAL: We propose an experiment that introduces a Temporal Graph Attention Network (TGAT) for multivariate time-series forecasting, allowing the model to learn integral relationships between temporal and spatial dependencies. - Vanilla graph attention networks
- GRU/LSTM-based models

PREDICTION: The proposed TGAT model is expected to significantly improve forecasting accuracy due to its ability to effectively capture both temporal and spatial dependencies in multivariate time-series data. TITLE:  Uncertainty-Aware Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting with Monte Carlo Sampling
PROPOSAL: We propose an experiment that introduces an uncertainty-aware multivariate time-series forecasting framework utilizing Monte Carlo sampling. The approach incorporates a factorization of the multivariate time-series data into a product of univariate time-series factors, allowing for efficient estimation of the forecasting uncertainty. We evaluate the proposed framework on a variety of real-world datasets from diverse domains, including electricity consumption forecasting, traffic flow forecasting, and solar power generation forecasting.
We compare the performance of our framework with state-of-the-art models, including the TGAT model, dual-path transformer, and hybrid forecasting super-resolution approach, as well as baselines that ignore uncertainty.
CONTROLS: 
- TGAT model
- Dual-path transformer
- Hybrid forecasting super-resolution approach
- Baseline with no uncertainty modeling
COST: 1068
PREDICTION: Our uncertainty-aware framework is expected to provide more accurate forecasting results than existing models by accounting for the uncertainty in the multivariate time-series data. However, the computational cost may increase due to the additional Monte Carlo sampling steps, which may be challenging to optimize for large-scale datasets.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Query-Based Channel-Selective Attention for Decoding
PROPOSAL: To address the limitations of simple linear projections in decoding future signals from encoded representations, we introduce a novel decoding method that selectively attends to informative channels based on the forecast horizon. The proposed method involves a query-based attention mechanism, where learned vectors (queries) are used to selectively focus on predictive variates at each time step. This allows the model to dynamically allocate attention weightings across channels in accordance with the forecast target and horizon. We also incorporate a modulating gate to attenuate learning of non-predictive signals.
CONTROLS: Compare against traditional linear projection and recent attention-based decoding methods, such as attentive pooling and permutation-invariant encoding (PIE).
COST: 11500 
PREDICTION: This approach is expected to yield 15% absolute improvements in forecasting accuracy over state-of-the-art methods for longer-term predictions, particularly in the domains of weather and solar power generation. The effectiveness may diminish for datasets with an abundance of uncorrelated signals, due to the model's tendency to over-allocate attention to less informative signals.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Revised Cross-Attention Enhanced Channel-Dependent Encoder
PROPOSAL: We revisit the cross-attention enhanced channel-dependent encoder proposed in Turn 1 and revise it to improve scalability and efficiency. Specifically, we replace the quadratic attention function with a learnable, low-rank approximation (e.g., using factorized quadratic attention). Additionally, we incorporate a dynamic channel weighting mechanism that adaptively adjusts the relative importance of different channels during training. This helps mitigate the risk of the model focusing excessively on high-variance channels and reduces the computational overhead.
CONTROLS: Compare against the original cross-attention enhanced encoder, a standard channel-independent encoder (1D CNN), and a simplified channel-dependent encoder without cross-attention.
COST: 16200 
PREDICTION: The revised encoder is expected to exhibit better handling of high-dimensional datasets and improved generalizability across different forecasting applications. A noticeable gain in forecasting accuracy of up to 10% within the traffic flow forecasting domain may be hindered by the difficulty in optimizing the dynamic channel weighting mechanism for certain datasets.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Minimally Supervised Training with Historical-Forward Sharing
PROPOSAL: To address the limitations of traditional pretraining-finetuning pipelines for time-series forecasting, we introduce a minimally supervised training approach that encourages sharing knowledge across historical and forward contexts. We utilize a masked segment reconstruction task with an additional historical-forward sharing component: a few forward segments are pseudo-masked and predicted by the model, while the corresponding historical segments are filled in as full supervision. This approach facilitates end-to-end learning of both encoding and decoding components, allowing the model to directly optimize for forecasting accuracy.
CONTROLS: Compare against pretraining-finetuning pipelines (BERT-inspired and standard unrehearsed pretraining), a direct supervision approach, and randomly sampled segments for the masked segment reconstruction task.
COST: 24000 
PREDICTION: This novel training approach is expected to significantly reduce the training time and improve the overall forecasting performance for datasets with complex temporal dependencies, as measured in the solar power generation forecasting domain. Potential issues include the increased sensitivity to initial model weights and the difficulty in determining the optimal amount of historical-forward sharing.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Explicit Channel Phenomenon Modeling for Incorporating Domain Knowledge
PROPOSAL: To incorporate domain-specific knowledge into the multivariate forecasting model, we introduce an explicit channel phenomenon modeling module. This component allows domain experts to specify and incorporate causal relationships between variables according to their knowledge, enabling the model to learn from and generalize these relationships. We propose representing these relationships as a directed acyclic graph (DAG) and incorporating it as a regularizer within the minimally supervised training framework introduced in Turn 3. This will help to reduce uncertainty in the model and provide more reliable forecasts.
CONTROLS: Compare against the original minimally supervised training approach and other state-of-the-art methods that incorporate knowledge into the forecasting process (e.g., incorporating physical laws based on temperature gradients).
COST: 31200 
PREDICTION: This approach is expected to achieve an average absolute percentage error (AAPE) of 15% lower than state-of-the-art methods across the traffic flow and electricity transformer temperature forecasting domains. Changes to the knowledge graphs and associated structures will require significant re-calibration of model weights, which could hinder training time and the model's ability to adapt to new data.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Adaptive Hierarchical Forecasting for Capturing Multi-Scale Dependencies
PROPOSAL: To capture diverse temporal and spatial complexities in multivariate time-series forecasting, we propose an adaptive hierarchical forecasting framework. This approach involves learning a Gaussian mixture model (GMM) to represent the distribution of temporal dependencies at multiple scales. By adaptively switching between the learned mixture components based on the forecast horizon and scale, the model can effectively handle diverse temporal patterns and spatial dependencies, improving overall forecasting performance.
CONTROLS: Compare against single-scale forecasting methods, multi-scale aggregation methods, and existing hierarchical forecasting approaches.
COST: 41513.28 
PREDICTION: This approach is expected to achieve a relative improvement of up to 25% in forecasting accuracy for medium to long-term predictions (H > 24 hours) in the electricity consumption forecasting domain, especially when dealing with grid-level forecasting. Model interpretability and scalability concerns may arise due to the added complexity of maintaining and updating the mixture models in real-time.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Revised Minimally Supervised Training with Historical-Forward Sharing
PROPOSAL: To improve the stability and efficiency of the minimally supervised training approach proposed in Turn 4, we revise it to incorporate an online knowledge distillation mechanism. This involves an additional distillation loss term that encourages the model to learn from a pre-trained forecasting model. We also introduce a refresh rate to control the frequency at which the state Knowledge distill is updated. This not only reduces the risk of over-reliance on the pre-trained model but also enables the model to adapt to new data and evolving relationships between variables.
CONTROLS: Compare against the original minimally supervised training approach and traditional pretraining-finetuning pipelines.
COST: 40200 
PREDICTION: This revised approach is expected to exhibit improved robustness and adaptability across different forecasting applications and datasets, with a noticeable reduction in training time for longer sequences. Oversmoothing of task structures and ineffective knowledge distillation can result from the learned weight initialization not being fully sampled for appropriately distant distilling.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: Phase-Aware Forecasting for Mitigating Seasonal and Trend Changes
PROPOSAL: To handle seasonality and trend changes in multivariate time-series forecasting, we introduce a phase-aware forecasting approach. This involves learning multiple phase-aware representations, each capturing the underlying dynamics within a specific phase of the time-series. We propose incorporating a modal-aware hierarchical attention mechanism, which selectively aggregates information from the different phases based on their relevance to the forecast horizon. This approach enables the model to capture both the rapid changes within each phase and the long-term trends between phases.
CONTROLS: Compare against traditional seasonal decomposition methods, trend-aware forecasting approaches, and existing phase-aware models (e.g., Fourier-series-based models).
COST: 55420 
PREDICTION: This approach is expected to achieve improved forecasting accuracy for seasonal and trend-based datasets, such as electricity consumption and solar power generation, with noticeable gains in low-phase noise regions (e.g., holidays, weekday sessions during shoulder months). However, the additional complexity may lead to increased model interpretability and hyperparameter tuning challenges.

CONTROLS: Compare against the original minimally supervised training approach and traditional pretraining-finetuning pipelines.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: Phase-Aware Forecasting for Mitigating Seasonal and Trend Changes
PROPOSAL: To handle seasonality and trend changes in multivariate time-series forecasting, we introduce a phase-aware forecasting approach. This involves learning multiple phase-aware representations, each capturing the underlying dynamics within a specific phase of the time-series. We propose incorporating a modal-aware hierarchical attention mechanism, which selectively aggregates information from the different phases based on their relevance to the forecast horizon. This approach enables the model to capture both the rapid changes within each phase and the long-term trends between phases.
CONTROLS: Compare against traditional seasonal decomposition methods, trend-aware forecasting approaches, and existing phase-aware models (e.g., Fourier-series-based models).
COST: 166510 
PREDICTION: This approach is expected to achieve improved forecasting accuracy for seasonal and trend-based datasets, such as electricity consumption and solar power generation, with noticeable gains in low-phase noise regions (e.g., holidays, weekday sessions during shoulder months). However, the additional complexity may lead to increased model interpretability and hyperparameter tuning challenges.

ACTION: REVISE 4
TITLE: Revised Explicit Channel Phenomenon Modeling for Incorporating Domain Knowledge
PROPOSAL: To further enhance the explicit channel phenomenon modeling module proposed in Turn 4, we introduce a novel hybrid approach that combines the strengths of both knowledge graphs and Gaussian process (GP) causal discovery. This involves learning a GP-based causal structure on top of the domain-specific knowledge graph, allowing for more flexible and adaptive modeling of complex relationships between variables. We propose incorporating this hybrid approach into the revised minimally supervised training framework and evaluating its performance on real-world forecasting tasks.
CONTROLS: Compare against traditional knowledge graph-based approaches, GP-based causal discovery, and existing hybrid models.
COST: 144420 
PREDICTION: This revised approach is expected to achieve improved forecasting accuracy and interpretability across different domains, with a noticeable reduction in the need for manual domain knowledge curation. However, the added complexity may lead to increased training time and model fragility to uncertain causal structures.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE:  Investigating Cross-Channel Interactions using a Novel Channel-Dependent Encoder
PROPOSAL: Design a new channel-dependent encoder architecture, dubbed "Multi-Task Vertex Graph Convolutional Network" (MTVGCN), composed of a vertex graph convolutional neural network (GCNN) that captures interactions among variates, and apply MTVGCN to three real-world datasets: weather forecasting (North America), electricity consumption forecasting (Germany), and traffic flow forecasting (London). Specifically, we will reformulate the existing graph attention mechanism as an optimization problem and solve it with global max pooling. This allows us to adaptively aggregate and weight feature representations across different channels, while navigating the trade-off between preserving spatial dependence and allowing flexibility in node connections. To demonstrate the superiority of MTVGCN over state-of-the-art channel-independent encoders, we establish a baseline comparison using a well-established peer model, briefly denoted as XT-attention [1], which has been broadly applied in the time-series domain.
CONTROLS: XT-attention [1] on the same dataset
COST: 1800
PREDICTION: MTVGCN should demonstrate competitive improvements over XT-attention in forecasting performance on all three datasets, specifically by providing lower error rates in multivariate predictions; however, model performance may drop when applied to datasets with an extremely large number of channels.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE:  A Linear Decoding Mechanism with Temporal Attention
PROPOSAL: Introduce a novel decoding mechanism, "Temporal Linear Attention Projection" (TLAP), that combines linear decoding with temporal attention mechanisms to predict future time series values from encoded representations. TLAP modulates linear projections using a temporal attention mechanism that evaluates the importance of each encoded step over the entire time series. TLAP is evaluated on the same three real-world datasets as MTVGCN: weather forecasting (North America), electricity consumption forecasting (Germany), and traffic flow forecasting (London). To compare against existing linear decoding strategies, we will consider the standard linear projection and its popular variants, briefly denoted as Lin-OLS [2] and Lin-LSTM [3] respectively.
CONTROLS: MTVGCN with standard linear decoding, Lin-OLS, Lin-LSTM, and XLNet's built-in linear forecasting model [4] on the same dataset
COST: 3600
PREDICTION: TLAP should outperform existing linear decoding strategies, especially on datasets with complex temporal dynamics, due to its improved flexibility and expressiveness; this gain is however sensitive to the complexity of the task and the encoder architecture used.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE:  Investigation of the Effects of Hyperparameters on Model Performance
PROPOSAL: Perform an in-depth analysis of the effects of hyperparameters on the performance of various time-series forecasting models, including XT-attention, TLAP, and the proposed MTVGCV. To this end, we design a systematic search for the optimal hyperparameters using a combination of grid search and random search methods. Our goal is to assess how different hyperparameters impact the forecasting performance across the datasets, including their influence on metrics such as Mean Absolute Error (MAE) and Mean Squared Error (MSE). The scope of our investigation will include adjusting learning rates, batch sizes, and the number of layers in the architecture as these parameters are known to have a significant influence on performance.
CONTROLS: XT-attention, TLAP, MTVGCV with random search and grid search on the same dataset

PROPOSAL: To improve model interpretability in time-series forecasting, we propose a novel method for visualizing and explaining the predictions made by our previously developed models, including TLAP and MTVGCV. Our proposed visualization method uses class activation mapping (CAM) to show which regions of the input data are most influential in making predictions, and also generates attention-weighted visualizations to highlight the most informative regions of the time series. Additionally, we utilize SHAP to assess the attribution of each feature to predictions made by our model. By visualizing and explaining our forecasted values, we can improve the trustworthiness of our models, make them more understandable, and even attempt to unveil causality for various temporal phenomena.
CONTROLS: TLAP, MTVGCV, SHAP, partial dependency and feature permutation importance on the same dataset
COST: 28518

ACTION: ADD
TITLE:  Investigating Cross-Channel Interactions using a Novel Channel-Dependent Encoder
PROPOSAL: Design a new channel-dependent encoder architecture, dubbed "Multi-Task Vertex Graph Convolutional Network" (MTVGCN), composed of a vertex graph convolutional neural network (GCNN) that captures interactions among variates, and apply MTVGCN to three real-world datasets: weather forecasting (North America), electricity consumption forecasting (Germany), and traffic flow forecasting (London). Specifically, we will reformulate the existing graph attention mechanism as an optimization problem and solve it with global max pooling. This allows us to adaptively aggregate and weight feature representations across different channels, while navigating the trade-off between preserving spatial dependence and allowing flexibility in node connections. To demonstrate the superiority of MTVGCN over state-of-the-art channel-independent encoders, we establish a baseline comparison using a well-established peer model, briefly denoted as XT-attention [1], which has been broadly applied in the time-series domain.
CONTROLS: XT-attention [1] on the same dataset
COST: 5400
PREDICTION: MTVGCN should demonstrate competitive improvements over XT-attention in forecasting performance on all three datasets, specifically by providing lower error rates in multivariate predictions; however, model performance may drop when applied to datasets with an extremely large number of channels.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE:  A Linear Decoding Mechanism with Temporal Attention
PROPOSAL: Introduce a novel decoding mechanism, "Temporal Linear Attention Projection" (TLAP), that combines linear decoding with temporal attention mechanisms to predict future time series values from encoded representations. TLAP modulates linear projections using a temporal attention mechanism that evaluates the importance of each encoded step over the entire time series. TLAP is evaluated on the same three real-world datasets as MTVGCN: weather forecasting (North America), electricity consumption forecasting (Germany), and traffic flow forecasting (London). To compare against existing linear decoding strategies, we will consider the standard linear projection and its popular variants, briefly denoted as Lin-OLS [2] and Lin-LSTM [3] respectively.
CONTROLS: MTVGCN with standard linear decoding, Lin-OLS, Lin-LSTM, and XLNet's built-in linear forecasting model [4] on the same dataset
COST: 10800
PREDICTION: TLAP should outperform existing linear decoding strategies, especially on datasets with complex temporal dynamics, due to its improved flexibility and expressiveness; this gain is however sensitive to the complexity of the task and the encoder architecture used.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISED Investigation of Mask-and-Reconstruction Tasks in Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: Extend our previous studies on pretraining-finetuning two-stage training strategies for multivariate time-series forecasting and focus on a novel masking objective designed to better align with the task. This "Domain-Aware Masking" (DAM) introduces an additional conditional masking scheme that incorporates the domain structure of the time series, mitigating the tendency to model uninformative patterns. We hypothesize that DAM will enhance the encoder-decoder architecture's ability to capture temporal dynamics and cross-channel dependencies in multivariate forecasting tasks. Performance evaluation will be conducted on the same three real-world datasets used for MTVGCN and TLAP: weather forecasting (North America), electricity consumption forecasting (Germany), and traffic flow forecasting (London). We compare our proposed DAM-based framework to various baselines, including the original pretraining-finetuning pipeline, by testing model performance on standard metrics for time-series forecasting, such as Mean Absolute Error (MAE).
CONTROLS: Original pretraining-finetuning pipeline, XT-attention with fine-tuning only, TLAP with fine-tuning only, MTVGCN with fine-tuning only on the same dataset
COST: 15200

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISED Investigating Cross-Channel Interactions using a Novel Channel-Dependent Encoder
PROPOSAL: REVISED Improve the convolutional architecture in MTVGCN by replacing the existing graph attention mechanism with a novel " backbone-stream fusion" (BSF) module, which integrate both local and global contexts. BSF combines self-attention and spatial convolution with a learned dynamic routing strategy to generate attentive spatial masks for local features. This new architecture will be employed on the same benchmarks and compared against XT-attention for state-of-the-art performance benchmarks on multivariate time-series datasets.
CONTROLS: XT-attention [1] on the same dataset
COST: 22560

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISED Investigating Cross-Channel Interactions using a Novel Channel-Dependent Encoder
PROPOSAL: REVISED Extensively incorporate the Structural Temporal Graph Convolution (STGCN) model to create a more sophisticated architecture: Multivariate Temporal Graph Convolutional Network (MTGCV). This design incorporates structural graph convolution and attention mechanisms to build on the principles of MTVGCV, but extends the abilities of the encoder model. We now aim to compare MTGCV against our previously proposed TLAP and other state-of-the-art models for enhanced performance and improved coverage of real-world multivariate time-series forecasting tasks on datasets such as solar power generation and electricity transformer temperature forecasting.
CONTROLS: TLAP, MTGCV, MTVGCV with attention mechanism, BERT-based pretraining and fine-tuning architecture on the same dataset
COST: 30240

ACTION: ADD
TITLE:  Investigation of the Effects of Hyperparameters on Model Performance
PROPOSAL: Perform an in-depth analysis of the effects of hyperparameters on the performance of various time-series forecasting models, including XT-attention, TLAP, and the proposed MTVGCV. To this end, we design a systematic search for the optimal hyperparameters using a combination of grid search and random search methods. Our goal is to assess how different hyperparameters impact the forecasting performance across the datasets, including their influence on metrics such as Mean Absolute Error (MAE) and Mean Squared Error (MSE). The scope of our investigation will include adjusting learning rates, batch sizes, and the number of layers in the architecture as these parameters are known to have a significant influence on performance.
CONTROLS: XT-attention, TLAP, MTVGCV with random search and grid search on the same dataset
COST: 43680

ACTION: ADD
TITLE:  Alignment of Encoder-Decoder Architecture with Training Objective
PROPOSAL: Introduce a novel pretraining objective for the encoder and decoder components of time-series forecasting models, focusing on learning cross-task representations that more accurately capture time-series patterns. This new pretraining scheme, "Dual-Temporal Masking" (DTM), when combined with a mask scheme that aligns with the downstream forecasting task, attains substantial benefits over state-of-the-art pretraining methods for model performance, particularly when tested on datasets such as traffic flow forecasting and weather forecasting. We perform a thorough comparison with established architectures, including TLAP and MTVGCV.
CONTROLS: TLAP with standard pretraining, MTVGCV with standard pretraining, MT-Transformer (a baseline stacking encoder, decoder and a masking scheme) on the same dataset
COST: 72880

PROPOSAL: Thoroughly investigate the effect of the Dual-Temporal Masking (DTM) training objective on training efficiency and generalizability across real-world multivariate time-series datasets. This study focused on the following: DTM paired with multitask learning strategy on a battery of time-series datasets, while looking for convergence speed, training loss, accuracy, and robustness to over-fitting. We use commonly used metrics in time-series analysis such as training time, AIC/BIC, model size, and calibration for better understanding the scope of proposed methods.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Efficient Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting with Channel-Aware Transformers
PROPOSAL: Implement a variant of the Transformer architecture, dubbed Channel-Aware Transformer (CAT), which models channel dependencies by adding channel-specific self-attention mechanisms on top of the Transformer encoder. This design aims to effectively capture cross-variable interactions without the high computational cost of channel-dependent encoders. Evaluate CAT on multivariate time-series forecasting benchmarks in weather forecasting, electricity consumption forecasting, and traffic flow forecasting using the Mean Absolute Error (MAE) metric.
CONTROLS: Transformer without channel dependencies ( vanilla Transformer encoder), CAT with only one channel-specific self-attention mechanism, and CAT without decoder linear layer to compare against previous work.
COST: 50000
PREDICTION: CAT is expected to outperform vanilla Transformer in forecasting accuracy across most domains due to its ability to model channel dependencies, but may fail in domains where simple, robust channel-independent encoders are sufficient.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Hierarchical Contrastive Learning with Adaptive Augmentation Routing
PROPOSAL: We propose a hierarchical contrastive learning framework that dynamically adapts the augmentation routing for each instance. At each level, the model partitions the views into disjoint clusters and learns a separate representation for each cluster, which encourages the model to focus on the most informative views for each instance. We use a novel variant of the InfoNCE loss function that enforces a hierarchical structure across the clusters, allowing the model to learn a more nuanced representation of semantic similarity. 
CONTROLS: We compare our method to the vanilla SimCLR framework and evaluate its performance on CIFAR-10, STL-10, and ImageNet datasets. To ablate the hierarchical structure, we test a variant where the model doesn't partition the views into clusters.
COST: 6000
PREDICTION: Our method should outperform SimCLR on the unsupervised clustering and linear evaluation tasks, especially on STL-10, due to its ability to focus on the most informative views. However, we anticipate that the hierarchical structure might become less effective for larger batch sizes, where the model might neglect smaller clusters.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Visualizing the Information Landscape of Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: We design a novel visualization tool to represent the information landscape of contrastive learning, providing insight into how the model represents semantic similarity between views. Our tool, called InfoMap, generates a graph where nodes represent individual samples, and edges represent the similarity between their representations. We also propose a new metric, called InfoDiversity, to quantify the diversity of information contributed by each view. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Contrastive Learning for Few-Shot Learning: A Unifying Framework
PROPOSAL: We propose a unifying framework for using contrastive learning for few-shot learning tasks. Our framework, called Few-Shot Contrastive Learning (FSCL), combines our hierarchical contrastive learning framework (proposal 1) with a few-shot evaluation mechanism. FSCL enables the model to learn a robust representation of each class and adapt to new classes with only a few examples. We design a novel evaluation protocol to benchmark FSCL and compare its performance to state-of-the-art few-shot learning methods.
CONTROLS: We compare FSCL to traditional few-shot learning methods, such as MAML and Protonet, and evaluate its performance on several benchmark datasets like CUB, Cars-196, and Stanford Online Products. To ablate the role of contrastive learning, we also test a variant of FSCL that uses only a few-shot learning mechanism.
COST: 27000
PREDICTION: Our FSCL framework should outperform state-of-the-art few-shot learning methods, especially on more challenging datasets, due to its ability to learn a robust representation of each class. However, we anticipate that the adaptability of FSCL might be limited to only few-shot scenarios, and it might not generalize well to new classes.

TITLE: Assessing Information Gain in Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: Investigate how the mutual information between views and the target representation changes over time during contrastive learning. Use a modified version of MINE (Mutual Information Neural Estimation) to estimate the mutual information. Train a range of automated augmentation models on the CIFAR-100 dataset, varying the level of transformation complexity, and evaluate the information gain for each instance over 50 epochs.
CONTROLS: Compare MINE against a zeroth-order information gain estimator and a strong supervised baseline; ablate the impact of target representation and view similarity.
COST: 240000
PREDICTION: We expect to see a nonlinear relationship between information gain and augmentation complexity, with a peak in information gain for moderate levels of transformation, confirming earlier intuitions about the representational trade-off. However, information gain might saturate prematurely due to the fixed augmentation pipeline, indicating a need for adaptive methods.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Contrastive Learning through Sample-Specific Augmentation
PROPOSAL: Develop an adaptive augmentation framework that uses the estimated mutual information gain from proposal 1 to determine the level of transformation complexity for each instance. This approach is grounded in a novel metric, termed 'information initiative', which measures the willingness of the model to learn new information and adjust its augmentations accordingly. For each instance, train a small auxiliary network to predict its information initiative and adjust augmentations to push the information gain beyond a predefined threshold. Validate this method on the ImageNet dataset and compare it to state-of-the-art contrastive learning frameworks.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the adaptive framework against MoCo and SimCLR with varying batch sizes, ablate the impact of the auxiliary network and the information initiative metric, and compare against a strong supervised baseline.
COST: 500000
PREDICTION: By dynamically adjusting augmentations, we expect the adaptive framework to consistently outperform static methods on information-theoretic metrics, demonstrating its potential for improved representational diversity and consistency. However, this comes at a cost in computation and potentially over-exploring less reliable regions of the augmentations space.

TITLE: Exploration-Exploitation Trade-off in Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: Investigate the exploration-exploitation trade-off during contrastive learning by integrating a simple, bi-level optimization approach, similar to Thompson sampling in bandit problems, to decide between information gain maximization and expressiveness maximization based on the information gain estimates from proposal 1. This will allow the model to switch between exploiting the known information and exploring the augmentation space for new information, with an adaptively controlled trade-off.
CONTROLS: Compare this integrated framework to our previously proposed adaptive framework (revised proposal 2), ablate different exploration strategies (e.g., epsilon-greedy), and evaluate the robustness to suboptimal exploration strategies.
COST: 600000
PREDICTION: We expect that balancing exploration and exploitation will lead to consistent improvements over purely adaptive methods, by avoiding premature convergence and better leveraging the representational capacity of the model. However, the optimal balance may still be sensitive to the choice of exploration strategy.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Impact of View Variance on Contrastive Learning through Meta-Learning
PROPOSAL: We will use a meta-learning approach to investigate how view variance affects the efficacy of self-supervised contrastive learning. Specifically, we will train a meta-model on a set of tasks where the objective is to match different augmented views of the same instance. The meta-model will learn to adapt its weights to the specific task and augmentation strategy, evaluating its performance on a validation set. We will use the ImageNet dataset and evaluate our approach using the accuracy metric.
CONTROLS: We will compare against a baseline where the meta-model is trained using a fixed augmentation strategy and without using meta-learning.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach may outperform the baseline in certain scenarios, especially when the augmentation strategy is complex, due to its ability to adapt to the task. However, it may not always generalize well to new tasks or augmentation strategies, which could lead to poor performance.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing Mutual Information Maximation under Class-Balanced Data Distributions
PROPOSAL: We will investigate how class-balance affects mutual information maximization in self-supervised contrastive learning. We will derive a lower bound on the mutual information between two augmented views of the same instance, and analyze its behavior under class-balance disturbances. Additionally, we will experimentally evaluate the impact of instance imbalance on class-based contrastive learning objectives using the CIFAR-100 dataset and the cross-entropy metric.
CONTROLS: We will compare against a baseline where the mutual information is maximized using a fixed, normal distribution.
COST: 180 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Analytically, we anticipate that class-balance negatively impacts mutual information maximization; experimentally, we expect that our approach improves performance under imbalanced data distributions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Uncertainty-Based Adaptive Augmentation for Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: We will propose an adaptive augmentation strategy using uncertainty estimation from a Bayesian neural network to select informative augmentations for each instance. The algorithm will use a Gaussian process to model uncertainty and select augmentations with low variance, indicating potential informativeness. We will evaluate its performance on the INFANT dataset and use the accuracy and diversity metrics.
CONTROLS: We will compare against a baseline using static, human-engineered augmentations and a second baseline using random augmentations.
COST: 270 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our method may significantly outperform the baselines by selecting augmentations that better match the structure of the data. However, its computational cost could be high due to the additional inference required for uncertainty estimation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing Contrastive Learning under Limited Batch Sizes
PROPOSAL: We will theoretically and empirically investigate the impact of batch size on the convergence of contrastive loss functions, focusing on the spectral clustering and noise-contrastive estimation properties. We will derive bounds on the convergence rate under certain assumptions and test these findings using simulated data and the Joseph-Fu-FDA benchmark dataset.
CONTROLS: We will compare against a baseline where batch size is unlimited and use a range of batch sizes to analyze the trade-off between batch size and convergence rate.
COST: 800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our theoretical analysis may reveal novel insights into the batch size convergence trade-off, and empirical evaluations may show that batch size affects the speed of convergence, but not the stability of the representation.

TITLE: Dynamic View Sampling for Efficient Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: We will propose a dynamic sampling strategy where the model adaptive chooses the number and spread of views for each instance, rather than relying on a fixed batch size or static augmentation pipeline. We will use a statistical process control approach to determine the optimal number of views, and evaluate its effectiveness using a traditional computer vision dataset such as ImageNet.
CONTROLS: We will compare against a baseline where the number of views is fixed and a second baseline with a random sampling strategy.
COST: 900 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our dynamic sampling approach may improve the efficiency and effectiveness of contrastive learning by adaptively selecting the most informative views for each instance, but may require additional computational resources to implement.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A Leaked Information Perspective on Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: We will analyze the concept of leaked information during contrastive learning, where some information from the target view is inadvertently conveyed to the source view. We will derive bounds on the leaked information using a mutual information-based perspective, and evaluate the practical impact of this phenomenon using a focus on ImageNet.
CONTROLS: We will compare against a baseline where no leakage control is implemented, as well as a second baseline where we try to remove the leakage through view augmentation.
COST: 1500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Leaked information may have a significant impact on the performance of contrastive learning methods, even if the individual views are carefully crafted; we anticipate that accounting for this information may lead to improved performance under certain circumstances.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Controlling Semantic Collusion in Contrastive Learning through Safe Augmentation
PROPOSAL: We will address the challenge of semantic collusion during contrastive learning, where different views convey semantically similar information. We will propose a novel safe augmentation method that learns to identify and disentangle semantically related features, reducing the risk of collusion. We will evaluate its effectiveness using the CUB dataset and a combination of metrics.
CONTROLS: We will compare against a baseline where no collusion control is implemented, as well as a second baseline where we use traditional augmentation methods.
COST: 1600 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our safe augmentation approach may effectively control semantic collusion and improve the robustness and generalizability of contrastive learning methods, while also reducing the risk of catastrophic forgetting in the presence of distributional shifts.

PROPOSAL: We will address the challenge of semantic collusion during contrastive learning, where different views convey semantically similar information. We will propose a novel safe augmentation method that learns to identify and disentangle semantically related features, reducing the risk of collusion. We will evaluate its effectiveness using the CUB dataset and a combination of metrics.
CONTROLS: We will compare against a baseline where no collusion control is implemented, as well as a second baseline where we use traditional augmentation methods.
COST: 14400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our safe augmentation approach may effectively control semantic collusion and improve the robustness and generalizability of contrastive learning methods, while also reducing the risk of catastrophic forgetting in the presence of distributional shifts.

PROPOSAL: We will study the transferability and robustness of contrastive learning methods on unseen data distributions using a suite of benchmarks and distractors from various domains, including unseen domains, novel classes, and anomalies. COST: 1800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This work will provide deeper insights into the nature of contrastive learning under transfer and out-of-distribution scenarios, with our proposed methods possibly exhibiting strong generalization performance and enabling the development of more robust AI systems.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Impact of View Variance on Contrastive Learning through Meta-Learning
PROPOSAL: We will use a meta-learning approach to investigate how view variance affects the efficacy of self-supervised contrastive learning. Specifically, we will train a meta-model on a set of tasks where the objective is to match different augmented views of the same instance. The meta-model will learn to adapt its weights to the specific task and augmentation strategy, evaluating its performance on a validation set. We will use the ImageNet dataset and evaluate our approach using the accuracy metric.
CONTROLS: We will compare against a baseline where the meta-model is trained using a fixed augmentation strategy and without using meta-learning.
COST: 360 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach may outperform the baseline in certain scenarios, especially when the augmentation strategy is complex, due to its ability to adapt to the task. However, it may not always generalize well to new tasks or augmentation strategies, which could lead to poor performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing Mutual Information Maximation under Class-Balanced Data Distributions
PROPOSAL: We will investigate how class-balance affects mutual information maximization in self-supervised contrastive learning. We will derive a lower bound on the mutual information between two augmented views of the same instance, and analyze its behavior under class-balance disturbances. Additionally, we will experimentally evaluate the impact of instance imbalance on class-based contrastive learning objectives using the CIFAR-100 dataset and the cross-entropy metric.
CONTROLS: We will compare against a baseline where the mutual information is maximized using a fixed, normal distribution.
COST: 540 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Analytically, we anticipate that class-balance negatively impacts mutual information maximization; experimentally, we expect that our approach improves performance under imbalanced data distributions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Uncertainty-Based Adaptive Augmentation for Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: We will propose an adaptive augmentation strategy using uncertainty estimation from a Bayesian neural network to select informative augmentations for each instance. The algorithm will use a Gaussian process to model uncertainty and select augmentations with low variance, indicating potential informativeness. We will evaluate its performance on the INFANT dataset and use the accuracy and diversity metrics.
CONTROLS: We will compare against a baseline using static, human-engineered augmentations and a second baseline using random augmentations.
COST: 810 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our method may significantly outperform the baselines by selecting augmentations that better match the structure of the data. However, its computational cost could be high due to the additional inference required for uncertainty estimation.

ACTION: REVISE
NUMBER: 3
TITLE: REVISED Uncertainty-Based Adaptive Augmentation for Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: We will refine the adaptive augmentation strategy using a simple, data-driven principle: it selects augmentations based on their ability to reduce the KL-divergence between the input distribution and the augmentation distribution. This shift emphasizes empirical performance over Bayesian inference, and is easier to compute. We will use the same dataset and metrics as before.
CONTROLS: We will compare against the revised baseline and a second baseline using random augmentations, and evaluate the effect of this change on accuracy and compute time.
COST: unchanged: 810 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our revised method may achieve better accuracy and lower computational cost compared to the previous method, making it more feasible for real-world applications.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing Contrastive Learning under Limited Batch Sizes
PROPOSAL: We will theoretically and empirically investigate the impact of batch size on the convergence of contrastive loss functions, focusing on the spectral clustering and noise-contrastive estimation properties. We will derive bounds on the convergence rate under certain assumptions and test these findings using simulated data and the Joseph-Fu-FDA benchmark dataset.
CONTROLS: We will compare against a baseline where batch size is unlimited and use a range of batch sizes to analyze the trade-off between batch size and convergence rate.
COST: 2400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our theoretical analysis may reveal novel insights into the batch size convergence trade-off, and empirical evaluations may show that batch size affects the speed of convergence, but not the stability of the representation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Dynamic View Sampling for Efficient Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: We will propose a dynamic sampling strategy where the model adaptive chooses the number and spread of views for each instance, rather than relying on a fixed batch size or static augmentation pipeline. We will use a statistical process control approach to determine the optimal number of views, and evaluate its effectiveness using a traditional computer vision dataset such as ImageNet.
CONTROLS: We will compare against a baseline where the number of views is fixed and a second baseline with a random sampling strategy.
COST: 2700 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our dynamic sampling approach may improve the efficiency and effectiveness of contrastive learning by adaptively selecting the most informative views for each instance, but may require additional computational resources to implement.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A Leaked Information Perspective on Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: We will analyze the concept of leaked information during contrastive learning, where some information from the target view is inadvertently conveyed to the source view. We will derive bounds on the leaked information using a mutual information-based perspective, and evaluate the practical impact of this phenomenon using a focus on ImageNet.
CONTROLS: We will compare against a baseline where no leakage control is implemented, as well as a second baseline where we try to remove the leakage through view augmentation.
COST: 4500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Leaked information may have a significant impact on the performance of contrastive learning methods, even if the individual views are carefully crafted; we anticipate that accounting for this information may lead to improved performance under certain circumstances.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Information Gain through Multiple Views of an Instance
PROPOSAL: Investigate the relationship between the mutual information between multiple views of an instance and the semantic consistency of those views using self-supervised contrastive learning.
CONTROLS: Compare with a baseline where views are randomly shuffled and a contrastive loss is applied.
COST: 1345.678925
PREDICTION: We expect to show a positive correlation between mutual information and semantic consistency, and that surge in mutual information over the course of training can serve as an upper bound for the improvements in downstream tasks, although the contribution of each individual view may vary and some potentially redundant or noisy information might spoil the improvements that could be made if each view was informative and independent.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Expansion of Diversity through Resource-Efficient Sampling
PROPOSAL: Investigate the effectiveness of adaptive sampling schedules that direct the model to seek out more informative views in early stages of training and gradually increase batch size as representational capacity expands.
CONTROLS: Compare with a fixed batch size schedule and a randomly sampled batch schedule.
COST: 1500
PREDICTION: We expect adaptive sampling to reduce the need for large batches, accelerate convergence and improve generalization, with a risk that early exposure to very informative, possibly overly mode-regularizing views could mislead the model away from exploration and thus suffer from overfitting.
