ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Augmentation-Aware Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: Propose a new contrastive learning framework that incorporates the intrinsic information gain through augmentation techniques by integrating the outputs of a view-specific centrality metric into the loss function for balanced importance of input views, cross-validation to dissimilar unrelated data points.
CONTROLS: Examine sensitivity to view order, comparing results to a baseline with randomly shuffled views.
COST: 1600
PREDICTION: Augmentation-aware training is expected to adapt to varying augmentation spaces improving data representation quality and increasing resilience against overfitting, while challenging modifications through a stronger, rather than experiential application of partial, multiself-world contrast could propel performance but introduce ambiguities into the contextual choice of adjustment parameters.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Redundancy and Noise in Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: Analyze the redundancy between views in state-of-the-art contrastive learning models, specifically investigating the effect of redundant views on the learned representations and proposing a regularization term to minimize redundancy and maximize informativeness of views.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of models trained with and without the proposed regularization term on a set of downsampled or filtered views; demonstrate that the regularization term can help reduce overfitting when augmenting small datasets.
COST: 1736.28903
PREDICTION: This proposal is expected to provide insights into the role of redundancy in contrastive learning, leading to improved robustness and generalizability of representations; however, the parameter learned through the regularization term might be sensitive to specific settings of hyperparameters, such as the learning rate, batch-size and alpha.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing Representational Diversity through Multidimensional Embeddings
PROPOSAL: Develop a method to visualize and compare the representational diversity of contrastive learning models using multidimensional embeddings, allowing for a qualitative assessment of how effectively the models capture intra- and inter-class variations.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the performance of different visualization techniques (t-SNE, PCA, UMAP) and compare the representational diversity of models trained with and without the proposed augmentation-aware framework.

PREDICTION: We expect to gain insights into the relationships between contrastive learning objectives, data augmentation strategies, and distributed representations, and demonstrate the usefulness of multidimensional embeddings as a complementary evaluation tool to traditional performance metrics. TITLE: Theoretical Foundations for Dynamic Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: Derive and analyze a set of theoretical bounds for the convergence rates of dynamic contrastive learning algorithms, providing insights into the scaling behavior of these methods and their ability to adapt to changing data distributions.
CONTROLS: Compare the derived bounds with existing bounds for static contrastive learning methods, and explore the implications of these bounds for the design of dynamic contrastive learning algorithms.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Augmentation via Population-Conditional Distribution Matching
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel framework for generating adaptive augmentations that leverage population-conditional distribution matching (PCDM) to optimize view diversity while maintaining semantic coherence. Specifically, we train a small auxiliary network to estimate the conditional distribution of augmentations given an instance's features, and use this distribution to sample augmentations during training.
CONTROLS: We compare PCDM-based augmentations with standard SimCLR and state-of-the-art (MoCo v3, NIC) augmentation schemes on a range of datasets.
COST: 180
PREDICTION: We anticipate PCDM to outperform standard augmentation methods by 5-15% in terms of convergence rate and model expressiveness, but may struggle with limited dataset availability, where biased augmentation distributions could emerge.

TITLE: Adaptive Augmentation via Population-Conditional Distribution Matching

PROPOSAL: We develop a novel approach to attribute-specific contrastive learning, which learns to recover the underlying contrastive dimensions that correspond to specific attributes (e.g., shape, texture, color) of the input data. PREDICTION: Our approach should capture more nuanced and explicit attribute relationships within the representations, but could fail if the attribute axis is not well-represented in the training data or if overfitting occurs due to a small number of attributes.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Measuring Mutual Information with Information Bottleneck Wasserstein Distances
PROPOSAL: We leverage recent advances in information-theoretic statistical inference to propose a novel method for measuring mutual information between random variables, based on density estimation via the Wasserstein distance. We apply this approach to study the evolution of mutual information along contrastive learning.
CONTROLS: We compare our estimated mutual information with existing methods and analyze the convergence behaviors of contrastive learning objectives on various datasets (e.g., ImageNet, MNIST).
COST: 5400
PREDICTION: Our Wasserstein-distance-based mutual information estimator should more accurately capture the learning dynamics and information flow in contrastive learning, but may not provide sufficient reduction in estimation complexity or computing resources.

PROPOSAL: We propose a novel framework for contrastive learning that explicitly embeds augmentation-aware distributions into the feature space. This enables the model to capture the semantics of augmentations and learn robust features that generalize across different view settings.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Characterizing View Information for Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: We design and experiment with an augmented view selection (AVS) mechanism that dynamically selects the most informative views for each instance during training, using a model-agnostic, frequency-based measure of mutual information. We test AVS on SimCLR with different datasets (e.g., CIFAR10, ImageNet) and measure its impact on contrastive learning's information-gathering efficiency and convergence rate.
CONTROLS: Baseline is standard SimCLR with random view selection.
COST: 150
PREDICTION: We expect AVS to improve information-gathering efficiency and convergence rate by 10-20%, and could fail if the frequency-based mutual information approximation is overly simplistic for complex datasets.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Augmentation via Population-Conditional Distribution Matching
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel framework for generating adaptive augmentations that leverage population-conditional distribution matching (PCDM) to optimize view diversity while maintaining semantic coherence. Specifically, we train a small auxiliary network to estimate the conditional distribution of augmentations given an instance's features, and use this distribution to sample augmentations during training.
CONTROLS: We compare PCDM-based augmentations with standard SimCLR and state-of-the-art (MoCo v3, NIC) augmentation schemes on a range of datasets.
COST: 540
PREDICTION: We anticipate PCDM to outperform standard augmentation methods by 5-15% in terms of convergence rate and model expressiveness, but may struggle with limited dataset availability, where biased augmentation distributions could emerge.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Episodic and Online Test-Time Adaptation Evaluation via Replication of Baseline Results
PROPOSAL: 
We attempt to reproduce the baseline results of prominent epitopic TTA methods, specifically DITTA and BC by Li et al., under consistent experimental settings (pre-trained model, text prompts, evaluation protocols) on the widely-used CLEVR dataset and ImageNet benchmark. We evaluate their performance using standard classification metrics (accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score). This controlled replication will allow for fair comparisons between TTA methods.
CONTROLS: 
- Baselines: unadapted CLIP model, DITTA, BC
- Controls: varying pre-trained model checkpoints, text prompts
COST: 30
PREDICTION: Reproduced baseline results will reveal whether existing observations about TTA methods are robust to experimental conditions, with discrepancies pointing towards opportunities for improvement; gains of newer methods over earlier ones may be overestimated due to varying experimental settings.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Systematic Evaluation of Test-Time Adaptation Methods on Fine-Tuned VLMs
PROPOSAL: 
We extend the replication of baseline results ( Proposal 1) to fine-tuned VLMs with pre-trained CLIP models optimized for CLEVR and ImageNet classification tasks, and further include the broader range of VLM architectures beyond CLIP, such as DALL-E and Detectron. We examine whether test-time adaptation still provides improvements over the fine-tuned models and explore whether adaptation complements or conflicts with training-time fine-tuning. We also compare the robustness of adapted models to adversarial attacks and evaluate their performance on secondary tasks like segmentation.
CONTROLS: 
- Baselines: fine-tuned CLIP model, DALL-E, Detectron
- Controls: varying fine-tuning schedules, adaptation scenarios
COST: 150
PREDICTION: Fine-tuned models will exhibit improved classification performance, but test-time adaptation may offer limited benefits under specific conditions; adaptation will likely enhance robustness against adversarial attacks but pose challenges to secondary tasks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Episodic and Online Test-Time Adaptation Evaluation via Replication of Baseline Results
PROPOSAL: 
We attempt to reproduce the baseline results of prominent epitopic TTA methods, specifically DITTA and BC by Li et al., under consistent experimental settings (pre-trained model, text prompts, evaluation protocols) on the widely-used CLEVR dataset and ImageNet benchmark. We evaluate their performance using standard classification metrics (accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score). This controlled replication will allow for fair comparisons between TTA methods.
CONTROLS: 
- Baselines: unadapted CLIP model, DITTA, BC
- Controls: varying pre-trained model checkpoints, text prompts

PREDICTION: Reproduced baseline results will reveal whether existing observations about TTA methods are robust to experimental conditions, with discrepancies pointing towards opportunities for improvement; gains of newer methods over earlier ones may be overestimated due to varying experimental settings.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Consistent Evaluation of Episodic Test-Time Adaptation Methods
PROPOSAL: Compare five state-of-the-art episodic TTA methods for VLMs on the ImageNet validation set using a consistent experimental setup and pre-trained CLIP checkpoint. Evaluate them under three different text prompts ('Default', 'Visual', and 'Textual') to assess their sensitivity. Additionally, compare their performance to a simple baseline where the model is frozen and only the classification layer is updated.
CONTROLS: Freeze-only baseline on ImageNet with CLIP pre-trained on ImageNet, ablating each TTA component on a held-out subset of ImageNet
COST: 6000
PREDICTION: Expected to see moderate gains (~1-2% top-1 accuracy) of the best episodic TTA method over the freeze-only baseline, with some degree of reduction in performance when text prompts change. However, TTA methods may fail to generalize across different architectural choices, limiting the applicability of this study.

TITLE: Online Test-Time Adaptation For Out-Of-Distribution Images
PROPOSAL: Develop an online TTA method for VLMs that leverages a specialized memory structure to store activations from a stream of test images. When encountering out-of-distribution (OOD) images, the method retrieves similar activations from memory to adapt the model in a data-efficient manner. Evaluate this method on responsively labeled datasets (e.g., ImageNet-V2 and DomainNet) and other benchmark OOD datasets.
CONTROLS: Adversariably trained CLIP baseline, ablating memory capacity and training procedure

PREDICTION: This method shows improved accuracy (~3-5% top-1 accuracy) on OOD images when compared to baselines and episodic TTA methods. Its potential to fail lies in its sensitivity to hyperparameters such as memory capacity and adaptation frequency.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Consistent Evaluation of Episodic Test-Time Adaptation Methods
PROPOSAL: Compare five state-of-the-art episodic TTA methods for VLMs on the ImageNet validation set using a consistent experimental setup and pre-trained CLIP checkpoint. Evaluate them under three different text prompts ('Default', 'Visual', and 'Textual') to assess their sensitivity. Additionally, compare their performance to a simple baseline where the model is frozen and only the classification layer is updated.
CONTROLS: Freeze-only baseline on ImageNet with CLIP pre-trained on ImageNet, ablating each TTA component on a held-out subset of ImageNet
COST: 18000
PREDICTION: Expected to see moderate gains (~1-2% top-1 accuracy) of the best episodic TTA method over the freeze-only baseline, with some degree of reduction in performance when text prompts change. However, TTA methods may fail to generalize across different architectural choices, limiting the applicability of this study.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Online Test-Time Adaptation For Out-Of-Distribution Images
PROPOSAL: Develop an online TTA method for VLMs that leverages a specialized memory structure to store activations from a stream of test images. When encountering out-of-distribution (OOD) images, the method retrieves similar activations from memory to adapt the model in a data-efficient manner. Evaluate this method on responsively labeled datasets (e.g., ImageNet-V2 and DomainNet) and other benchmark OOD datasets.
CONTROLS: Adversariably trained CLIP baseline, ablating memory capacity and training procedure
COST: 30000
PREDICTION: This method shows improved accuracy (~3-5% top-1 accuracy) on OOD images when compared to baselines and episodic TTA methods. Its potential to fail lies in its sensitivity to hyperparameters such as memory capacity and adaptation frequency.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Systematic Evaluation of Episodic and Online Test-Time Adaptation for Vision-Language Models
PROPOSAL: We will conduct a controlled and systematic evaluation of existing episodic and online TTA methods for VLMs on the real-world AVA V2+EVA-Lab image-text retrieval benchmark, using the CLIP-ViT-B-32 model as the baseline. We will compare the performance of five episodic and three online TTA methods under identical experimental settings, and measure their gains in terms of accuracy, mean normalized discounted cumulative gain (MDCG), and mean over all relevant videos (MAV) metrics. We will also benchmark the performance of these methods on out-of-distribution (OOD) data from the COCO image-text retrieval and the Yelp Fusion text-image retrieval benchmarks.
CONTROLS: The baseline will be the CLIP-ViT-B-32 model without any test-time adaptation, and we will also compare our results to the original work of each TTA method to ensure direct and fair comparison.
COST: 170
PREDICTION: We expect to achieve significant gains over the baseline model for episodic and online TTA methods, with the best performing methods improving the accuracy by at least 5% and MDCG, MAV by at least 10% and 15% respectively. However, some methods might fail on OOD data or struggle with small-scale test sets.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Reproducibility of Episodic Test-Time Adaptation for VLMs
PROPOSAL: We will reproduce and extend the episodic test-time adaptation methods on CLIP with a consistent experimental setup, using a MCMC inference strategy to obtain an ensemble of adapted models. We will compare the performance of these adapted models to the original CLIP model on several image classification benchmarks and investigate the dependence on different architectures, pre-training checkpoints, and evaluation protocols.
CONTROLS: We will use the following baselines: (1) original CLIP model, (2) CLIP fine-tuned with text prompts, (3) CLIP adapted using other episodic TTA methods. We will also experiment with ablating the MCMC inference strategy and investigating the effect of different architectures, pre-training checkpoints, and evaluation protocols.
COST: 3600
PREDICTION: We expect to see a consistent improvement in accuracy for the adapted models over the original CLIP model, but the absolute improvement may be small due to the robustness of the pre-trained CLIP model. Failure may arise if the MCMC inference strategy is not efficient, or if the adapted models are overly specialized to the test set.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Systematic Investigation of Online Test-Time Adaptation for VLMs
PROPOSAL: We will systematically evaluate online test-time adaptation methods for VLMs on a range of image and video classification benchmarks, focusing on the trade-off between adaptation accuracy and robustness. We will investigate the effect of different online adaptation mechanisms, such as gradient update and distribution shift regularizers, on the model's robustness and adaptation quality.
CONTROLS: We will compare the online TTA methods to the original pre-trained VLM and to episodic TTA methods. We will also experiment with ablating the online adaptation mechanisms and investigating the effect of different model architectures, hyperparameters, and evaluation protocols.
COST: 5400
PREDICTION: We expect to see an improvement in adaptation accuracy and a degradation in robustness for the online TTA methods compared to the episodic TTA methods, but the degree of improvement and degradation may depend on the specific benchmarks and adaptation mechanisms used. Failure may arise if the online adaptation mechanisms are not effective or if the model's robustness is compromised too much.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient Discrete Video Tokenizer via Multi-Resolution Image Tokenizer Transfer
PROPOSAL: Investigate pruning Image GPT (IGPT) from larger image synthesis models (e.g. Variance-Gamma Codebook), and then fuse it into discrete video tokenizers, comparing low-frequency image glyphs' transfer against direct video tokenizer training. To evaluate the effectiveness of IGPT pruning, compare the former against each of the following three baselines: (1) full image tokenizer initialization, (2) uniform random initialization, and (3) in-domain video tokenizer training.
CONTROLS: IGPT pruning comparison, optimally-tuned full image tokenizer with downstream video tasks, this and the above baselines on 480p/720p YouTube-8M, LIP, and UCF-101.
COST: 20800
PREDICTION: While direct video tokenizer training delivers highest video fidelity, pruning and transferring an IGPT should show competitive performance with one-fifth of the costs and training times of direct video tokenizer training, albeit with degraded video quality and/or smaller tensor sizes.

CONTROLS: Standard diffusion models, pure autoregressive models, and their weighted combinations without additional sophisticated

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient Dynamic Contextual Encoding for Long-Term Temporal Consistency in Discrete Video Generation
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of dynamic contextual encoding techniques to efficiently capture and maintain long-term temporal consistency in discrete video generation models. This approach aims to reduce the computational requirements and memory usage associated with maintaining large contextual histories, while preserving the model's ability to generate coherent and temporally consistent video sequences. We will evaluate this approach by comparing it to the state-of-the-art models in video generation tasks such as text-to-video generation, image-to-video generation, and video extrapolation.
CONTROLS: Baseline models without dynamic contextual encoding, fixed-size contextual encoding, and caching-based contextual encoding.
COST: 150000
PREDICTION: The proposed dynamic contextual encoding approach is expected to improve the efficiency and temporal consistency of discrete video generation models, while maintaining or improving their visual quality and generative capabilities.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Learning to Inpaint and Recover Missing Frames for Video Generation
PROPOSAL: Develop a new approach that leverages the strengths of video inpainting and frame recovery to improve the robustness and flexibility of discrete video generation models. This approach will involve learning to inpaint missing frames in the input video sequence, and recovering missing frames during the generation process. We will evaluate this approach by comparing it to the state-of-the-art models in video generation tasks such as text-to-video generation, image-to-video generation, and video extrapolation.
CONTROLS: Baseline models without inpainting and frame recovery, models with inpainting but not frame recovery, and models with frame recovery but not inpainting.
COST: 400000
PREDICTION: The proposed inpainting and frame recovery approach is expected to significantly improve the robustness and flexibility of discrete video generation models, making them more suitable for real-world applications with missing or corrupted input data.

PROPOSAL: Implement an autoregressive model (e.g., Implicit Video Navigator) in conjunction with Entropic Graph Neural Networks (EGNNs) to capture the temporal evolution of video data. TITLE: Attention-Guided Relational Modeling for Temporal Tokenization
PROPOSAL: We propose to develop an attention-guided relational modeling (AGR) for temporal tokenization, which leverages both spatial and temporal dependencies to capture coherent motion in videos. The model will incorporate a graph attention mechanism to explore the relationships between tokens within a video sequence and assign weights to edges based on features learned from a graph neural network. This approach aims to improve the quality of generated videos by focusing on the spatial and temporal relationships within the temporal token sequence. We will evaluate the performance of this model on text-to-video synthesis tasks.
CONTROLS: AGR model with random attention mechanism and without graph attention mechanism
COST: 1584
PREDICTION: AGR model will demonstrate significant improvements over traditional temporal tokenization methods, but may require large-scale training data to accurately capture complex temporal relationships in videos.

TITLE: Long-Term Context-Aware Discrete Video Generation with Hierarchical Self-Attention
PROPOSAL: We propose a hierarchical self-attention mechanism to dynamically manage long-term context for discrete video generation. The model consists of a coarse-grained self-attention module, which captures global context, and a fine-grained self-attention module, which explores specific details. By iteratively refining the context representation, the model learns to balance the need for both long-term consistency and fine-grained details. This approach aims to improve the generation of long videos with coherent motion.

COST: 2158.75
PREDICTION: The proposed model will achieve state-of-the-art results on text-to-video synthesis tasks, particularly for long videos, but may require careful tuning of hyperparameters for optimal performance.

TITLE: Query-Based Video Editing and Manipulation using Discrete Video Synthesis
PROPOSAL: We propose a query-based video editing and manipulation framework that uses discrete video synthesis to modify and edit existing videos. The model takes a query video and a target video as input, and generates a new video that is a transformation of the target video based on the query video. We also investigate the use of attention-based mechanisms to focus on specific regions of the target video and apply the transformations accordingly. This approach aims to enable fast and efficient video editing and manipulation.

TITLE: Interactive coarse-to-fine Discrete Video Synthesis using Generative Decision Trees
PROPOSAL: We propose an interactive coarse-to-fine discrete video synthesis framework that uses generative decision trees to enable efficient and flexible video generation. The model generates videos in a coarse-to-fine manner, with each decision tree node representing a specific level of detail. The user can interact with the model by making decisions at each node, effectively guiding the video generation process. We also investigate the use of uncertainty estimation to handle ambiguous user inputs. This approach aims to enable fast and flexible video generation, as well as enabling users to control the generation process.

PREDICTION: The proposed model will achieve state-of-the-art results on interactive video generation tasks, particularly for complex query videos, but may require careful tuning of hyperparameters for optimal performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Unified Video Generation via Multi-Scale Discrete Autoregressive Modeling
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel discrete autoregressive architecture, called UVAL (Unified Visual Autoregressive Learner), which approaches high-resolution video generation through multi-scale next-token prediction, learning diffusions at different spatial and temporal scales. We extend VAR's next-scale prediction framework to videos by incorporating pyramid-like hierarchical representations of the spatiotemporal context and introduce a self-modulating mechanism to dynamically adjust the context size. For video text-to-image synthesis, UVAL incorporates a text encoder, while for into-video generation, we learn a glimpse-based multi-frame attentions.
CONTROLS: VQ-GAN++, realizing discrete image tokenizers and demonstrating their unsuitability for video; Emu3, to show the scalability and attention required in autoregressive video prediction.
COST: 1600
PREDICTION: UVAL outperforms Emu3 on 720p text-to-video generation with lower inference latency, but may struggle with coherent motion and face hallucination in long videos with many interactions.

TITLE: Efficient Pretraining for Discrete Video Tokenizers
PROPOSAL: To overcome the computational bottleneck of training discrete video tokenizers from scratch, we introduce VidVAE (Video Variational Autoencoder), a pretraining framework that leverages a probabilistic latent space to guide tokenizer learning, promoting efficient and fast convergence on video tokens. VidVAE consists of a spatiotemporal encoder, a probabilistic tokenizer module, and a video reconstruction head. By pretraining the tokenizer on a large, diverse video dataset, we enable downstream models to focus on the challenging task of video-to-video synthesis.
CONTROLS: UVAL-1 (without VidVAE pretraining), demonstrating time-consuming training; supervised learning for tokenizers to show its relative inefficiency in preserving reconstruction features and temporal consistency.
COST: 12825
PREDICTION: VidVAE's pretraining significantly reduces tokenizer training time to 1/3 of baseline, potentially weakening overall performance and requiring reoptimization of VidVAE parameters to post-integrate with UVAL, specifically risk-stabilization training by pre-training VidVAE withśnie cyclic arg loss, stagging weight and hyper parameter reset.

PROPOSAL: To further improve the efficiency and quality of video generation, we propose an adaptive progressive framework, APVG, which leverages the strengths of UASNET (from Proposal 5) and UVAL (from Proposal 1) in a hierarchical manner. APVG first generates a low-resolution video outline using UASNET, and then refines it in a progressive manner using multiple iterations of UVAL, progressively increasing the resolution and detail of the generated video.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Accelerating APVG with Task-Aware Quantization and Knowledge Distillation
PROPOSAL: To accelerate the inference of APVG (Adaptive Progressive Video Generation) and its UASNET components, we propose TAQKD (Task-Aware Quantization and Knowledge Distillation), a novel method that applies task-aware quantization to the shared encoder and decoder of UASNET, and fine-tunes a student model using knowledge distillation from the teacher model. This approach reduces the computational cost of APVG while maintaining its high-quality output.
CONTROLS: Baseline APVG without TAQKD, to evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed acceleration method, and ablation studies on individual components of TAQKD.
COST: 115200
PREDICTION: TAQKD achieves a significant reduction in inference time (up to 70%) and opens up new applications of APVG in real-time video generation, facial animation, and more, but may require careful hyperparameter tuning to achieve optimal trade-offs between speed and accuracy.

TITLE: Unified Video Generation via Multi-Scale Discrete Autoregressive Modeling
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel discrete autoregressive architecture, called UVAL (Unified Visual Autoregressive Learner), which approaches high-resolution video generation through multi-scale next-token prediction, learning diffusions at different spatial and temporal scales. We extend VAR's next-scale prediction framework to videos by incorporating pyramid-like hierarchical representations of the spatiotemporal context and introduce a self-modulating mechanism to dynamically adjust the context size. For video text-to-image synthesis, UVAL incorporates a text encoder, while for into-video generation, we learn a glimpse-based multi-frame attentions.
CONTROLS: VQ-GAN++, realizing discrete image tokenizers and demonstrating their unsuitability for video; Emu3, to show the scalability and attention required in autoregressive video prediction.
COST: 4800.00
PREDICTION: UVAL outperforms Emu3 on 720p text-to-video generation with lower inference latency, but may struggle with coherent motion and face hallucination in long videos with many interactions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient Pretraining for Discrete Video Tokenizers
PROPOSAL: To overcome the computational bottleneck of training discrete video tokenizers from scratch, we introduce VidVAE (Video Variational Autoencoder), a pretraining framework that leverages a probabilistic latent space to guide tokenizer learning, promoting efficient and fast convergence on video tokens. VidVAE consists of a spatiotemporal encoder, a probabilistic tokenizer module, and a video reconstruction head. By pretraining the tokenizer on a large, diverse video dataset, we enable downstream models to focus on the challenging task of video-to-video synthesis.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient Discrete Video Tokenizers via Multi-Task Learning
PROPOSAL: We explore a novel multi-task learning approach to train discrete video tokenizers. The model is trained on both video reconstruction and keyframe extraction tasks to leverage the strengths of both paradigms. Specifically, we use a dual-head architecture to jointly predict video frames and keyframes. Our hope is that this multi-task learning setup will lead to a more robust and accurate discrete video tokenizer.
CONTROLS: We will compare our proposed approach with tokenizers trained on either task in isolation (e.g. only video reconstruction) and with pre-trained image tokenizers (as a baseline for discrete video tokenizers).
COST: 1440
PREDICTION: Our multi-task learning approach will achieve state-of-the-art performance on video reconstruction and outperform pre-trained image tokenizers. However, it may be sensitive to hyperparameters and require careful tuning.

TITLE: Temporal Modeling for Video Generation using Adaptive Attention Interpolation
PROPOSAL: We propose an adaptive attention interpolation mechanism for temporal modeling in our discrete video generator. The model will dynamically adjust the attention weights over time to focus on relevant parts of the context sequence. This allows the model to adapt to the pace of the input sequence and better handle long-range temporal dependencies.
CONTROLS: We will compare the adaptive attention interpolation with a fixed attention mechanism and with baseline methods that use a fixed-size context window.

TITLE: Hierarchical Discrete Video Modeling for Efficient Long-Term Video Generation
PROPOSAL: We introduce a hierarchical discrete video modeling framework that breaks down the video generation process into a sequence of smaller sub-tasks. Each sub-task will be represented as a separate autoregressive model, which can be learned and evaluated independently. This hierarchical structure will enable efficient long-term video generation by allowing the model to focus on a specific subset of the video at a time.
CONTROLS: We will compare our hierarchical approach with a single-tier autoregressive model and with diffusion-based video generation methods.
COST: 4320
PREDICTION: Our hierarchical framework will achieve state-of-the-art results for long-term video generation while significantly reducing inference latency. However, it may struggle with tasks that require complex temporal relationships between frames.

TITLE: Uncovering Properties of Gradient-Based Training for Out-of-Context Reasoning
PROPOSAL: We will use a theoretically grounded analysis to investigate the properties of transformer models that enable them to infer implications for unseen subjects. Assuming a SystemZ-like training regime with Masked Language Modeling (MLM), we will derive a set of mathematical bounds that describe how the model updates its weights according to the gradient flow during training. We will then analyze how these bounds relate to the model's ability to perform out-of-context reasoning.
CONTROLS: We will compare our bounds with two baselines: the "Random Initialization" baseline, where the model is initialized with random weights, and the "No Training" baseline, where the model is not updated during training.
COST: 500
PREDICTION: We expect to find that the matrix structure of the transformer weights, particularly the self-attention matrices, play a crucial role in enabling the model to perform out-of-context reasoning. However, we may also observe that the model's ability to generalize is sensitive to the specific training dynamics, and that in certain cases, the model may not be able to infer implications even when the training regime is carefully designed.

TITLE: Analyzing the Effect of Knowledge Graph Structure on Out-of-Context Reasoning
PROPOSAL: We will experimentally investigate how the structure of the knowledge graph, in terms of the relationships between entities, affects the model's ability to perform out-of-context reasoning. We will use a synthetic dataset with varying levels of graph complexity, and fine-tune a pre-trained LLM on each dataset to observe how the model's performance changes. Specifically, we will analyze the impact of singleton entities (entities that appear only once in the graph), mereological relationships (relationships between entities that imply spatial or partonomic relationships), and relationship hierarchies on out-of-context reasoning.
CONTROLS: We will compare our results with two baselines: the "Random KGE" baseline, where the knowledge graph embeddings are randomly initialized, and the "NoFineTuning" baseline, where the model is not fine-tuned on the knowledge graph.

PREDICTION: We expect to find that models perform better on out-of-context reasoning tasks when the knowledge graph structure is well-defined and hierarchical, but may struggle when the graph is highly disconnected or with singleton entities. However, we may also observe that the model's performance is highly sensitive to the specific fine-tuning procedure and dataset.

TITLE: Empirical Study of Ripple Effects in Out-of-Context Reasoning
PROPOSAL: We will experimentally investigate the phenomenon of ripple effects in out-of-context reasoning, where the model's ability to associate two events is affected by the presence of other entities in the training data. We will use the HOPE dataset, which contains events with multiple subjects and relations, and fine-tune a range of pre-trained LLMs on the dataset. We will then evaluate the model's performance on tasks that require out-of-context reasoning, such as inferring the implications of a given fact. Specifically, we will analyze how the model's performance changes when the training set includes multiple subjects, and how the introduction of new entities affects the model's ability to generalize.
CONTROLS: We will compare our results with two baselines: the "Single Event" baseline, where the model is trained on single-event datasets, and the "No Ripple" baseline, where the model is trained without any ripple effects (i.e., without any entities that appear in multiple events).
COST: 3322
PREDICTION: We expect to find that the model's performance is highly sensitive to the presence of ripple effects, and that the model is more likely to exhibit over- or under-association in tasks that require out-of-context reasoning. However, we may also observe that certain models are more robust to ripple effects due to their knowledge graph architectures.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Role of Induction Heads in Out-of-Context Reasoning
PROPOSAL: We will conduct a theoretical analysis of the role of induction heads in out-of-context reasoning. Specifically, we will examine how induction heads contribute to the model's ability to infer implications from learned facts, and how they interact with other components of the transformer model to enable out-of-context reasoning. We will use a combination of mathematical analysis and qualitative probing to understand the functional role of induction heads in enabling the model to reason across different events and entities.
CONTROLS: We will compare our results with two theoretical baselines: the "No Induction" baseline, where the model does not have induction heads, and the "All Induction" baseline, where the model has multiple induction heads that are fully connected.
COST: 2692
PREDICTION: We expect to find that induction heads play a crucial role in enabling the model to reason across different events and entities, but that their effect is highly dependent on the specific architecture of the model and the characteristics of the training data. However, we may also observe that induction heads can sometimes lead to over-association or inaccurate generalization if not properly calibrated.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Robustness of Out-of-Context Reasoning to Adversarial Attacks
PROPOSAL: We will conduct an empirical study to evaluate the robustness of out-of-context reasoning to adversarial attacks, where we intentionally introduce errors or misleading information into the training data to test the model's ability to reason correctly. We will use a range of adversarial attacks, including noise injection, data poisoning, and adversarial examples, and evaluate the model's performance on tasks that require out-of-context reasoning. We will also analyze the robustness of different models to different types of attacks and identify potential vulnerabilities in the models.
CONTROLS: We will compare our results with two theoretical baselines: the "Perfect Model" baseline, where the model is assumed to be perfectly robust to all attacks, and the "Adversarially Trained" baseline, where the model is trained on adversarial examples.
COST: 6000
PREDICTION: We expect to find that the model's performance is highly vulnerable to adversarial attacks, particularly those that target the model's understanding of relationships and entities. However, we may also observe that certain models are more robust to certain types of attacks due to their architecture or training procedure.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Uncovering Properties of Gradient-Based Training for Out-of-Context Reasoning
PROPOSAL: We will use a theoretically grounded analysis to investigate the properties of transformer models that enable them to infer implications for unseen subjects. Assuming a SystemZ-like training regime with Masked Language Modeling (MLM), we will derive a set of mathematical bounds that describe how the model updates its weights according to the gradient flow during training. We will then analyze how these bounds relate to the model's ability to perform out-of-context reasoning.
CONTROLS: We will compare our bounds with two baselines: the "Random Initialization" baseline, where the model is initialized with random weights, and the "No Training" baseline, where the model is not updated during training.
COST: 1500
PREDICTION: We expect to find that the matrix structure of the transformer weights, particularly the self-attention matrices, play a crucial role in enabling the model to perform out-of-context reasoning. However, we may also observe that the model's ability to generalize is sensitive to the specific training dynamics, and that in certain cases, the model may not be able to infer implications even when the training regime is carefully designed.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing the Effect of Knowledge Graph Structure on Out-of-Context Reasoning
PROPOSAL: We will experimentally investigate how the structure of the knowledge graph, in terms of the relationships between entities, affects the model's ability to perform out-of-context reasoning. We will use a synthetic dataset with varying levels of graph complexity, and fine-tune a pre-trained LLM on each dataset to observe how the model's performance changes. Specifically, we will analyze the impact of singleton entities (entities that appear only once in the graph), mereological relationships (relationships between entities that imply spatial or partonomic relationships), and relationship hierarchies on out-of-context reasoning.
CONTROLS: We will compare our results with two baselines: the "Random KGE" baseline, where the knowledge graph embeddings are randomly initialized, and the "NoFineTuning" baseline, where the model is not fine-tuned on the knowledge graph.
COST: 5000
PREDICTION: We expect to find that models perform better on out-of-context reasoning tasks when the knowledge graph structure is well-defined and hierarchical, but may struggle when the graph is highly disconnected or with singleton entities. However, we may also observe that the model's performance is highly sensitive to the specific fine-tuning procedure and dataset.

However, we may also observe that the added number of parameters in Hotpot fades under a snag that competes against paradigm walkthroughs.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Probing the Generalization Capability of Large Language Models
PROPOSAL: Investigate the relationship between the capacity of an LLM to deduce implications from learned facts and its architecture, specifically by manipulating the layer-wise attention patterns and weights of a BERT-like model. Empirically analyze the downstream performance on a standardized set of test-time implication-deduction tasks, controlled for the type and scope of the implications.
CONTROLS: Test the performance of the model on a held-out test set of implication-deduction tasks without injected knowledge, compared to a baseline model which has undergone standard fine-tuning.
COST: 10
PREDICTION: I anticipate that modifying the layer-wise attention patterns of the model will result in improved performance on some subsets of implication-deduction tasks, but show little overall improvement or may actually decrease performance when the implications require a combination of facts at multiple hops in the knowledge graph, potentially due to reduced model capacity or effects such as the exposure problem.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Empirical Evaluation of Ripple Effects in Open-Domain Question Answering
PROPOSAL: Investigate the capability of LLMs in inferring facts not explicitly stated in the input but implied by the context. Employ a dataset specifically designed for measuring ripple effects, and assess the model's ability to recognize relationships between entities, relationships, and events. Evaluate the performance on a battery of standardized tests designed to elicit open-domain question answering behaviors concerning implication detection and inferential reasoning.
CONTROLS: Compare the results to human performance on the same set of tasks and evaluate different models' abilities to exploit information from the context.
COST: 50
PREDICTION: I anticipate that the results will reveal significant variations in the ability of LLMs to engage in ripple effects across different models, and that even high-performing models will struggle to accurately identify distant implications in complex contexts, possibly due to squashing of long-range dependencies in self-attentive architectures.

TITLE: A Synthetic Dataset for Investigating Out-of-Context Reasoning and Hallucinations in LLMs
PROPOSAL: Develop a synthetic dataset of triples (s, r, a) with their implications for LLM fine-tuning, where some subjects are only present in the fact and others are also present in their implication. For example, the dataset could include the combinations {(Alice, lives in, Paris), (Alice, speaks, French)}, {(Bob, lives in, New York), (Bob, speaks, English)}, {(Alice, lives in, Paris), (Alice, speaks, Italian)}, and so on. The goal is to generate a large amount of data that mirrors real-world scenarios but with complete control over the underlying facts and implications.
CONTROLS: Compare to baseline models fine-tuned on random combinations of triples with no implications, and provide a benchmark for evaluating generalization.
COST: 6000
PREDICTION: The synthetic dataset will allow for a more systematic investigation of out-of-context reasoning and hallucinations in LLMs and should reveal a nuanced relationship between these phenomena and the complexity of the fact-implication chains. It might fail if the generated data underrepresent the variety of real-world knowledge graphs.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Fine-Grained Calibrated Analysis of the Frequency Domain for DFF
PROPOSAL: We revise the original Proposal 3, introducing a novel energy-based frequency analysis framework to better understand how different frequency components contribute to the modeling of DFF. This framework leverages a novel energy decomposition method to identify and isolate the essential frequency components in the focal stack. By incorporating this framework into our analysis, we can gain a deeper understanding of how frequency components impact DFF performance and potentially improve model robustness.
CONTROLS: To validate the effectiveness of our new analysis framework, we will compare its performance to the original frequency analysis and also evaluate its ability to improve model performance on challenging DFF scenarios
COST: 270000
PREDICTION: Energy-based framework significantly improves frequency analysis' interpretability, enabling better insight into DFF's frequency characteristics; better frequency modeling likely to improve model robustness and performance on challenging scenarios.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: Uncertainty-Aware Focus Estimation for Depth-from-Focus Models
PROPOSAL: We propose to develop an uncertainty-aware focus estimation module for DFF models, which can provide a direct measure of the uncertainty associated with focus estimation. This module will be integrated with existing DFF models to enhance their robustness to noise, ambiguity, and variations in focus features. We will evaluate the performance of our uncertainty-aware DFF model on various real-world datasets.
CONTROLS: To validate the benefits of our uncertainty-aware focus estimation module, we will compare its performance to that of the original DFF model and also evaluate its ability to improve model robustness in challenging scenarios
COST: 312000
PREDICTION: Uncertainty-aware focus estimation significantly improves model robustness and accuracy on real-world datasets; benefits of uncertainty-aware approach will be most evident in challenging scenarios with high focus ambiguity or noise.

TITLE: Learning to Simulate Defocus for Depth Estimation
PROPOSAL: We will train a generative adversarial network to simulate focal stacks from a single image, using a dataset of real-world images with ground-truth depth and synthetic focal stacks. This simulated data will then be used to train a depth estimation network that learns to predict depth directly from the simulated focal stacks. In contrast to direct depth estimation from a single image, this approach incorporates the physical principles of focus and focal stacks, potentially leading to more accurate and robust depth estimation.
CONTROLS: We will compare our method against baseline depth estimation methods that simply infer depth from a single image, as well as a method that uses a similar architecture but is trained on real-world focal stacks rather than simulated ones.
COST: 3600
PREDICTION: We expect our method to outperform baseline methods in terms of accuracy, especially in low-texture regions and at abrupt depth changes, while also being more robust to misleading focus cues. However, we may see a degradation in performance in scenes with high-frequency textures or transparent objects, where the simulated focal stacks may not accurately capture the physical principles of depth-of-field.

PROPOSAL: We will investigate the use of a novel gradient transform that combines information from multiple focal planes to improve depth estimation. This transform, which we call the Focal-Stack Gradient Transform (FSGT), is designed to amplify the contrast between true depth edges and texture-induced gradients, while also reducing the variability of focus cues across the focal stack. We will evaluate the FSGT in conjunction with a variety of depth estimation models, including our previously-proposed simulated defocus network.
CONTROLS: We will compare our method against baseline depth estimation methods that use traditional gradient operators, as well as against our simulated defocus network without the FSGT.

PREDICTION: We expect our method to improve the accuracy and robustness of depth estimation, especially in scenes with high-frequency textures or transparent objects, where traditional gradient operators may struggle to distinguish between true depth edges and texture-induced gradients. However, we may see a decrease in performance in scenes with low-texture regions, where the FSGT may not effectively amplify the contrast between true depth edges and texture-induced gradients.

TITLE: Scene-Aware Metropolis-Hastings Algorithm for Focal Stack Inference
PROPOSAL: Develop a scene-aware Metropolis-Hastings algorithm to jointly optimize the focal stack and depth map inference, taking into account the spatial and focal consistency of the input image. This model will utilize a customized hierarchical prior that enforces focus consistency across adjacent pixels and focal planes, leading to improved depth estimation results. Evaluation will be performed on the NYU Depth V2 dataset and a subset of real-world focal stacks.
CONTROLS: Compare to the traditional physics-informed model and Metropolis-Hastings algorithm without scene-aware prior, on the aforementioned datasets.

PREDICTION: Notable improvement in depth estimation accuracy, especially in scenes with complex and sparse depth structures; potential limitations in scenes with fine textures or abrupt depth changes due to the computational complexity of the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm.

PROPOSAL: Develop a scene-aware Metropolis-Hastings algorithm to jointly optimize the focal stack and depth map inference, taking into account the spatial and focal consistency of the input image. This model will utilize a customized hierarchical prior that enforces focus consistency across adjacent pixels and focal planes, leading to improved depth estimation results. Evaluation will be performed on the NYU Depth V2 dataset and a subset of real-world focal stacks.
CONTROLS: Compare to the traditional physics-informed model and Metropolis-Hastings algorithm without scene-aware prior, on the aforementioned datasets.
COST: 6000
PREDICTION: Notable improvement in depth estimation accuracy, especially in scenes with complex and sparse depth structures; potential limitations in scenes with fine textures or abrupt depth changes due to the computational complexity of the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: Adversarial Defense for Focal Stack Depth Estimation against Adversarial Attacks
PROPOSAL: Develop a robust focal stack depth estimation framework that incorporates an adversarial defense mechanism to counter adversarial attacks, which can significantly degrade the performance of focal stack-based depth estimation models. This model will utilize a discriminator network to detect and mitigate the effects of adversarial attacks, ensuring the robustness and reliability of the depth estimation results. Evaluation will be performed on the NYU Depth V2 dataset and a subset of real-world focal stacks.
CONTROLS: Compare to the traditional physics-informed model and baseline models without adversarial defense, on the aforementioned datasets.
COST: 7500
PREDICTION: Notable improvement in adversarial robustness, with a significant reduction in the impact of adversarial attacks on focal stack depth estimation; potential trade-off with model accuracy in benign scenarios due to the added complexity of the adversarial defense mechanism.

ACTION: ADD 7
TITLE: Uncertainty Quantification for Focal Stack Depth Estimation using Ensemble Methods
PROPOSAL: Develop a focal stack depth estimation framework that incorporates uncertainty quantification using ensemble methods to provide a measure of confidence in the estimated depth map. This model will utilize multiple instantiations of the physics-informed model, trained on different subsets of the focal stack data, to estimate both the depth map and its associated uncertainty. Evaluation will be performed on the NYU Depth V2 dataset and a subset of real-world focal stacks.
CONTROLS: Compare to the traditional physics-informed model and baseline models without uncertainty quantification, on the aforementioned datasets.
COST: 9000
PREDICTION: Notable improvement in uncertainty estimation, with a significant increase in the accuracy and reliability of the depth estimation results; potential trade-off with model speed and complexity due to the need to train multiple instantiations of the model.

ACTION: ADD 8
TITLE: Multi-Task Learning for Focal Stack Depth Estimation with Uncertainty-aware Confidence Measurement
PROPOSAL: Develop a focal stack depth estimation framework that incorporates multi-task learning to simultaneously predict depth, uncertainty, and confidence scores, and to utilize a novel uncertainty-aware confidence measurement mechanism to select the most reliable depth map estimates. This model will leverage a shared encoder-decoder architecture to learn robust and accurate depth and uncertainty estimates, and then apply a confidence measurement module to detect and exclude noisy or uncertain predictions. Evaluation will be performed on the NYU Depth V2 dataset and a subset of real-world focal stacks.
CONTROLS: Compare to the traditional physics-informed model, uncertainty quantification model and baseline models without multi-task learning or uncertainty-aware confidence measurement, on the aforementioned datasets.
COST: 12000
PREDICTION: Notable improvement in accuracy, reliability, and robustness of the depth estimation results, with a significant increase in the confidence of the predicted depth maps; potential trade-off with model speed and complexity due to the need to train a multi-task model with uncertainty-aware confidence measurement.

ACTION: ADD 9
TITLE: Holistic Focal Stack Depth Estimation via Graph Convolutional Networks and Self-Supervised Learning
PROPOSAL: Develop a holistic focal stack depth estimation framework that leverages graph convolutional networks and self-supervised learning to effectively model the spatial and focal relationships within the focal stack data. This model will utilize a graph-structured representation of the focal stack data, and then apply a self-supervised learning approach to learn robust and accurate depth estimates from the graph-structured representation. Evaluation will be performed on the NYU Depth V2 dataset and a subset of real-world focal stacks.
CONTROLS: Compare to the traditional physics-informed model, uncertainty quantification model, multi-task learning model and baseline models without graph convolutional networks or self-supervised learning, on the aforementioned datasets.
COST: 15000
PREDICTION: Notable improvement in accuracy, reliability, and robustness of the depth estimation results, with a significant increase in the confidence of the predicted depth maps; potential trade-off with model speed and complexity due to the need to train a graph-structured model with self-supervised learning.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Designing Physics-Informed Features for DFF using Multi-Modal Learning
PROPOSAL: We develop a multi-modal learning approach that incorporates physics-informed features directly learned from simulated focal stacks and paired with corresponding all-in-focus images. The learned features focus on capturing salient properties of the focusing process, such as gradual changes in sharpness, and encode real-world geometric cues missed by standard image features.
CONTROLS: The performance of the proposed multi-modal approach will be compared against existing learning-based DFF models that solely rely on image features, and we will analyze its impact on noise robustness, texture-induced artifacts, and focal-stack utilization.
COST: 750
PREDICTION: By explicitly accounting for the physical principles involved, the proposed approach should outperform traditional learning-based methods in handling fine textures and abrupt depth changes while maintaining accurate depth estimations.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A Theoretical Analysis of Focal-Stack Utilization in Learning-Based DFF
PROPOSAL: We establish a theoretical framework to formalize and analyze the effectiveness of using focal stacks in learning-based DFF. We develop bounds on the generalization error of learning-based methods when incorporating focal stacks, demonstrating their potential to represent a broader image formation model than conventional methods. Furthermore, we provide conditions for the accuracy and robustness of depth recovery for focal stacks with varying levels of texture, noise, and focal ambiguity.
CONTROLS: Theoretical analysis against simplified modeling scenarios, reduced modeling, and a blanket removal of the incorporation of focal stacks.
COST: 1000
PREDICTION: Our theoretical analysis should confirm the benefits of including focal stacks for robust depth estimation and reveal key parameter and regularization sensitivities governing the success of focal-stack exploitation in our model, especially highlighting difficulties in fine textures or ambiguity scenarios.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Focal Priors: Introducing Domain-Specific Regularization for DFF
PROPOSAL: We design a set of domain-specific regularization terms for learning-based DFF models that leverage prior knowledge about the structure of focal stacks and real-world indoor scenes. We also explore integrating these focal priors into existing approaches, adapting their architecture to benefit from the physics-informed regularization. Our goal is to improve model robustness by reducing texture-induced artifacts and focal ambiguity in scenes with complex geometry and varying lighting conditions.
CONTROLS: We compare our focal prior-regularized models against state-of-the-art learning-based DFF models, using both qualitative and quantitative evaluation metrics.
COST: 1400
PREDICTION: By explicitly encoding knowledge about the physics and structure of focal stacks in our learned model, our focal prior-regularized approach should exhibit improved depth estimation accuracy and robustness in scenes with fine textures, NF backgrounds, or varying lighting, establishing a solid foundation for our subsequent experiments.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Training with Noise-Aware Synthetic Data for Robust Learning in DFF
PROPOSAL: We generate synthetic focal stack data with added noise and proceeding to train and validate our learning-based DFF models on these noisy data. We will leverage both explicit noise sources and implicit, physics-based noise models that are more comprehensive than existing ones. This uncovers the best way to explicitly degrade synthetic images under physics-like contexts, expected to enable near-optimal noise-driven regularization and bring robustness to real-world focus-related challenges.
CONTROLS: Our learned models will be evaluated on both real-world and synthetic datasets, comparing its performance to the established counterparts when focal degradation is quite high.
COST: 1834.56
PREDICTION: By augmenting the training process with synthetic focal stacks featuring added noise, our models should efficiently apply noise tolerance in complicated depth scenes, thereby matching State-of-art performance with considerable accuracy.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Comparative Study of Joint vs. Sequential Methods for Simultaneous Depth and Focus Estimation
PROPOSAL: We conduct an exhaustive study to investigate the difference between joint and sequential approaches for the simultaneous inference of depth and focus from a given focal stack or focal plane. Our joint approach involves learning a shared representation of the input data, while our sequential approach solves the two tasks step by step, directly linking the solutions of each individual task.
CONTROLS: The depth and focus recovery performance of both approaches will be evaluated and compared on a set of real-world and synthetic benchmark datasets, along with evaluation of inference complexity, practical deployment considerations, data-driven representations.
COST: 2160
PREDICTION: The study should reveal that the joint neural network approach outperforms the sequential alternative, reaching robust results especially in fine textures and ambiguities, where depth and sharpness accurately coupled virtually overcome visible artifacts in inferred scenes, showcasing considerable advances both over prior works and Baselines.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Quantifying Impact of Token Overlap on MoE Specialization in Diffusion Transformers
PROPOSAL: Investigate the impact of token overlap on MoE specialization by systematically manipulating the number of tokens assigned to each expert. Use a grid search over different overlap ratios (e.g., 25%, 50%, 75%) and expert capacities, and evaluate the resulting expert specialization using metrics such as intra-expert token mutual information. Compare with a baseline of uniform token assignment.
CONTROLS: Compare with a uniform token assignment baseline and ablate the effect of different overlap ratios on expert capacity. Use the Diffusion Transformer's built-in "none" step as a reference point (i.e., when nodes at the same noise level are fully connected to each other) to compare with the results from random subsets.
COST: 400
PREDICTION: This study may uncover that token overlap hinders expert specialization, and higher overlap ratios lead to a decrease in intra-expert mutual information. However, it may also reveal that with sufficiently large expert capacity, the MoE can adapt to and learn from spatially overlapping tokens, potentially mitigating the effect of token overlap on specialization.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Role of Visual Token Semantics in Expert Learning and Mode Coverage
PROPOSAL: Investigate how different visual token representations (e.g., raw pixel values, feature maps from a pre-trained convolutional network) affect MoE learning and mode coverage in DiTs. Use a combination of quantitative metrics (e.g., expert mutual information, mode coverage) and qualitative visualizations (e.g., t-SNE embeddings of learned expert representations) to understand how different token representations contribute to expert specialization and generalizability.
CONTROLS: Compare with a baseline of dense DiT models and ablate the effect of using different pre-trained convolutional networks for generating visual token features. Evaluate the robustness of the findings by using multiple pre-trained networks and analyzing their differences.
COST: 600
PREDICTION: This study may reveal that certain visual token representations create a stronger inductive bias towards expert specialization, but also lead to a decrease in generalizability and mode coverage. This could indicate that the choice of token representation is crucial in MoE-DiT design and should be optimized for the specific task at hand.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Expert Routing Heterogeneity for Diffusion Transformers with Mixture-of-Experts
PROPOSAL: Design and test a novel routing mechanism that allows for heterogeneous (different in topology) expert routing for DiTs. Specifically, modify the existing routing weights calculation to introduce a routing multiplicity factor that randomly splits the output of each expert into multiple sub-experts, each processed individually through an additional set of routing weights. Compare this topology-aware routing mechanism against the original routing method.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original dense DiT model and ablate the effect of injecting multiplicity factors into individual routing paths.
COST: 367.2
PREDICTION: By injecting diverse routing topologies, MoE-DiTs may improve their ability to handle complex patterns and semantically distinct regions within the input, leading to better generation quality and robustness to different input scenarios.

TITLE: Investigating Token Rouge-Accord in DiT Models
PROPOSAL: This experiment compares the token-level parameters and gradients of DiTs with and without MoE routing to analyze how token properties impact MoE layer performance. DiT variants will be evaluated on text-to-image benchmarks (e.g., COCO) using FID and IS scores as metrics. Controls include a baseline dense DiT model and a comparison with routing methods such as token-choice and expert-choice, which focus on distinguishing token characteristics.
CONTROLS: Dense DiT model, token-choice DiT-MoE, expert-choice EC-DiT
COST: 1000
PREDICTION: Expected results will reveal differences in token parameters, activation patterns, and gradient flow, hinting at challenges in inducing specialization among visual tokens. Failures could stem from differences in baseline models or misspecification of the overfitting-rare sensor model to vocational capture.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Characterizing Patch Types and Sparsity in DiT Models
PROPOSAL: This experiment uses a combination of statistical analysis and visualization techniques to study the distribution of patches and their corresponding feature maps within DiTs, possibly identifying the "difficulty spectrum" of patches in a denoising process. Fourier transform and patch-level density metrics will be used to analyze these properties. Another key focus is exploring the sparsity of activations in different DiT layers to understand how expert routing might leverage such sparsity. On text-to-image datasets like Flickr30k, FID, and IS scores will be used as evaluation metrics.
CONTROLS: Dense DiT model, previous Token Rouge-Accord results, patch attribute analysis using FFT and patchStats to check presumed conception orientations
COST: 1500
PREDICTION: Expected results will highlight specific patterns in patch difficulty and activations' sparsity, providing critical underpinnings for MoE layer design, routing, and parameter redistribution of visual information. Possible pitfalls may involve missing critical features of visual tokens or overfitting patch decomposition models.

WMF is a factorization technique that can identify latent patterns in matrices and can be used to reduce the dimensionality of the routing process in MoE-DiT models. We aim to develop a WMF-based approach that efficiently routes tokens to experts in DiT models, and evaluate its performance on text-to-image benchmarks like COCO using metrics FID and IS scores.

COST: 3800
PREDICTION: Expected results will provide a framework for efficient MoE routing in DiT models, and demonstrate its effectiveness on text-to-image tasks. Challenges lie in developing a WMF approach that efficiently captures the complex relationships between tokens, experts, and patches in MoE-DiT models.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Grid-based Token Routing for Expert Specialization in DiT-MoE
PROPOSAL: Implement a grid-based token router for DiT-MoE, where each token is routed to the expert that processes the spatial feature maps covering its location in the image grid, aiming to leverage the spatial structure of visual tokens to foster expert specialization. Compare this approach to the existing token-choice routing and expert-choice routing in DiT-MoE using the LSUN-Bedroom dataset and the FID score.
CONTROLS: Compare to both token-choice routing and expert-choice routing in DiT-MoE, as well as a baseline dense DiT model. Measure the influence of grid size and routing strategies on expert specialization.
COST: 30000
PREDICTION: We predict that the grid-based token router will improve the quality of generation compared to token-choice routing and expert-choice routing, potentially achieving gains of up to 10% in FID scores. However, it may underperform the baseline dense DiT, indicating that currently, no Mixture-of-Experts routing strategy outperforms dense activations for visual synthesis.

PROPOSAL: Undertake a comprehensive analysis of the visual tokens processed by a DiT, characterizing their feature distributions, spatial structure, and learned representations, aimed at identifying attributes that can facilitate or hinder expert specialization. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Expert Quotas vs. Token Quotas: Adaptive Allocation for Expert Specialization in DiT-MoE
PROPOSAL: Investigate the interaction between expert quotas (each expert has a fixed quota of tokens) and token quotas (each token selects its top experts) in DiT-MoE, comparing the performance of variants that adaptively adjust quotas as a function of token feature distributions, spatial structure, or learned representations, discovered through visual token analysis. Test the adaptive allocation strategies on the LSUN-Bedroom dataset and Cifar-10 dataset using a combination of FID score and per-expert metrics (e.g., uniformity of token allocation).
CONTROLS: Compare to non-adaptive expert-choice and token-choice routing in DiT-MoE, with fixed quotas, as well as a dense baseline DiT model.
COST: 60000
PREDICTION: We predict that adaptive quotas based on token features and spatial structure will yield performance improvements of up to 15% in FID scores, while the uniformity of token allocation per expert may significantly drop, highlighting the role of adaptive allocation in driving expert specialization.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Expert Quotas vs. Token Quotas: Adaptive Allocation for Expert Specialization in DiT-MoE (Revised)
PROPOSAL: Modify the adaptive allocation strategy to incorporate a meta-learning mechanism, where the quota adjustment is itself cast as a sequence prediction problem, solved using a variant of the adapter module from LLMs, fine-tuned on a held-out validation set. This should enable the quota adapter to generalize to unseen token distributions. Compare this optimized strategy to its static and non-adaptive baseline counterparts, and the predefined adaptive schemes studied in previous experiments, on the LSUN-Bedroom and Cifar-10 datasets using both FID score and intersection over union (IoU) of expert token predictions as metrics.
CONTROLS: Compare only to non-adaptive expert-choice and token-choice routing in DiT-MoE with fixed quotas, as well as a dense baseline DiT model.
COST: 75000
PREDICTION: We expect the meta-learning quota allocation mechanism to improve FID scores and increase IoU of expert token predictions by up to 18% and 12% respectively over static and predefined strategies, demonstrating significant generalization to unseen token distributions and robustly fostering expert specialization across datasets.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Tied Experts: Ensembling for Inter-Expert Consistency and Improved Specialization
PROPOSAL: Explore a novel L2-regularized tied expert formulation, where the output weights of all experts are tied across tasks and input tokens, forcing the experts to agree on their contribution to the overall model output. This can be seen as a regularization technique for expert specialization, promoting more consistent and accurate predictions. Evaluate the effect of tied experts on stability, generalization, and generation quality across the LSUN-Bedroom and Cifar-10 datasets, comparing it to a baseline of untied experts with adaptive allocation.
CONTROLS: Compare tied experts with both a dense DiT baseline and an untied DiT-MoE model with progressive allocation strategy, to assess if the benefits of tied experts come from the regularization or from leveraging a specific routing.
COST: 90000
PREDICTION: We anticipate that tied experts will significantly improve model stability and reduce overfitting, leading to 5-10% improvements in FID scores, and potentially providing a useful Regularization tool to reduce the risk of poor-quality generations due to inconsistent expert involvement.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Gradual Routing and Progressive Training for DiT-MoE
PROPOSAL: Introduce a gradual routing mechanism where at each training time step, a growing fraction of tokens are routed using the learned expert weights and a diminishing fraction of tokens follow the default dense routing. This progressive approach allows the model to smoothly transition from a uniformly dense DiT to an MoE with a diverse set of experts, potentially mitigating challenges in training and routing such as dead zones and inconsistent performance. Evaluate the effectiveness of gradual routing and training on the LSUN-Bedroom and Cifar-10 datasets, measuring convergence rate, FID scores, and generation diversity.
CONTROLS: Compare to (i) the conventional token-choice routing in DiT-MoE, (ii) a dense DiT baseline, and (iii) a variant with fixed routing schedules (e.g., routing 20% of tokens at the start, 80% by the end).
COST: 105000
PREDICTION: We expect gradual routing and progressive training to facilitate faster convergence (up to 20% reduction in steps to reach peak FID score), better FID scores (up to 12% improvement), and increased diversity of generated outputs, ultimately leading to improved robustness and quality in the output of the DiT-MoE model.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Attention-based Expert Consulting for DiT-MoE
PROPOSAL: Modify the DiT-MoE architecture to incorporate attention mechanisms that allow each expert to selectively draw information from other experts, thus establishing a self-supervised learning and collaboration regime that enables experts to compensate for their own limitations by leveraging the strengths of others. Evaluate this consulting mechanism's ability to boost FID scores, diversity of generations, and convergence speed on the LSUN-Bedroom and Cifar-10 datasets, in comparison with existing DiT-MoE variants.
CONTROLS: Compare to standard DiT-MoE, tied experts, and gradual routing with progressive training, to isolate the added value of expert consultation in each scenario.
COST: 120000
PREDICTION: We expect attention-based expert consulting to provide improved accuracy, diversity, and convergence speed (by up to 15%), fostering more synchronized and cross-informed expert discussions, but also increasing the risk of non-determinism in training and routing, possibly impacting model interpretability.
