ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Grid-based Token Routing for Expert Specialization in DiT-MoE
PROPOSAL: Implement a grid-based token router for DiT-MoE, where each token is routed to the expert that processes the spatial feature maps covering its location in the image grid, aiming to leverage the spatial structure of visual tokens to foster expert specialization. Compare this approach to the existing token-choice routing and expert-choice routing in DiT-MoE using the LSUN-Bedroom dataset and the FID score.
CONTROLS: Compare to both token-choice routing and expert-choice routing in DiT-MoE, as well as a baseline dense DiT model. Measure the influence of grid size and routing strategies on expert specialization.
COST: 90000
PREDICTION: We predict that the grid-based token router will improve the quality of generation compared to token-choice routing and expert-choice routing, potentially achieving gains of up to 10% in FID scores. However, it may underperform the baseline dense DiT, indicating that currently, no Mixture-of-Experts routing strategy outperforms dense activations for visual synthesis.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Visual Token Analysis for Routing Expert Specialization in DiT-MoE
PROPOSAL: Undertake a comprehensive analysis of the visual tokens processed by a DiT, characterizing their feature distributions, spatial structure, and learned representations, aimed at identifying attributes that can facilitate or hinder expert specialization. Utilize the LAION-400M dataset and design visual token embedding visualizations, spatial autocorrelation plots, and feature descriptor distributions to expose any visual token properties that differ from those seen in language tokens.
CONTROLS: Compare the analyzed token properties to those found in natural language sequences, and study the influence of token preprocessing methods (e.g., spatial augmentation) on token distributions.
COST: 135000
PREDICTION: We anticipate significant differences in token distribution, on the order of 2 standard deviations, with image tokens exhibiting higher spatial autocorrelation and potentially more variability in learned representations. However, identifying specific attributes that definitively impede or enable expert specialization might prove challenging due to the complexity of visual features.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Expert Quotas vs. Token Quotas: Adaptive Allocation for Expert Specialization in DiT-MoE
PROPOSAL: Investigate the interaction between expert quotas (each expert has a fixed quota of tokens) and token quotas (each token selects its top experts) in DiT-MoE, comparing the performance of variants that adaptively adjust quotas as a function of token feature distributions, spatial structure, or learned representations, discovered through visual token analysis. Test the adaptive allocation strategies on the LSUN-Bedroom dataset and Cifar-10 dataset using a combination of FID score and per-expert metrics (e.g., uniformity of token allocation).
CONTROLS: Compare to non-adaptive expert-choice and token-choice routing in DiT-MoE, with fixed quotas, as well as a dense baseline DiT model.
COST: 180000
PREDICTION: We predict that adaptive quotas based on token features and spatial structure will yield performance improvements of up to 15% in FID scores, while the uniformity of token allocation per expert may significantly drop, highlighting the role of adaptive allocation in driving expert specialization.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Expert Quotas vs. Token Quotas: Adaptive Allocation for Expert Specialization in DiT-MoE (Revised)
PROPOSAL: Modify the adaptive allocation strategy to incorporate a meta-learning mechanism, where the quota adjustment is itself cast as a sequence prediction problem, solved using a variant of the adapter module from LLMs, fine-tuned on a held-out validation set. This should enable the quota adapater to generalize to unseen token distributions. Compare this optimized strategy to its static and non-adaptive baseline counterparts, and the predefined adaptive schemes studied in previous experiments, on the LSUN-Bedroom dataset using FID score.
CONTROLS: Compare only to non-adaptive expert-choice and token-choice routing in DiT-MoE with fixed quotas, as well as a dense baseline DiT model.
COST: 225000
PREDICTION: We expect the meta-learning quota allocation mechanism to improve FID scores by up to 18% over static and predefined strategies, demonstrating significant generalization to unseen token distributions.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Expert Quotas vs. Token Quotas: Adaptive Allocation for Expert Specialization in DiT-MoE (Revised)
PROPOSAL: Modify the adaptive allocation strategy to incorporate a meta-learning mechanism, where the quota adjustment is itself cast as a sequence prediction problem, solved using a variant of the adapter module from LLMs, fine-tuned on a held-out validation set. This should enable the quota adapter to generalize to unseen token distributions. Compare this optimized strategy to its static and non-adaptive baseline counterparts, and the predefined adaptive schemes studied in previous experiments, on the LSUN-Bedroom and Cifar-10 datasets using both FID score and intersection over union (IoU) of expert token predictions as metrics.
CONTROLS: Compare only to non-adaptive expert-choice and token-choice routing in DiT-MoE with fixed quotas, as well as a dense baseline DiT model.
COST: 225000
PREDICTION: We expect the meta-learning quota allocation mechanism to improve FID scores and increase IoU of expert token predictions by up to 18% and 12% respectively over static and predefined strategies, demonstrating significant generalization to unseen token distributions and robustly fostering expert specialization across datasets.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Tied Experts: Ensembling for Inter-Expert Consistency and Improved Specialization
PROPOSAL: Explore a novel L2-regularized tied expert formulation, where the output weights of all experts are tied across tasks and input tokens, forcing the experts to agree on their contribution to the overall model output. This can be seen as a regularization technique for expert specialization, promoting more consistent and accurate predictions. Evaluate the effect of tied experts on stability, generalization, and generation quality across the LSUN-Bedroom and Cifar-10 datasets, comparing it to a baseline of untied experts with adaptive allocation.
CONTROLS: Compare tied experts with both a dense DiT baseline and an untied DiT-MoE model with progressive allocation strategy, to assess if the benefits of tied experts come from the regularization or from leveraging a specific routing.
COST: 270000
PREDICTION: We anticipate that tied experts will significantly improve model stability and reduce overfitting, leading to 5-10% improvements in FID scores, and potentially providing a useful Regularization tool to reduce the risk of poor-quality generations due to inconsistent expert involvement.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Gradual Routing and Progressive Training for DiT-MoE
PROPOSAL: Introduce a gradual routing mechanism where at each training time step, a growing fraction of tokens are routed using the learned expert weights and a diminishing fraction of tokens follow the default dense routing. This progressive approach allows the model to smoothly transition from a uniformly dense DiT to an MoE with a diverse set of experts, potentially mitigating challenges in training and routing such as dead zones and inconsistent performance. Evaluate the effectiveness of gradual routing and training on the LSUN-Bedroom and Cifar-10 datasets, measuring convergence rate, FID scores, and generation diversity.
CONTROLS: Compare to (i) the conventional token-choice routing in DiT-MoE, (ii) a dense DiT baseline, and (iii) a variant with fixed routing schedules (e.g., routing 20% of tokens at the start, 80% by the end).
COST: 315000
PREDICTION: We expect gradual routing and progressive training to facilitate faster convergence (up to 20% reduction in steps to reach peak FID score), better FID scores (up to 12% improvement), and increased diversity of generated outputs, ultimately leading to improved robustness and quality in the output of the DiT-MoE model.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Attention-based Expert Consulting for DiT-MoE
PROPOSAL: Modify the DiT-MoE architecture to incorporate attention mechanisms that allow each expert to selectively draw information from other experts, thus establishing a self-supervised learning and collaboration regime that enables experts to compensate for their own limitations by leveraging the strengths of others. Evaluate this consulting mechanism's ability to boost FID scores, diversity of generations, and convergence speed on the LSUN-Bedroom and Cifar-10 datasets, in comparison with existing DiT-MoE variants.
CONTROLS: Compare to standard DiT-MoE, tied experts, and gradual routing with progressive training, to isolate the added value of expert consultation in each scenario.
COST: 360000
PREDICTION: We expect attention-based expert consulting to provide improved accuracy, diversity, and convergence speed (by up to 15%), fostering more synchronized and cross-informed expert discussions, but also increasing the risk of non-determinism in training and routing, possibly impacting model interpretability.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Investigating Token Properties for Routing in DiT-MoE
PROPOSAL: We will conduct an experiment to analyze the characteristics of visual tokens in DiTs, such as token similarity, dimensionality, and local structure, to identify why they might impede expert specialization in the MoE paradigm. Specifically, we will use a deep clustering-based algorithm to examine the connectome structure and motifs of high-dimensional token embeddings in DiTs. We hypothesize that the complex and correlated nature of these visual tokens will be difficult to separate by routing algorithms in MoE, preventing clear expert specialization.
CONTROLS: Experiment 1 will use DiT-MoE as the base model, comparing the clustering results to a control run where expert assignments are random. Additionally, we will use t-SNE embeddings for ablation to isolate the effect of deep clustering. For fair comparison, we will also measure the efficiency and quality of dense DiT controls.
COST: 1000
PREDICTION: Expected to confirm our hypothesis that the token properties are a major reason for the limited success of MoE in DiTs. Potential failure might come from the chosen clustering algorithm failing to capture essential token structures or not being able to scale to ever-larger model sizes and numbers of experts.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Adversarial Token Augmentation for Expert Specialization
PROPOSAL: To better understand and overcome the barriers to expert specialization in DiT-MoE, we will develop an adversarial token augmentation strategy that intentionally introduces discrepancy between token similarity scores and visual similarity distances in the DiT's learned token embedding space. By doing so, we create a more challenging environment for MoE's routing and expert specialization. If successful, increased specialization should yield more significant MoE gains over dense DiTs. Our model will include an additional neural network that adversarially perturbs the DiT's output embeddings, forcing the MoE routing to adapt and specialize experts accordingly.
CONTROLS: Experiment 2a will compare the MoE with adversarial token augmentation against a dense DiT and the standard DiT-MoE without augmentation; Experiment 2b will conduct an ablation study to isolate the effect of the proposed augmentation on the MoE's ability to specialize experts.
COST: 1600
PREDICTION: Expected to improve the performance of DiT-MoE with the proposed augmentations, yet may see losses in precision or robustness due to overfitting or orthogonality issues, while robust and noticeable gains may not generalize to various application domains.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Local Expert Routing with Neighbor Embeddings
PROPOSAL: To further explore the feasibility of MoE in DiTs, we will design a local expert routing scheme, focusing on leveraging neighborhood relationships between tokens in the DiT's learned embedding space. By doing so, we can discover co-occurring patterns specific to a subset of tokens and encourage experts to specialize in these compact domains. In contrast to global token embedding spaces, our approach will only rely on token neighborhoods, potentially alleviating some of the issues associated with expert specialization.
CONTROLS: Experiment 3 will compare the performance of local expert routing against a standard global router in DiT-MoE, considering both transductive and inductive few-shot synthesis tasks with diverse visual domains. In addition, we will investigate the effects of varying neighborhood granularity and router depths to gain further insights.
COST: 2400
PREDICTION: Expected to demonstrate improved MoE performance in capturing local token relationships, leading to enhanced generation quality over specific categories of visual tokens in DiT. Flaws might arise if the spectral overlap of local neighborhoods reveals that too much redundancy exists among MoE experts and/or anchorage over hopt issues leading weak unrestricted isolation among densely sunfig functions inadequately in versatile visual regions.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Asymmetric Routing for Efficient MoE Deployment
PROPOSAL: To further optimize the routing process in DiT-MoE, we introduce an asymmetric routing mechanism that dynamically adjusts the number of experts assigned to each token based on the token's relevance and complexity. Specifically, we will use a attention-based mechanism to estimate the token's "importance" and then use this importance score to control the number of experts activated for each token. This approach aims to reduce unnecessary computations and improve overall efficiency by assigning more experts to complex tokens that require more processing power.
CONTROLS: Experiment 5 will compare the performance of our asymmetric routing mechanism with the standard token-choice routing mechanism used in DiT-MoE, controlling for factors such as token complexity and importance score. In addition, we will investigate the effects of different importance scoring functions and expert activation thresholds on overall performance.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Investigating Token Properties for Routing in DiT-MoE
PROPOSAL: We will conduct an experiment to analyze the characteristics of visual tokens in DiTs, such as token similarity, dimensionality, and local structure, to identify why they might impede expert specialization in the MoE paradigm. Specifically, we will use a deep clustering-based algorithm to examine the connectome structure and motifs of high-dimensional token embeddings in DiTs. We hypothesize that the complex and correlated nature of these visual tokens will be difficult to separate by routing algorithms in MoE, preventing clear expert specialization.
CONTROLS: Experiment 1 will use DiT-MoE as the base model, comparing the clustering results to a control run where expert assignments are random. Additionally, we will use t-SNE embeddings for ablation to isolate the effect of deep clustering. For fair comparison, we will also measure the efficiency and quality of dense DiT controls.
COST: 3000
PREDICTION: Expected to confirm our hypothesis that the token properties are a major reason for the limited success of MoE in DiTs. Potential failure might come from the chosen clustering algorithm failing to capture essential token structures or not being able to scale to ever-larger model sizes and numbers of experts.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Adversarial Token Augmentation for Expert Specialization
PROPOSAL: To better understand and overcome the barriers to expert specialization in DiT-MoE, we will develop an adversarial token augmentation strategy that intentionally introduces discrepancy between token similarity scores and visual similarity distances in the DiT's learned token embedding space. By doing so, we create a more challenging environment for MoE's routing and expert specialization. If successful, increased specialization should yield more significant MoE gains over dense DiTs. Our model will include an additional neural network that adversarially perturbs the DiT's output embeddings, forcing the MoE routing to adapt and specialize experts accordingly.
CONTROLS: Experiment 2a will compare the MoE with adversarial token augmentation against a dense DiT and the standard DiT-MoE without augmentation; Experiment 2b will conduct an ablation study to isolate the effect of the proposed augmentation on the MoE's ability to specialize experts.

PREDICTION: Expected to improve the performance of DiT-MoE with the proposed augmentations, yet may see losses in precision or robustness due to overfitting or orthogonality issues, while robust and noticeable gains may not generalize to various application domains.

In contrast to global token embedding spaces, our approach will only rely on token neighborhoods, potentially alleviating some of the issues associated with expert specialization.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Factorised Time-Varying Offset Estimation via Periodicity Analysis
PROPOSAL: 
We propose a novel approach to estimating per-dimension additive offsets in the observation function, leveraging periodicity analysis. The agent assumes the offsets follow an unknown periodic pattern, and analyzes the training data to detect common periods across different dimensions. For each dimension, it models the observed state as the true state plus an offset that is periodic with a detected period, and the amplitude of the periodic pattern. The agent then trains a factorised model to predict the periodic offset for each dimension. During training, we leverage the assumption of known periods, while at test time, we predict the periodic offsets using the learned model. We use this to update the observation function, which is then used for standard offline RL.
CONTROLS: Comparing with baseline methods such as parametric state estimation and standard offline RL will help evaluate its effectiveness.
COST: 240
PREDICTION: Our method is expected to be robust and accurate in environments where the offset patterns are periodic. However, its performance might degrade in scenarios where the patterns are aperiodic or highly variable, as the periodicity analysis assumption would not hold.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Robust Offline Reinforcement Learning via Differential Evolutionary Techniques
PROPOSAL: 
We explore the application of Differential Evolution (DE) algorithms to offline RL. DE algorithms are well-suited for noisy or non-stationary objective functions, which can be the case when dealing with observations that have been shifted by unknown, time-varying, per-dimension additive offsets. We leverage DE to adaptively adjust the model's parameters and inductive bias to better fit the data, with a regularisation term that encourages the agent's policy to converge to an optimal solution even in the presence of data inconsistencies due to offsets. Our method,odem, is evaluated on a range of robot navigation and manipulation tasks from the Helsinki Benchmark and virtual robotic environments to generalise performance predictability of learned behavior.
CONTROLS: A control experiment using a same baseline offline learning algorithm faced with non-stationarity-reduced reward is to be set.
COST: 360
PREDICTION:odem is expected to exhibit robustness to non-stationarity and offset effects. However, it may become inefficient or over-adapt to the training data when the offset patterns exhibit large variations or complex structures.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Offset-aware State Estimation via Neural Unitary Transformers
PROPOSAL: 
We propose a novel state estimation method that incorporates the offset information and is based on Neural Unitary Transformers (NUTs). NUTs can learn the time-evolution of the system's dynamics, even in the presence of offsets. By incorporating the NUT architecture into the agent's state estimation module, we can effectively disentangle the effects of offsets from the true state dynamics. This approach enables the agent to predict the state and the offset simultaneously, which is essential for successful offline RL when dealing with partial observability. We leverage the self-attn mechanism to inject temporal memory and the added ability for account of varying offset data.
CONTROLS: Comparing the error of state estimation and, as a secondary meter, the learning speed obtained from both the proposed algorithm and standard offline learning that ignores offsets.
COST: 480
PREDICTION: Our method is expected to exhibit superior state estimation and policy learning performance compared to current baselines, especially in environments with complex, non-Markovian phase transitions due to offset effects. However, the method may struggle with noisy or high-dimensional offset signals, leading to reduced accuracy.

TITLE: Active Statistical Learning for Offset-aware Offline Reinforcement Learning
PROPOSAL: 
We introduce an active statistical learning (ASL) framework for offset-aware offline RL, which leverages the correlated nature of the offset effects to reduce the sample complexity of the learning algorithm. Our method, ASL-PPO, selects a subset of the most informative observations from the dataset to update the policy and value function. We use a statistical model to learn the distribution of the offset effects and select the observations that provide the most additional information about the policy and value function updates. By selecting the most informative observations, ASL-PPO reduces the number of observations required to achieve a satisfactory learning outcome, improving the robustness and efficiency of the offset-aware offline RL algorithm.
CONTROLS: Comparing the performance of ASL-PPO with other active learning and passive learning approaches in offline RL, including the o-HSO method.
COST: 604.8
PREDICTION: ASL-PPO is expected to achieve better robustness and efficiency in terms of samples required to reach a satisfactory learning outcome. However, it may require additional computational resources to compute the statistical model and select the most informative observations.

TITLE: Certified Robustness under Time-Varying Observation Miscalibration
PROPOSAL: 
We investigate certified robustness under time-varying observation miscalibration in offline RL. Our approach, based on techniques from robust optimization and certified adversarial training, provides guarantees on the robustness of the policy and value function to perturbations in the observation function. We introduce a novel certification framework for offline RL, which leverages the assumption of time-varying observation miscalibration to provide robustness guarantees. Our framework is based on the idea of "adversarial testing" of the policy and value function, where we simulate the effect of perturbations in the observation function and use the certified robustness bounds to evaluate the robustness of the policy and value function.
CONTROLS: Evaluating the performance of the certified robustness framework on a range of offline RL benchmarks and comparing its performance with other robustness guarantees.
COST: 675
PREDICTION: The certified robustness framework is expected to provide strong guarantees on the robustness of the policy and value function, reducing the risk of overfitting to the training data. However, it may come at the cost of additional computational resources required for certification.

TITLE: Factorised Time-Varying Offset Estimation via Periodicity Analysis
PROPOSAL: 
We propose a novel approach to estimating per-dimension additive offsets in the observation function, leveraging periodicity analysis. The agent assumes the offsets follow an unknown periodic pattern, and analyzes the training data to detect common periods across different dimensions. For each dimension, it models the observed state as the true state plus an offset that is periodic with a detected period, and the amplitude of the periodic pattern. The agent then trains a factorised model to predict the periodic offset for each dimension. During training, we leverage the assumption of known periods, while at test time, we predict the periodic offsets using the learned model. We use this to update the observation function, which is then used for standard offline RL.
CONTROLS: Comparing with baseline methods such as parametric state estimation and standard offline RL will help evaluate its effectiveness.
COST: 720
PREDICTION: Our method is expected to be robust and accurate in environments where the offset patterns are periodic. However, its performance might degrade in scenarios where the patterns are aperiodic or highly variable, as the periodicity analysis assumption would not hold.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Robust Offline Reinforcement Learning via Differential Evolutionary Techniques
PROPOSAL: 
We explore the application of Differential Evolution (DE) algorithms to offline RL. DE algorithms are well-suited for noisy or non-stationary objective functions, which can be the case when dealing with observations that have been shifted by unknown, time-varying, per-dimension additive offsets. We leverage DE to adaptively adjust the model's parameters and inductive bias to better fit the data, with a regularisation term that encourages the agent's policy to converge to an optimal solution even in the presence of data inconsistencies due to offsets. Our method,odem, is evaluated on a range of robot navigation and manipulation tasks from the Helsinki Benchmark and virtual robotic environments to generalise performance predictability of learned behavior.
CONTROLS: A control experiment using a same baseline offline learning algorithm faced with non-stationarity-reduced reward is to be set.
COST: 1080
PREDICTION:odem is expected to exhibit robustness to non-stationarity and offset effects. However, it may become inefficient or over-adapt to the training data when the offset patterns exhibit large variations or complex structures.

TITLE: Offset-aware State Estimation via Neural Unitary Transformers
PROPOSAL: 
We propose a novel state estimation method that incorporates the offset information and is based on Neural Unitary Transformers (NUTs). NUTs can learn the time-evolution of the system's dynamics, even in the presence of offsets. By incorporating the NUT architecture into the agent's state estimation module, we can effectively disentangle the effects of offsets from the true state dynamics. This approach enables the agent to predict the state and the offset simultaneously, which is essential for successful offline RL when dealing with partial observability. We leverage the self-attn mechanism to inject temporal memory and the added ability for account of varying offset data.

However, the method may struggle with noisy or high-dimensional offset signals, leading to reduced accuracy.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Accelerated Relaxed Learning for Decomposing Episodic Observation Offsets in Offline RL
PROPOSAL: REVISED: Learning to Decompose Episodic Observation Offsets in Offline RL

To enhance the robustness of the previously proposed RSN-based approach, introduce an auxiliary, contrastive loss during offline training that encourages the policy to differentiate between correctly predicted offsets and those that deviate significantly from the true offsets. This can be formulated as an instance of multiclass classification, with each potential offset serving as a class label. Train the predictive model to output a probability distribution over the possible offset values, using a contrastive loss function (e.g., triplet loss) to ensure the predicted probability distribution reflects the correct offset's similarity to the ground-truth value, while encouraging the other potential offsets to be deemed significantly less plausible. The additional contrastive loss is added to the standard RL objective.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original RSN-based method without contrastive loss, as well as with other robust offline RL methods that explicitly handle non-stationarity in observation functions, and examine the impact of varying the frequency of providing the contrastive signal during training.
COST: 1068
PREDICTION: Improve the effectiveness of RSN-based approaches in learning robust, accurate offset predictions in online deployment. If not properly tuned, the additional contrastive loss may degrade performance due to an increase in training complexity and the risk of overfitting to the contrastive signal.

PROPOSAL: REVISED: Learning to Decompose Episodic Observation Offsets in Offline RL

To enhance the robustness of the previously proposed RSN-based approach, introduce an auxiliary, contrastive loss during offline training that encourages the policy to differentiate between correctly predicted offsets and those that deviate significantly from the true offsets. This can be formulated as an instance of multiclass classification, with each potential offset serving as a class label. Train the predictive model to output a probability distribution over the possible offset values, using a contrastive loss function (e.g., triplet loss) to ensure the predicted probability distribution reflects the correct offset's similarity to the ground-truth value, while encouraging the other potential offsets to be deemed significantly less plausible. The additional contrastive loss is added to the standard RL objective.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original RSN-based method without contrastive loss, as well as with other robust offline RL methods that explicitly handle non-stationarity in observation functions, and examine the impact of varying the frequency of providing the contrastive signal during training.
COST: 3200
PREDICTION: Improve the effectiveness of RSN-based approaches in learning robust, accurate offset predictions in online deployment. If not properly tuned, the additional contrastive loss may degrade performance due to an increase in training complexity and the risk of overfitting to the contrastive signal.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adversarial Offset Quantization for Offline RL
PROPOSAL: We propose a two-stage approach to handle non-stationarity in offline RL. First, we define a novel quantity - the Offset Quantization Distance (OQD) - representing the disagreement between a trained agent's predictions on the stationary offline dataset and its predictions at test time under different possible offsets. Second, during test time, the agent learns a small neural network that takes in the estimated OQD and outputs a "quantized" offset, which is used to adjust the agent's predictions. This quantization process can be seen as a form of robust regression, and we motivate its theoretical and practical benefits via the concept of Minimal Description Length (MDL) and statistical learning theory.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: Train a standard offline RL algorithm on the stationary dataset; Baseline 2: Train offline RL with a pre-trained noise model that imitates the effect of offsets.
COST: 665.042
PREDICTION: This proposal has high potential for improving robustness by leveraging the OQD distance. However, it might struggle with high-dimensional state spaces and/or complex offset patterns, limiting its scalability.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Offset-Agnostic Offline Policy Distillation
PROPOSAL: Given the available stationary offline dataset, we attempt to "distill" a robust policy into a lightweight, offset-agnostic neural network that can withstand deviations in the observation function at test time. To achieve this, we route the input data from the offline dataset through both the robust policy and the original policy, and then compare their outputs using a suitable loss function. This encourages the robust policy to produce outputs that are invariant under different possible offsets, while still being consistent with the original policy's predictions on the stationary dataset.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: Train the original offline RL algorithm for longer; Baseline 2: Train a standard offline RL algorithm on the stationary dataset, then fine-tune a new network on a proxy dataset generated by applying random offsets to the observations.
COST: 1050
PREDICTION: This method may lead to improved robustness in offline RL, but its performance gain will likely depend heavily on the characteristics of the offset-agnostic learning objective.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Transition-Estimation Robustification (TER)
PROPOSAL: To address the partially observable test-time environment, we embed a transition estimation component that iteratively adjusts its internal parameters to better match the agent's observations and the empirically observed persistence of offsets across episodes. This allows it to distill insight from the offline data into a distribution over the offsets, which is then used to compute a likelihood of the observed states given the learned transition dynamics. This probability distribution can guide the agent's actions during test time and help to reject potentially incompatible observations.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: Implement a simple history-based approach to diagnostically measure residual mismatch and thus address the episodes; Baseline 2: Train an original offline RL algorithm on a augmented stationary dataset that already takes the transfer learning into account.
COST: 1345.678925
PREDICTION: Transition-Estimation Robustification (TER) has the potential to better handle complex time-series patterns in offsets, but precise tuning of its internal parameters may be challenging. It requires development of an internal transition-prediction framework, and its performance may well rely significantly on that.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adversarial Offset Quantization for Offline RL
PROPOSAL: We propose a two-stage approach to handle non-stationarity in offline RL. First, we define a novel quantity - the Offset Quantization Distance (OQD) - representing the disagreement between a trained agent's predictions on the stationary offline dataset and its predictions at test time under different possible offsets. Second, during test time, the agent learns a small neural network that takes in the estimated OQD and outputs a "quantized" offset, which is used to adjust the agent's predictions. This quantization process can be seen as a form of robust regression, and we motivate its theoretical and practical benefits via the concept of Minimal Description Length (MDL) and statistical learning theory.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: Train a standard offline RL algorithm on the stationary dataset; Baseline 2: Train offline RL with a pre-trained noise model that imitates the effect of offsets.
COST: 2000
PREDICTION: This proposal has high potential for improving robustness by leveraging the OQD distance. However, it might struggle with high-dimensional state spaces and/or complex offset patterns, limiting its scalability.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Offset-Agnostic Offline Policy Distillation
PROPOSAL: Given the available stationary offline dataset, we attempt to "distill" a robust policy into a lightweight, offset-agnostic neural network that can withstand deviations in the observation function at test time. To achieve this, we route the input data from the offline dataset through both the robust policy and the original policy, and then compare their outputs using a suitable loss function. This encourages the robust policy to produce outputs that are invariant under different possible offsets, while still being consistent with the original policy's predictions on the stationary dataset.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: Train the original offline RL algorithm for longer; Baseline 2: Train a standard offline RL algorithm on the stationary dataset, then fine-tune a new network on a proxy dataset generated by applying random offsets to the observations.
COST: 3150
PREDICTION: This method may lead to improved robustness in offline RL, but its performance gain will likely depend heavily on the characteristics of the offset-agnostic learning objective.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Transition-Estimation Robustification (TER)
PROPOSAL: To address the partially observable test-time environment, we embed a transition estimation component that iteratively adjusts its internal parameters to better match the agent's observations and the empirically observed persistence of offsets across episodes. This allows it to distill insight from the offline data into a distribution over the offsets, which is then used to compute a likelihood of the observed states given the learned transition dynamics. This probability distribution can guide the agent's actions during test time and help to reject potentially incompatible observations.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: Implement a simple history-based approach to diagnostically measure residual mismatch and thus address the episodes; Baseline 2: Train an original offline RL algorithm on a augmented stationary dataset that already takes the transfer learning into account.
COST: 4000
PREDICTION: Transition-Estimation Robustification (TER) has the potential to better handle complex time-series patterns in offsets, but precise tuning of its internal parameters may be challenging. It requires development of an internal transition-prediction framework, and its performance may well rely significantly on that.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISED: Transition-Estimation Robustification (TER)
PROPOSAL: To enhance the effectiveness of TER, we extend its transition estimation component by introducing an uncertainty-aware mechanism, allowing it to assess the reliability of its internal parameters and adapt a more conservative approach when observing drastic changes in the observation function. This can be achieved through integrating a state-of-the-art uncertainty estimation module, such as the Bayesian neural network or Monte Carlo dropout based reliability estimation, into the internal transition-prediction framework. This enlarged capability will enable TER to more effectively model uncertainty introduced by non-stationarity.
CONTROLS: REVISED: (i) a diagnosis framework for tracking TER predictions to distinguish between genuine outcomes and improbability terms ; (ii) Evaluation with standard cross-validation with a multi-objective approach that aims to find a set that balances accuracy and robustness .
COST: 4700
PREDICTION: This revised approach has the potential to improve TER's ability to handle ambiguous, unseen offset patterns, although thorough adaptation and development of the internal transition-prediction framework may be required to fully unleash its potential.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Impact of Offset Distribution on Offline Robustness
PROPOSAL: Experimentally evaluate the effect of different offset distribution shapes (e.g., uniform, normal, periodic, and real-world patterns) on the performance of standard offline RL algorithms when deployed under non-stationarity. Use a Gaussian process-based simulator to generate datasets with known offset distributions, and evaluate performance using mean reward and standard deviation of returns on a stationary test environment. Compare with a simple baseline that uses a fixed offset (i.e., always predicts a zero offset).
CONTROLS: Compare with self-play methods for Intergated Thoery Exploration (ITE) that are offline, i.e., no interaction is assumed when training the estimator of the distribution of the planner's values.
COST: 1500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The simulation will show that certain offset distributions (e.g., normal or periodic) result in better performance than others, and that standard offline RL algorithms perform surprisingly well under realistic non-stationarity – which might fail if we mistakenly assume that real-world offsets follow Gaussian patterns.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Reparameterized Q-Networks for Offline Robustness
PROPOSAL: Introduce a new type of Q-network that incorporates the unknown, per-dimension additive offsets as an additional latent parameter. The network is trained offline using policy evaluation with the reparameterized action-value function, where the offset is treated as a learned parameter rather than a fixed, known quantity. This approach aims to reduce the mismatch between the training and test environments by learning a function that is equivariant to the time-varying offsets.
CONTROLS: Compare with standard offline Q-learning, and investigate ablations without reparameterization or with different types of latent offset representations (e.g., categorical or sinusoidal).
COST: 2400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This reparameterization method shows improved offline robustness, especially when the offset patterns are complex and have a small number of samples, by implicitly modeling the time-varying structure. Failing assumptions in the likelihood model might lead to poor performance when the offsets are high-dimensional or not capturing intrinsic temporal patterns.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Offline Offset Learning with an Unknown, Time-Varying Structure
PROPOSAL: Design a novel, offline method for learning the time-varying, additive offsets from the data without explicit access to the offsets or their history. The approach leverages the fact that the agent's policy, learned from the stationary data, can be used as a proxy to infer the offsets. The method trains a separate network to predict the offsets from the agent's actions and current observations, while the agent's policy is updated based on the inferred offsets. This method combines the benefits of reparameterization with the ability to learn the offsets directly from the data.
CONTROLS: Test this method with various ablations, including removing the separate network or using a fixed offset estimation strategy, and also compare it with other offline methods.
COST: 3600 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This method will demonstrate significant offline robustness in scenarios with diverse offset patterns, particularly when the initial offset is zero or the offsets evolve at a moderate pace. However, it may struggle with high-dimensional or rapidly changing offsets due to limitations in learning the time-varying structure.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Transfer Learning for Offline Robustness in Non-Stationary Environments
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of transfer learning to improve the robustness of offline RL policies in non-stationary environments with time-varying offsets. The method involves training a base policy offline using a stationary dataset and then fine-tuning it using a small amount of data from a new, non-stationary environment with a similar offset distribution. This approach aims to leverage the knowledge learned from the base policy to quickly adapt to the changing environment.
CONTROLS: Test with different types of base policies (e.g., tabular or deep), offset distributions, and fine-tuning regimes (e.g., batch or online).
COST: 5000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Transfer learning can significantly improve offline robustness in non-stationary environments, especially when the fine-tuning data is plentiful and the offset distribution remains similar. However, its performance may degrade in scenarios with high-dimensional or highly non-stationary offsets, or when the fine-tuning process is too small.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploration-Exploitation Trade-off in Offline Robustness under Non-Stationarity
PROPOSAL: Investigate the exploration-exploitation trade-off in offline robustness under non-stationarity, where the agent must balance the cost of exploring different options versus exploiting the knowledge gained from the stationary training data. This will be achieved by incorporating an exploration-exploitation module into the existing offline robustness methods, which selects between exploration and exploitation based on the likelihood of the current policy to be robust to the changing environment.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the performance of the exploration-exploitation module on various non-stationary scenarios and compare it with other offline RL methods that do not explicitly address the exploration-exploitation trade-off.
COST: 6650.42 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The exploration-exploitation trade-off will be crucial in offline robustness under non-stationarity, and incorporating an explicit module to balance these two forces can significantly improve performance. However, if not designed carefully, this module may lead to over-exploration, reducing the overall robustness.

PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of transfer learning to improve the robustness of offline RL policies in non-stationary environments with time-varying offsets. The method involves training a base policy offline using a stationary dataset and then fine-tuning it using a small amount of data from a new, non-stationary environment with a similar offset distribution. This approach aims to leverage the knowledge learned from the base policy to quickly adapt to the changing environment.
CONTROLS: Test with different types of base policies (e.g., tabular or deep), offset distributions, and fine-tuning regimes (e.g., batch or online).

PREDICTION: Transfer learning can significantly improve offline robustness in non-stationary environments, especially when the fine-tuning data is plentiful and the offset distribution remains similar. However, its performance may degrade in scenarios with high-dimensional or highly non-stationary offsets, or when the fine-tuning process is too small.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: CoT-GAN: Combining Chain-of-Thought and Image-to-Image Translation Models for Unified Multi-Modal Reasoning
PROPOSAL: Train a chain-of-thought (CoT) based generative adversarial network (GAN) (https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.05939) on a multimodal dataset that includes text and images, where the generator produces both a reasoned text sequence and an image based on the input prompt and visual state. The discriminator evaluates both the coherence of the text sequence and the correctness of the generated image.

PREDICTION: This approach should significantly improve performance on reasoning-intensive tasks, such as visual question answering and jigsaw puzzle solving, while also producing more coherent image and text outputs. However, it may require large amounts of computational resources due to the need to train a GAN that can generate both text and images, and may struggle with long and complex reasoning chains.

TITLE: Unified Multi-Modal Reasoning with Efficient Sequence Visualization via Graph-Structured Tokens
PROPOSAL: We will evaluate a novel, sequence-visualization-based, sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) model, GraphVis, that conveys visual state transitions through graph-structured tokens, replacing traditional autoregressive generation with a more compact and flexible representation. GraphVis leverages a graph transformer architecture to learn and interactively generate visual state updates alongside textual logic within the same sequence. This representation enables more efficient sequence lengths and allows the model to learn from long-range dependencies with lower computational expense.

PROPOSAL: We propose to conduct experiments on leveraging stability-enhancing techniques commonly used in the domain of natural language processing, particularly with an LSTM/transformer language model conditioned on an auxiliary multimodal signal. We want to compare how these modalities affect multimodal language and image associations. Baseline will be transformer-based MLLM, and we exchange stability-enhancing techniques with Esim, conformer and MLM-based attention. We use a vision-language dataset established via simulated terrain environments including recognized scene objects. Its multimodal training patches (256 x 256) emphasize conditioning effects with test images represented as sprites 128 x 128. We evaluate the performance with NLL training per time-step, Number of vector collected when generate prediction and average averages criterion from all steps objective
CONTROLS: Transformers-Only MLLM; LSTM MLLM.
COST: 2070
PREDICTION: Conditional multimodal techniques improves multimodal coherence for prompt understanding, leading to fewer incoherent predictions downstream; however, sparse implementation might struggle on multiple object types and poor spectral analysis as told in sampled experiment.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Hierarchical Chain-of-Thought Reasoning through Vision-Language Transformers (H-CoTR)
PROPOSAL: We propose H-CoTR, a hierarchical architecture for multimodal chain-of-thought reasoning that leverages the strengths of vision-language transformers to tackle complex, visually grounded tasks. H-CoTR consists of a sequence of layers, each processing a different aspect of the input scene or prompt. We first apply an object detection module to identify relevant objects and contextualize the input scene. Next, a visual feature extractor captures salient visual features surrounding these objects. These features are then processed by a visual transformer, which generates a high-level understanding of the scene. Concurrently, a language transformer processes the input prompt and generates intermediate reasoning steps. The visual and language transformers communicate through a inter-modal attention module, allowing the model to align and integrate visual and textual information. We evaluate H-CoTR on a range of tasks, including visual question answering, instruction-based image editing, and jigsaw puzzle solving.
CONTROLS: ViLBERT milCot, ALBEF
COST: 2948.92952
PREDICTION: H-CoTR demonstrates competitive performance on various multimodal tasks and offers a new architectural perspective on the challenges of multimodal chain-of-thought reasoning; however, the computational costs of processing multiple layers may outweigh the benefits for extremely long sequence lengths.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Meta Learning for Visual Reasoning with Adversarial Sampling
PROPOSAL: We introduce a meta-learning approach to adapt visual reasoning models to new tasks and environments. Our method, MetaVis, leverages adversarial sampling to generate diverse and challenging input samples during training. We train a visual reasoning model on a set of pretext tasks, and then use the adversarial samples to adapt the model to a new task. MetaVis also employs a meta-controller that uses the trained model to predict the likelihood of each sample being a good fit for the target task. The meta-controller is trained to minimize the difference between the predicted likelihood and the actual likelihood of each sample being relevant to the target task. We evaluate MetaVis on a range of visual reasoning tasks, including visual question answering and instruction-based image editing.
CONTROLS: H-CoTR, IGRL
COST: 2851.8
PREDICTION: MetaVis shows promising results on various visual reasoning tasks and offers a flexible way to adapt to new tasks and environments, but its performance might be hindered by the need to generate adversarial samples and the computational costs of meta-learning.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Parallel Chain-of-Thought for Efficient Multimodal Reasoning
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel method for efficient multimodal reasoning by introducing a parallel chain-of-thought architecture. This architecture splits the reasoning process into two separate parallel chains: one for textual reasoning and another for visual reasoning. TITLE: Hierarchical Chain-of-Thought Reasoning through Vision-Language Transformers (H-CoTR)
PROPOSAL: We propose H-CoTR, a hierarchical architecture for multimodal chain-of-thought reasoning that leverages the strengths of vision-language transformers to tackle complex, visually grounded tasks. H-CoTR consists of a sequence of layers, each processing a different aspect of the input scene or prompt. We first apply an object detection module to identify relevant objects and contextualize the input scene. Next, a visual feature extractor captures salient visual features surrounding these objects. These features are then processed by a visual transformer, which generates a high-level understanding of the scene. Concurrently, a language transformer processes the input prompt and generates intermediate reasoning steps. The visual and language transformers communicate through a inter-modal attention module, allowing the model to align and integrate visual and textual information. We evaluate H-CoTR on a range of tasks, including visual question answering, instruction-based image editing, and jigsaw puzzle solving.

PROPOSAL: To alleviate the computational burden and improve the coherence of visual transitions, we propose a novel attention-aware visual module that dynamically selects relevant visual features based on the textual context. This module is integrated into the standard MLLM architecture and is trained jointly with the textual generation component. Specifically, we design the module to have a hierarchical attention mechanism that first focuses on the most relevant regions of the image based on a textual query, and then refines the attention over time based on the generated text output at each reasoning step.

TITLE: Efficient End-to-End Multi-Modal Chain-of-Thought Reasoning via Early Stopping and Knowledge Sharing
PROPOSAL: To address the training instability and computational burden associated with long multi-modal reasoning chains, we propose an efficient end-to-end multi-modal CoT reasoning framework that incorporates early stopping and knowledge sharing. Specifically, we employ a knowledge sharing mechanism that encourages the model to reuse previously generated intermediate results, and use a dynamic early stopping criterion that adaptively terminates the reasoning process when the model converges to a coherent solution. This framework is designed to alleviate the need for expensive cross-modal dynamics updates and stabilizes the training process.
CONTROLS: Baselines: standard MLLM architecture without knowledge sharing or early stopping; ablations: different early stopping criteria and knowledge sharing mechanisms
COST: 4800
PREDICTION: The proposed framework is anticipated to demonstrate improved training stability and efficiency, particularly on tasks with long and compositional reasoning chains, but may also lead to decreased performance if the early stopping criterion is overly conservative, preventing the model from exploring optimal solutions.

TITLE: Task-Agnostic Transfer Learning for Multi-Modal Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
PROPOSAL: To improve the model's generalizability and reduce overfitting on specific tasks, we propose a task-agnostic transfer learning method for multi-modal CoT reasoning. The approach involves pre-training the model on a large and diverse set of tasks, followed by fine-tuning on the target task. We define a set of task-agnostic loss functions that capture the commonality of multi-modal CoT reasoning across tasks, such as the consistency loss between intermediate results and the final output. Additionally, we employ a meta-reinforcement learning framework to adapt the model's policy and critic networks to the target task.

TITLE: Evaluating the Role of Input and Output Distillation in Multi-Modal Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
PROPOSAL: To further improve the model's performance and efficiency, we investigate the effectiveness of input and output distillation techniques in multi-modal CoT reasoning. Specifically, we explore two types of distillation: input distillation, which compresses the input visual data into a more compact representation, and output distillation, which compresses the model's output into a more concise form. We examine the impact of these distillation techniques on the model's performance, both individually and in combination, and explore different distillation methods, such as knowledge distillation and teacher-student learning.

This framework is designed to alleviate the need for expensive cross-modal dynamics updates and stabilizes the training process.
CONTROLS: Baselines: standard MLLM architecture without knowledge sharing or early stopping; ablations: different early stopping criteria and knowledge sharing mechanisms
COST: 14400
PREDICTION: The proposed framework is anticipated to demonstrate improved training stability and efficiency, particularly on tasks with long and compositional reasoning chains, but may also lead to decreased performance if the early stopping criterion is overly conservative, preventing the model from exploring optimal solutions.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Efficient End-to-End Multi-Modal Chain-of-Thought Reasoning via Early Stopping and Knowledge Sharing
PROPOSAL: To further enhance the efficiency and effectiveness of our proposed framework, we revise the early stopping criterion to adaptively balance between training stability and solution quality. This is achieved by incorporating a fidelity loss term that quantifies the model's adherence to the optimal solution found in previous iterations. The revised early stopping criterion uses a scaled-down version of the fidelity loss to dynamically adjust the stopping criterion, allowing the model to balance between solution quality and training stability. Additionally, we adapt the knowledge sharing mechanism to selectively share information from previous iterations based on their relevance to the current reasoning task.
CONTROLS: Baselines: standard MLLM architecture without knowledge sharing or early stopping; ablations: different early stopping criteria, fidelity loss functions, and knowledge sharing strategies
COST: 21600
PREDICTION: The revised framework is anticipated to demonstrate improved solution quality while maintaining training stability, particularly on tasks with long and compositional reasoning chains; potential failure: if the fidelity loss is set too aggressively, it may cause the model to over-explore and decrease training efficiency.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Task-Agnostic Transfer Learning for Multi-Modal Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
PROPOSAL: To improve the model's generalizability and reduce overfitting on specific tasks, we propose a task-agnostic transfer learning method for multi-modal CoT reasoning. The approach involves pre-training the model on a large and diverse set of tasks, followed by fine-tuning on the target task. We define a set of task-agnostic loss functions that capture the commonality of multi-modal CoT reasoning across tasks, such as the consistency loss between intermediate results and the final output. Additionally, we employ a meta-reinforcement learning framework to adapt the model's policy and critic networks to the target task.
CONTROLS: Baselines: standard MLLM architecture without transfer learning; ablations: different pre-training tasks, loss functions, and meta-learning strategies

PREDICTION: The proposed transfer learning method is anticipated to improve the model's transferability and generalizability across diverse tasks, but may require careful tuning to ensure the meta-reinforcement learning framework adapts to the target task without introducing overfitting; potential failure: if the pre-training and fine-tuning processes lead to an unstable or inconsistent policy update.

We examine the impact of these distillation techniques on the model's performance, both individually and in combination, and explore different distillation methods, such as knowledge distillation and teacher-student learning.

TITLE: Investigating Gaze Estimation from Text and Video
PROPOSAL: We design a multimodal fusion experiment that incorporates text and video inputs to estimate gaze points on an egocentric video dataset. We train a model that jointly optimizes gaze estimation and LLM performance using a multi-task loss function. This setup can benefit from a text-based description of the user's gaze, such as speech or notes, in conjunction with video input.

PREDICTION: The text-video fusion model should improve gaze estimation accuracy, particularly in noisy or low-quality video environments where the model can benefit from additional contextual information about the user's gaze. However, the impact may depend on the accuracy and quality of the text-based descriptions.

PROPOSAL: Investigate and compare the performance of state-of-the-art multimodal large language models (MLLMs) on various egocentric video question answering benchmarks, including those with and without gaze signals, on real-world datasets. Specifically, we will assess the ability of MLLMs to answer questions about a user's intentions and actions without relying heavily on complex prompting.
CONTROLS: Compare MLLM performance on different benchmarks, including Gaze-Aided Egocentric Question Answering (GAEQA) and Egocentric Action Recognition through Gaze-indexed Attention (EARtGA) datasets, with and without gaze signals.
COST: 2000
PREDICTION: Expected result: significant performance variation among MLLMs and benchmarks, highlighting the value of incorporating egocentric gaze signals. The result might fail if benchmarks lack sufficient gaze data or if the tested MLLMs are not adapted for egocentric video tasks.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Evaluating Egocentric Gaze-Aware MLLMs on Everyday Video Question Answering
PROPOSAL: We will evaluate the standard egocentric video question answering benchmark (Egocentric-QA) on a new gaze-aware variant of the general-purpose language model, BART. We will add a new module to the model's visual transformer to take the input gaze data and learn gaze-aware features. We will use a real-world egocentric video dataset, such as EGTEA Gaze+, and split it into development and test sets.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of the gaze-aware BART to a gaze-agnostic baseline, i.e., the original BART model without gaze input, on Egocentric-QA.
COST: 5000
PREDICTION: We expect to see significant improvements in accuracy due to the inclusion of gaze-aware features, especially in questions that require understanding the user's attention and focus. However, the benefit hinges on the model's ability to interpret the gaze signal, which may decrease in accuracy due to noisy or missing gaze data.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Investigating the Role of Gaze in Egocentric Visual Pre-training for MLLMs
PROPOSAL: We will investigate whether pre-training general-purpose MLLMs (such as BART and RoBERTa) on egocentric video datasets with gaze annotations can improve their understanding of user intent and attention. We will train a gaze-pre-trained model on the EGTEA Gaze+ dataset and compare its performance on Egocentric-QA to the gaze-aware model from proposal 1 and standard pre-training on exocentric video data.
CONTROLS: We will evaluate all models on the standard Egocentric-QA benchmark and their respective baselines (gaze-aware BART and standard BART).
COST: 6000
PREDICTION: Pre-training on egocentric video with gaze annotations will provide the model with valuable information about user attention and focus, leading to improved performance on Egocentric-QA. However, the pre-training dataset may not fully capture the complexities of real-world gaze data, limiting the model's transferability.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Gaze Estimation and Temporal Alignment for Egocentric Video Understanding
PROPOSAL: We will develop a gaze estimation module that outputs gaze coordinates for each frame in egocentric videos. We will then temporally align the gaze estimates with the visual features extracted by the model, ensuring that the gaze-aware features are synchronized with the corresponding video frames. This alignment is crucial for effectively exploiting gaze cues in MLLMs.
CONTROLS: We will evaluate the impact of suboptimal temporal alignment on gaze-aware feature extraction and assess the performance of different gaze estimation methods in the context of Egocentric-QA.
COST: 6650.42
PREDICTION: The quality of gaze estimation will directly impact the performance of gaze-aware features. While state-of-the-art gaze estimation models may produce accurate results, their performance may degrade in real-world datasets with varied lighting, occlusions, and other effects that compromise gaze tracking accuracy.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Evaluating Egocentric Gaze-Aware MLLMs on Everyday Video Question Answering
PROPOSAL: We will evaluate the standard egocentric video question answering benchmark (Egocentric-QA) on a new gaze-aware variant of the general-purpose language model, BART. We will add a new module to the model's visual transformer to take the input gaze data and learn gaze-aware features. We will use a real-world egocentric video dataset, such as EGTEA Gaze+, and split it into development and test sets.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of the gaze-aware BART to a gaze-agnostic baseline, i.e., the original BART model without gaze input, on Egocentric-QA.
COST: 15000
PREDICTION: We expect to see significant improvements in accuracy due to the inclusion of gaze-aware features, especially in questions that require understanding the user's attention and focus. However, the benefit hinges on the model's ability to interpret the gaze signal, which may decrease in accuracy due to noisy or missing gaze data.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Investigating the Role of Gaze in Egocentric Visual Pre-training for MLLMs
PROPOSAL: We will investigate whether pre-training general-purpose MLLMs (such as BART and RoBERTa) on egocentric video datasets with gaze annotations can improve their understanding of user intent and attention. We will train a gaze-pre-trained model on the EGTEA Gaze+ dataset and compare its performance on Egocentric-QA to the gaze-aware model from proposal 1 and standard pre-training on exocentric video data.
CONTROLS: We will evaluate all models on the standard Egocentric-QA benchmark and their respective baselines (gaze-aware BART and standard BART).
COST: 18000
PREDICTION: Pre-training on egocentric video with gaze annotations will provide the model with valuable information about user attention and focus, leading to improved performance on Egocentric-QA. However, the pre-training dataset may not fully capture the complexities of real-world gaze data, limiting the model's transferability.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Gaze Estimation and Temporal Alignment for Egocentric Video Understanding
PROPOSAL: We will develop a gaze estimation module that outputs gaze coordinates for each frame in egocentric videos. We will then temporally align the gaze estimates with the visual features extracted by the model, ensuring that the gaze-aware features are synchronized with the corresponding video frames. This alignment is crucial for effectively exploiting gaze cues in MLLMs.
CONTROLS: We will evaluate the impact of suboptimal temporal alignment on gaze-aware feature extraction and assess the performance of different gaze estimation methods in the context of Egocentric-QA.
COST: 20000
PREDICTION: The quality of gaze estimation will directly impact the performance of gaze-aware features. While state-of-the-art gaze estimation models may produce accurate results, their performance may degrade in real-world datasets with varied lighting, occlusions, and other effects that compromise gaze tracking accuracy.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Gaze Estimation and Temporal Alignment for Egocentric Video Understanding
PROPOSAL: We will expand the scope of proposal 3 to not only develop a gaze estimation module but also investigate the impact of different gaze estimation methods on the performance of MLLMs in egocentric video question answering. We will compare the accuracy of different gaze estimation models (e.g., multi-task learning, attention-based approaches) and evaluate their effect on the model's ability to understand user intent and attention.
CONTROLS: We will evaluate the performance of different gaze estimation models in the context of Egocentric-QA, comparing their impact on gaze-aware feature extraction and the model's overall performance.
COST: 22000
PREDICTION: Different gaze estimation methods will vary in their accuracy and robustness, affecting the model's ability to understand user intent and attention. We expect that more accurate gaze estimation methods will lead to better performance in egocentric video question answering, but the model's overall performance may also depend on other factors, such as gaze-aware feature extraction and temporal alignment techniques.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Analyzing the Impact of Gaze Accuracy on Egocentric MLLMs
PROPOSAL: We will systematically analyze the effect of gaze accuracy on the performance of MLLMs in egocentric video question answering. We will generate synthetic gaze data with varying levels of accuracy and incorporate it into the Egocentric-QA benchmark. This will allow us to evaluate how MLLMs generalize to different gaze accuracy scenarios, shedding light on the robustness of gaze-aware features in real-world applications.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of MLLMs on Egocentric-QA with different levels of gaze accuracy, from controlled synthetic data to real-world eye-tracking data.
COST: 24000
PREDICTION: While gaze-aware features will improve model performance in egocentric video question answering, the influence of gaze accuracy on model performance will be significant. We anticipate that models will be less accurate in scenarios with noisy or missing gaze data, highlighting the importance of developing robust gaze-aware features that can generalize to a wide range of gaze accuracy levels.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: User-Centric Evaluation of Egocentric MLLMs through Human-Robot Interaction
PROPOSAL: We will design a human-robot interaction (HRI) experiment to assess the effectiveness of egocentric MLLMs in real-world user-centric scenarios. Participants will interact with a robot companion equipped with an MLLM, providing feedback on the robot's ability to understand their intentions and attention. We will evaluate the impact of gaze-aware features on user satisfaction and task completion rates.
CONTROLS: We will compare the user-centric performance of egocentric MLLMs with and without gaze-aware features in various real-world HRI scenarios.

However, user-centered evaluations may also reveal limitations of the current MLLMs, such as potential biases or assumptions about user intentions, highlighting areas for future model improvement.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Egocentric MLLMs on Exocentric Visual Understanding
PROPOSAL: We will examine how well current multimodal large language models (MLLMs) perform on standard exocentric visual question answering (VQA) benchmarks, despite being primarily trained on egocentric data. This will serve as a baseline for research focused on improving the egocentric-centric performance of MLLMs. We will use a combination of existing datasets (e.g., VQA, Visual Genome, Hateful Memes) and metrics (e.g., accuracy, F1-score, BERTScore). Controls will include various baseline models (e.g., BERT, RoBERTa, Vision Transformer).
CONTROLS: BERT, RoBERTa, Vision Transformer
COST: 12000
PREDICTION: Current egocentric MLLMs may already show strong performance on exocentric VQA benchmarks due to transfer learning effects, but still may underperform due to the lack of egocentric-specific annotations and the ambiguities in scene contexts. They might fail in correctly predicting visual attributes for the person in the frame in heavily packed environments.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Egocentric Video Question Answering with Gaze Signals
PROPOSAL: We propose to conduct an extensive study investigating how MLLMs perform on egocentric video question answering benchmarks (issue 9-I in [1]), with a focus on this task's difficulty in the absence of gaze signals. We will leverage the recent egocentric video question answering benchmarks (e.g., EPIC-Kitchens, EGVQAV, and Actor-ActionNet) to understand the performance gap of MLLMs in understanding user intent, identifying gaze-related challenges, and pushing the limits of state-of-the-art models. For this phase, we plan to split our evaluation into three controlled comparisons with existing MLLMs (BiT, CLIPViL-BERT, and GazeGPT): (1) performance on egocentric video question answering tasks, (2) performance when evaluated without gaze cues, and (3) baseline performance using human-annotated gaze.
CONTROLS: BiT, CLIPViL-BERT, GazeGPT (human-annotated gaze baseline included)
COST: 106.8
PREDICTION: This study would likely highlight the MLLMs’ weakness in interpreting gaze cues and reveal that MLLMs exhibit significant gaps when handling egocentric video question answering tasks with and without gaze data - but performance we get for BiT and CLIPViL-BERT without gaze data is significantly better than the one without our new human landmark model. However, introducing inaccurate or missing gaze cues may lead to inconsistent model performance due to the task's inherent difficulty.

TITLE: EG UserRole Model + Gaze Modality Fusion
PROPOSAL: To complement the previous study, we propose adding a multimodal model experiment that exploits gaze and egocentric video hyperlinking for gaining more informative user intent from egocentric videos. Our approach revolves around fusing two models: EGUserRole, a pre-existing model designed to map the user's role and ego-centric action into structured semantic representations, and TP-Gaze model, our original extension of the popular BERT-Resize-GAN estimation architecture. This creates the first egocentric multimodal model that not only provides useful structural representations to phrases of our questions from action knowledge as detected from egocentric vision but also exerts a constant conditioning force of the your visual spread, locally conditioned by sensed visual and phenomenological human gaze parameters. TITLE: Evaluating Gaze Data Quality and Its Impact on Egocentric Video Question Answering
PROPOSAL: The previous studies highlighted the potential benefits of incorporating gaze data into MLLMs for egocentric video question answering. However, the effectiveness of gaze data can vary significantly depending on its quality and accuracy. Our new proposal aims to investigate how different qualities and accuracy levels of gaze data impact MLLM performance on egocentric video question answering tasks. We will generate a set of synthetic gaze data with varying qualities (accuracy, coverage, and resolution) and evaluate how it affects MLLM performance compared to using more accurate human-collected gaze data. This will provide insights into the sensitivity of MLLMs to gaze data quality and inform strategies for improving gaze-based MLLM architectures.

TITLE: Developing a Metric for Evaluating Egocentric Video Question Answering Performance with Gaze Signals
PROPOSAL: While the previous studies have demonstrated the potential benefits of incorporating gaze signals into MLLMs for egocentric video question answering, there is a lack of suitable metrics for evaluating performance in this task. Our new proposal aims to develop a novel metric that captures the synergy between gaze signals and the understanding of egocentric video content. The metric should provide a comprehensive evaluation of the model's ability to infer user intent and actions from the visual context and gaze data. We will investigate different combinations of standard metrics (e.g., accuracy, precision, recall) and gaze-specific metrics (e.g., gaze attention, fixation duration) to develop a robust and interpretable evaluation framework.

TITLE: Investigating Egocentric Video Question Answering with Gaze Signals
PROPOSAL: We propose to conduct an extensive study investigating how MLLMs perform on egocentric video question answering benchmarks (issue 9-I in [1]), with a focus on this task's difficulty in the absence of gaze signals. We will leverage the recent egocentric video question answering benchmarks (e.g., EPIC-Kitchens, EGVQAV, and Actor-ActionNet) to understand the performance gap of MLLMs in understanding user intent, identifying gaze-related challenges, and pushing the limits of state-of-the-art models. For this phase, we plan to split our evaluation into three controlled comparisons with existing MLLMs (BiT, CLIPViL-BERT, and GazeGPT): (1) performance on egocentric video question answering tasks, (2) performance when evaluated without gaze cues, and (3) baseline performance using human-annotated gaze.

However, introducing inaccurate or missing gaze cues may lead to inconsistent model performance due to the task's inherent difficulty.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Layer-wise Modality Similarity Analysis for AR UMMs
PROPOSAL: Train an AR UMM with modality-shared transformer layers on the WebVQA benchmark, and compute the layer-wise Cosine Similarity (CS) between text and image gradders to quantify modality conflicts. We will also ablate the normalization scheme for the visual input token embeddings, examining if CS improves or worsens when using instance normalization, group normalization, or batch normalization.
CONTROLS: Baseline AR UMM with no normalization scheme change, and a parallel set of experiments with vision and text inputs separated in two distinct transformer blocks.
COST: 1000
PREDICTION: Layer-wise analysis will reveal modality conflicts increase through the depth of the network, with the largest discrepancy observed between layers 5-7. Ablation studies will show instance normalization improves CS, while group and batch normalization degrade it.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Layer-wise Modality Similarity Analysis for AR UMMs
PROPOSAL: Train an AR UMM with modality-shared transformer layers on the WebVQA benchmark, and compute the layer-wise Cosine Similarity (CS) between text and image gradders to quantify modality conflicts. We will also ablate the normalization scheme for the visual input token embeddings, examining if CS improves or worsens when using instance normalization, group normalization, or batch normalization.
CONTROLS: Baseline AR UMM with no normalization scheme change, and a parallel set of experiments with vision and text inputs separated in two distinct transformer blocks.
COST: 3000
PREDICTION: Layer-wise analysis will reveal modality conflicts increase through the depth of the network, with the largest discrepancy observed between layers 5-7. Ablation studies will show instance normalization improves CS, while group and batch normalization degrade it.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Empirical Study on Visual Tokenization Schemes for AR UMMs
PROPOSAL: Implement three visual tokenization schemes – eleven neuron (11N), seventeen neuron (17N), and encapsulated channel-wise (ECC) – in an AR UMM and compare their effects on visual question answering task performance on Visual 7W.
CONTROLS: Use the baseline AR UMM implemented in proposal 1 and compare the performance of the three visual tokenization schemes.
COST: 45000
PREDICTION: The eleven neuron and seventeen neuron schemes will exhibit comparable performance improvements over the baseline AR UMM, whereas the ECC scheme will show better performance and computational efficiency, but with potential loss in semantic expressiveness, which may impact future tasks.

ACTION: ADD

PREDICTION: Gradient normalization will reduce modality conflicts detected by proposal 1's layer-wise analysis and improve performance in all tasks, but with diminishing returns as optimization techniques target modality conflicts more directly, suggesting employment of multiple techniques can offer the best trade-off between improvement and complexity.
