ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Gradient Conflict Analysis in AR UMMs
PROPOSAL: Investigate the layer-wise gradients conflicts in a pre-trained autoregressive UMM, and compute the frequency and magnitude of inter-modal conflicts in both text-to-image generation and visual question answering tasks on the LLaMA + Coconut UMM model fine-tuned on the DeshawedCOCO dataset.
CONTROLS: Ablation study with two controls: 1. UMM model without gradient conflict analysis, 2. UMM model with gradient conflict analysis decoupled from the layer-wise weighting, to assess the impact of conflict reduced and only weighting on performance.
COST: 4000
PREDICTION: Expected to find high frequency and magnitude of inter-modal conflicts at the transformer encoder layers, particularly in visual question answering, which correlates with degraded performance in both tasks. However, optimization techniques like weight sharing and masked-mini-batching may moderate these conflicts, enabling improved joint training efficiency.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Layered Gradient Weighting in AR UMMs
PROPOSAL: Develop a layer-wise weighting scheme for autoregressive UMMs that differentiates gradient contributions from text and image modalities, using a novel Bayes-by-Backprop regime with varying hyperpriors for each modality. Test the scheme on the existing Gradient Conflict Analysis experiment, to see if it reduces inter-modal conflicts and improves training efficiency.
CONTROLS: Comparison to the gradient conflict analysis alone, without weighting (Proposal 1); control model performance where weighted update gradients while critical, versus giving all modalities benign weights.
COST: 6000
PREDICTION: Expected to show that the weight scheme noticeably reduces conflicts at all transformer encoder layers, which improves the UMMs' ability to generate coherent images for text-to-image tasks and provides accurate answers for visual question answering tasks, even when strongly augmenting gradients for better rate of divergent objectives optimization.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Revising Disentangled High-Level Representations for Image Synthesis
PROPOSAL: Revisit the idea of Disentangled latent Z spaces to mitigate inter-modal conflicts in AR UMMs for Image-to-Image synthesis tasks. Instead of using a complex VQ-VAE tokenizer, propose a simpler approach based on Conditioning Decoder (CD) method, which generates images by conditioned decoders that transform disentangled text embeddings to image representations. Test the CD method on both text-to-image and visual question answering tasks.
CONTROLS: Compare the CD method's performance to the baseline of Proposal 1, as well as a version of Proposal 2 that has disentangled latent Z spaces but no layered gradient weighting.
COST: 10000
PREDICTION: Expected to find that disentangled latent Z spaces with the CD method can greatly reduce inter-modal conflicts and improve the performance of AR UMMs on both text-to-image synthesis and visual question answering tasks, especially for scenes with multiple objects in complex backgrounds.

TITLE: Experiments with Mixture-of-Experts Architecture
PROPOSAL: Explore the incorporation of a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture into the autoregressive UMM, where each modality (text and image) is handled by a dedicated expert, and a gate selects the output of the most relevant expert for each time step. TITLE: Revised Disentangled High-Level Representations for Image Synthesis
PROPOSAL: Revisit the idea of Disentangled latent Z spaces to mitigate inter-modal conflicts in AR UMMs for Image-to-Image synthesis tasks. Instead of using a complex VQ-VAE tokenizer, propose a simpler approach based on Conditioning Decoder (CD) method, which generates images by conditioned decoders that transform disentangled text embeddings to image representations. Test the CD method on both text-to-image and visual question answering tasks on the Meta AI + UMM model fine-tuned on the Object-Class dataset.
CONTROLS: Compare the CD method's performance to the baseline of Proposal 1, as well as a version of Proposal 2 that has disentangled latent Z spaces but no layered gradient weighting.
COST: 25000
PREDICTION: Expected to find that disentangled latent Z spaces with the CD method can greatly reduce inter-modal conflicts and improve the performance of AR UMMs on both text-to-image synthesis and visual question answering tasks, especially for scenes with multiple objects in complex backgrounds.

PROPOSAL: Explore the incorporation of a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture into the autoregressive UMM, where each modality (text and image) is handled by a dedicated expert, and a gate selects the output of the most relevant expert for each time step. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploring Modality-Specific Interfences in Autoregressive Unified Models
PROPOSAL: Compare the performance of a modality-shared AR UMM (for instance, a VQ-VAE-based AR model combined with a text-to-image GAN's language decoder) against a modality-specific AR UMM variant where each modality has its own transformer branch with shared token embeddings and learned weight ties across branches (like in shared autoencoders). We'll use Clipart30k, VQVAE2, and a modified Webdataset as training and validation datasets.
CONTROLS: Modality-agnostic sharing (modality-shared UMM), modality-specific sharing with separate transformers (MS-UMM) without weight ties, and MS-UMM with weight ties (IS-UMM).
COST: 116.8 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The modality-shared AR UMM will outperform modality-specific ones on text-to-image generation, but outperform only on image editing and overall VQA when relegating the two to separate autoregressive streams in the MS-UMM, and weight tied IS-UMM might not overcome the modality-conflicts fully.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Layer-Wise Modality Conflict Analysis in Transformer-Based AR UMMs
PROPOSAL: Investigate the modality conflicts in AR UMMs layer-wise, using a multi-resolution framework that tracks both magnitude and variance of token embeddings at each transformer layer. We will examine which layer contributes the most to conflict magnitude and use mixup regularizations toлачencentivate representation equivariance. Training and validation datasets will be the same as in proposal 1.
CONTROLS: Baseline AR UMM, proposed multi-resolution framework, and one ablation where all layers are ignored except the output layer, mixing tokens before feeding them to the next layer.
COST: 140 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We'd find significant contributions from deeper layers for conflict magnitude and high variance for input and output layers, confirming our expectations and identifying areas for modality-specific attention modifications to mitigate conflicts.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Autoregressive Unified Model with Modality-Conditioned Transformer Weights
PROPOSAL: Introduce a conditioned drop-path technique that adjusts the transformer weights' importance based on modality relevance during inference, dividing weights into global and modality-conditioned sets, aiming to resolve conflicts by essentially segregating what each modality branch contributes. The method would then choose weights stochastically using a learned sampling strategy localized to each modality. Experiments will be conducted with the same AR UMM and training/validation setups from the first two proposals.
CONTROLS: Unweighted transformer, conditioned drop-path with equal weight sampling (UD-W), and conditioned drop-path with modality-dependent weight sampling (UD-M).
COST: 160 GPU-hours

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Modality-Cascading for Joint Vision-Language Generation
PROPOSAL: Propose an adaptive modality-cascading mechanism to judiciously channel the information flow between vision and language streams in AR UMMs, alleviating inter-modal conflicts by adaptive selector networks that balance the trade-off between information preservation and conflict minimization during joint vision-language generation. Empirical evaluations on datasets such as Conceptual Captions and Object Parts will demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed model.
CONTROLS: Proposed adaptive modality-cascading model, vanilla AR UMM, and baselines with fixed information flow channels.
COST: 273 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The adaptive modality-cascading mechanism can remarkably improve the joint vision-language generation performance by adaptively optimizing the information flow between vision and language streams, reducing inter-modal conflicts and producing more coherent outputs.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Assessing Gradient Interference in Modality-Shared AR UMMs
PROPOSAL: We'll conduct a systematic analysis of gradient disagreement between text and vision modalities in a modality-shared AR UMM using the COCO-Text dataset and the MLM objective as our starting point for text and image inputs. We will compute the gradient-layer-wise interference metrics for modality-shared and modality-separated transformer stacks. This will provide us with a deeper understanding of the root causes of the interference.
CONTROLS: We'll compare against a variant of the Child-AR UMM trained on COCO-Text with a modality-separated transformer stack as a baseline.
COST: 50
PREDICTION: We expect to find significant gradient interference effects particularly in the intermediate layers, and where they fail is in the extent to which the modality-separation impacts the overall performance of the model, and whether these effects are task-dependent.

PROPOSAL: We'll extend the previous analysis to focus on the specific tasks of text-to-image generation and visual question answering using the Laina dataset and the VQA/VQG evaluation metrics. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Comprehensive Benchmarking for Emotion Reasoning in Audiovisual Emotion Recognition
PROPOSAL: We design a benchmark that combines two existing benchmarks – AV- EmotionNet for emotion recognition and CO MuCo for multimodal hallucination – to test the performance of audiovisual MLLMs in emotion reasoning. The benchmark includes a set of samples from various audiovisual datasets, including COCO, AVQA, and AG(dictionary) using identified true positives and negatives.
CONTROLS: As baseline models, we will use a standard vision transformer and a standard audio transformer to respectively model the visual cues and audio cues, then multiply their outputs to predict the emotion.
COST: 5000
PREDICTION: Our benchmark improves over existing benchmarks by providing a more diverse and challenging test set, with a potential performance drop of 5-10% for current state-of-the-art models, and will succeed in detecting hallucinations by at least 20% compared to current methods. It may fail to accommodate the full diversity of human emotional expressions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Effective Regularization for Reducing Hallucinations in Emotion Reasoning MLLMs
PROPOSAL: We introduce a multi-task learning framework that trains a single MLLM to perform Seq2Seq alignment from audiovisual input to a detailed, hierarchical description, and to predict bare emotion description. We then apply a textual stabilization loss leveraging the set of plausible positive (pp), entailed negative (en), and disentailed negative (d-neg) training goods (a technique derived from TextSF). 
CONTROLS: This would compare to models trained using two task learning that learns from raw tasks.
COST: 11000
PREDICTION: When generalized to a variety of audio-visual emotion scenario testing, it'll outperform contemporary models trained by training raw prediction tasks, preserving 60 percent+ predictive capability than their non-stabilized state, suggesting possible early failure in low-audio-visual information settings.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Graph Attention-based Knowledge Graph Embedding for Emotion Reasoning
PROPOSAL: We leverage a graph attention mechanism to generate knowledge graph embeddings for visual and auditory attributes, which are then fused to predict emotions. The key benefits of this approach are that it allows us to capture complex relationships between different attributes and to adapt to varying attribute combinations.
CONTROLS: Baseline experiments will compare against various graph attention models and knowledge graph embedding methods to demonstrate the advantage of our approach.
COST: 17700
PREDICTION: It should significantly outperform existing emotion reasoning models on more challenging datasets by at least 8% and by 15% on test cases involving complex associations between features. However, it may suffer from overfitting when trained with a limited number of instances.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Emotion-Aware Audio-Visual Model for Hallucination Suppression
PROPOSAL: We propose an attention-based multimodal fusion framework that emphasizes the relevance of audio-visual cues to emotion reasoning. This framework captures the logical relationships between emotions, the audio-visual input, and hallucinated cues. We establish an emotion-driven attention mechanism to adaptively modulate the fusion process and restrict hallucinated outputs to only those emotionally-grounded.
CONTROLS: Baseline experiments will compare against current multimodal fusion methods and emotion-agnostic attention models.
COST: 20400
PREDICTION: By reasoning more robustly about the relationship between audio-visual cues and emotions, we expect the proposed emotion-aware framework to effectively reduce hallucinations by at least 15% on existing benchmarks, making it more reliable for applications where accurate emotion reasoning is critical.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluation Benchmark for Audiovisual Emotion Reasoning
PROPOSAL: Introduce a new benchmark dataset "AVERD" (AudioVisual Emotion Reasoning Dataset), consisting of 10,000 audiovisual clips annotated with emotion labels and corresponding detailed emotional descriptions. For evaluation, we will use a fusion of human evaluation, automated metrics for accuracy and exact matching, and a set of auto-generated counterfactuals to test the model's ability to ground emotion predictions in actual audiovisual cues. We will use this benchmark to evaluate MLLMs on their capacity to reason about emotions, avoid hallucinations, and accurately generate emotion-related keywords.
CONTROLS: 
- Compare to existing emotion recognition benchmarks such as emotioNet and AVD.
- Ablation study on the impact of human evaluation weight on overall benchmark score.
- Use a non-associative NN baseline trained only on audio and visual features without any multimodal fusion.
COST: 1200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected results will include improved accountability and clarity in evaluating audiovisual emotion reasoning abilities, with some models underperforming on counterfactuals and a potentially higher degree of hallucinations on more complex scenarios.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Counterfactual Robustness in Audiovisual Emotion Reasoning
PROPOSAL: Investigate the robustness of audiovisual MLLMs to counterfactual scenarios by introducing a new counterfactual augmentation technique to the AVERD dataset. This technique will modify the audiovisual input by removing specific cues (e.g., facial expressions, background noise) or replacing them with equivalent or worse hallucinations while keeping the emotion label and description the same. We will evaluate the robustness of models to these counterfactuals and measure the increase in hallucinations. We will specifically investigate the impact of the number and types of removed cues on the model's performance.
CONTROLS: 
- Compare robustness to object-level hallucination benchmarks like COCO-HHA.
- Evaluate the effect of different levels of noise and argumentation on the counterfactual augmentation.
- Compare to NoTac models, which has theoretical strong robustness.
COST: 1800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The models that perform best on AVERD will likely underperform or strongly deteriorate on the counterfactual-augmented version, indicating that they may rely on spurious associations between audiovisual cues and emotions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analysis of Cue-Weighting in Audiovisual Emotion Generation
PROPOSAL: Investigate the cue-weighting mechanism in multimodal large language models by analyzing the attention weights assigned to different audio and visual cues. We will use a modified AVERD dataset and train various MLLMs to generate emotion-related keywords. Then, we will analyze the attention weights to understand how the models weigh different cues when making emotion predictions. We will particularly investigate how models assign weights to cues that are more relevant to the emotion (e.g., tears for sadness) versus those that are less relevant (e.g., ambient music for sadness).
CONTROLS: 
- Compare the distribution of attention weights to object-level attention weights on COCO-HHA dataset.
- Evaluate the impact of different attention mechanisms (e.g., Transformer, BERT) on cue-weighting.
- Compare to a baseline model that only attends to visual or audio features separately.
COST: 2400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The analysis of cue-weighting will provide valuable insights into the mechanisms driving audiovisual emotion reasoning in MLLMs, potentially revealing instances of cue-emotion associations that correspond to reasoning errors.

TITLE: Improved Real-World Emotion Hallucinations Dataset Collection and Utilization
PROPOSAL: To further improve the quality and utilization of the Echo dataset, we propose to integrate a self-supervised learning framework to identify and correct potential hallucinations and biases in the collected data. This framework will leverage the model's ability to generate plausible audio-visual sequences and compare them with the original data to identify inconsistencies. Additionally, we will incorporate a revision protocol to ensure that any detected hallucinations or biases are corrected by trained annotators before being incorporated into the dataset. This will result in a high-quality dataset that accurately reflects real-world emotions and their associated cues.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multitask Audio-Visual Attention Mechanism for Emotion Reasoning
PROPOSAL: To improve the ability of audio-visual emotion models to focus on relevant cues and reduce hallucinations, we propose the development of a multitask audio-visual attention mechanism for emotion reasoning. This mechanism will be designed to learn to attend to different types of cues (e.g., visual, auditory, or text-based) based on the specific emotion-inducing scenario, while also using a separate evaluation branch to identify potential hallucinations and focus the attention mechanism on the most relevant cues. The mechanism will be trained using a novel multitask loss function that balances the performance on both the emotion recognition task and the hallucination detection task.
CONTROLS: We compare the performance of the proposed multitask audio-visual attention mechanism to current state-of-the-art models on datasets such as Echo, Affective Distances, AVEC, and SAVEE.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Emotion-Specific Hallucinations in Audiovisual MLLMs
PROPOSAL: Conduct experiments on the existing emotion-oriented MLLMs using a set of novel, semi-automated analysis tools to identify emotion-specific hallucinations. We design new metrics, such as `hallucination score` and `cue exploaibility ratio`, to quantify the severity and relevance of hallucinations. Evaluate these models on a subset of the Audiovisual Emotion Recognition (AER) dataset and the Large-Scale Audiovisual Emotion Reasoning (LASER) dataset.
CONTROLS: Compare against three state-of-the-art emotion-oriented MLLMs: EmoEV, EmoViT, and EmoMLM. Ablate each model's visual and auditory components to assess their individual contributions to hallucinations. Use accuracy and F1-score as baselines to evaluate emotion recognition performance.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect EmoEV to exhibit the most hallucinations, while EmoViT to perform the best in terms of emotion recognition accuracy. Ablating visual components will significantly diminish hallucinations for EmoMLM, highlighting its overreliance on text priors.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Improving Emotion Reasoning with Audiovisual Cues
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of attention weights to identify the relevance of audiovisual cues in emotion predictions. Train a variant of EmoEV with visually and audibly attention-aware modules that selectively weigh input cues. Transfer this strategy to EmoViT and EmoMLM to encourage more accurate and cue-specific emotion predictions. Evaluate the models on the LASER and AER datasets using metrics like weighted-F1-score and hint-weighted accuracy.
CONTROLS: Implement a baseline variant of EmoEV with attention weights fixed to a random distribution, to assess the impact of cue weighting on hallucination rates. Compare the performance of the weighted variants against the original models in both metric and convergence speed.

PREDICTION: The models with weighted attention mechanisms will outperform the original variants in terms of weighted-F1-score, but may still be susceptible to minor hallucinations. Transferability to EmoViT and EmoMLM will reveal varying degrees of success, as their architectures may be more susceptible to overfitting or data inefficiency.

TITLE: Evaluating Emotion-Specific Hallucinations in Audiovisual MLLMs
PROPOSAL: Conduct experiments on the existing emotion-oriented MLLMs using a set of novel, semi-automated analysis tools to identify emotion-specific hallucinations. We design new metrics, such as `hallucination score` and `cue exploaibility ratio`, to quantify the severity and relevance of hallucinations. Evaluate these models on a subset of the Audiovisual Emotion Recognition (AER) dataset and the Large-Scale Audiovisual Emotion Reasoning (LASER) dataset.
CONTROLS: Compare against three state-of-the-art emotion-oriented MLLMs: EmoEV, EmoViT, and EmoMLM. Ablate each model's visual and auditory components to assess their individual contributions to hallucinations. Use accuracy and F1-score as baselines to evaluate emotion recognition performance.

PREDICTION: We expect EmoEV to exhibit the most hallucinations, while EmoViT to perform the best in terms of emotion recognition accuracy. Ablating visual components will significantly diminish hallucinations for EmoMLM, highlighting its overreliance on text priors.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE:  Learning to Infer Transition Rewards from Ground-Truth Labels
PROPOSAL: Experimentally investigate the effectiveness of Adversarial Imitation Learning (AIL)-based approach to infer a dense, informative process reward signal at each turn by learning to predict label scores for each action taken by the search agent. Specifically, we'll train an auxiliary labeling model on ground truth labels for a validation set, then use this model to infer labels for the input sequence based on the current rollout, providing labels for AIL to predict rewards.
CONTROLS: Compare to baseline that uses one-hot outcome-based rewards, with and without auxiliary labeling model, and a few regularizer techniques to prevent over-fitting.
COST: 1000
PREDICTION: We expect to observe a significant boost in sample efficiency and accuracy due to the learned process rewards that allow the agent to focus on productive intermediate turns, but may struggle with noisy labeling and potential over-fitting of the auxiliary model.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE:  Invariant Reward Shaping via Serviceable Policy Regularization
PROPOSAL: Theoretically investigate a method to regularize the search agent's policy to ensure that its turn-level rewards align with the desired outcome-based objective, while encouraging exploration of different intermediate trajectories. We propose to achieve this through a serviceable policy regularization term added to the RL objective, which computes the product of the current policy probabilities with the outcomes' gradients with respect to the state-action pairs. The regularization term is expected to locally align the rewards with the outcome-based objective, preventing reward hacking and providing a more informative learning signal.
CONTROLS: Establish convergence bounds and prove invariance to various system parameters and hyperparameters.
COST: 1600
PREDICTION: We expect this method to achieve robust policy learning with stronger performance on complex multi-turn search tasks under sparse outcome-based rewards.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE:  Invariant Reward Shaping via Serviceable Policy Regularization
PROPOSAL: amend the original proposal, replacing the serviceable policy regularization term with a relaxation of the term, using a gradient inpainting approach to stabilize the optimization process and promote exploration of various intermediate actions. This involves defining an auxiliary function that tiles the space of state-action pairs and extends their outcomes through interpolation, posing as a contextual corrector which learns how to build correct paths in a policy's vicinity. Improved multimodal representations then strengthen the local alignment of the learned process rewards with the desired outcome-based objective.
CONTROLS: Establish the theoretical soundness of this approach, focusing on marginal stability of the relaxation around gradients, towards improving overall analytic performance with external feedback.
COST: 1800
PREDICTION: By amending the approach and adding necessary theoretical foundations, this method is expected to provide a flexible and effective framework for alignment, stabilization, and exploration of process rewards, and exhibit further robust learning under complex search tasks.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE:  Learning to Infer Transition Rewards from Ground-Truth Labels
PROPOSAL: Amend the original proposal to incorporate a meta-learning component, training an auxiliary model to predict the relevance of each intermediate turn to the final outcome. By doing so, we can predict turn-level rewards that capture not only the correct information but also its importance in achieving the final goal. This meta-learning component is trained to minimize the difference between the predicted turn-level rewards and the true outcome-based rewards. We expect this revision to improve the sample efficiency and accuracy of the search agent.
CONTROLS: Compare to the original baseline and the revised contrastive process reward learning framework to evaluate the effectiveness of the meta-learning component.
COST: 2400
PREDICTION: We expect this revised approach to provide a more nuanced understanding of the importance of each intermediate turn, leading to more accurate and sample-efficient search agents.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE:  Hierarchical Attention Mechanism for Intermediate Turn Selection
PROPOSAL: Introduce a hierarchical attention mechanism that selectively focuses on the most informative intermediate turns in a search trajectory. This mechanism consists of two attention layers: a co-attention layer and a predictive attention layer. The co-attention layer attends to the relationships between the search history and intermediate turns, while the predictive attention layer attends to the relationships between the intermediate turns and the final outcome. By selecting the most informative intermediate turns, this mechanism aims to improve the sample efficiency and accuracy of the search agent.
CONTROLS: Examine the effect of different attention weights, number of layers, and hierarchical structures on the performance of the search agent.
COST: 2800
PREDICTION: We expect this hierarchical attention mechanism to effectively filter out redundant or irrelevant information, leading to improved performance on complex search tasks.

TITLE:  Model-Agnostic Process Reward Learning via Active Learning
PROPOSAL: Introduce an active learning framework that actively selects a subset of intermediate turns to be labeled by the agent itself, based on uncertainty estimates and relevance scores. We propose to use a decision tree-based active learning algorithm that iteratively selects the most informative and uncertain intermediate turns to be labeled. By selectively labeling the most relevant intermediate turns, we aim to reduce the labeling burden and improve the sample efficiency and accuracy of the search agent.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE:  Learning to Infer Transition Rewards from Ground-Truth Labels
PROPOSAL: Amend the original proposal to incorporate a meta-learning component, training an auxiliary model to predict the relevance of each intermediate turn to the final outcome. By doing so, we can predict turn-level rewards that capture not only the correct information but also its importance in achieving the final goal. This meta-learning component is trained to minimize the difference between the predicted turn-level rewards and the true outcome-based rewards. We expect this revision to improve the sample efficiency and accuracy of the search agent.
CONTROLS: Compare to the original baseline and the revised contrastive process reward learning framework to evaluate the effectiveness of the meta-learning component.

PREDICTION: We expect this revised approach to provide a more nuanced understanding of the importance of each intermediate turn, leading to more accurate and sample-efficient search agents.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE:  Hierarchical Attention Mechanism for Intermediate Turn Selection
PROPOSAL: Introduce a hierarchical attention mechanism that selectively focuses on the most informative intermediate turns in a search trajectory. This mechanism consists of two attention layers: a co-attention layer and a predictive attention layer. The co-attention layer attends to the relationships between the search history and intermediate turns, while the predictive attention layer attends to the relationships between the intermediate turns and the final outcome. By selecting the most informative intermediate turns, this mechanism aims to improve the sample efficiency and accuracy of the search agent.
CONTROLS: Examine the effect of different attention weights, number of layers, and hierarchical structures on the performance of the search agent.
COST: 8400
PREDICTION: We expect this hierarchical attention mechanism to effectively filter out redundant or irrelevant information, leading to improved performance on complex search tasks.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE:  Model-Agnostic Process Reward Learning via Active Learning
PROPOSAL: Introduce an active learning framework that actively selects a subset of intermediate turns to be labeled by the agent itself, based on uncertainty estimates and relevance scores. We propose to use a decision tree-based active learning algorithm that iteratively selects the most informative and uncertain intermediate turns to be labeled. By selectively labeling the most relevant intermediate turns, we aim to reduce the labeling burden and improve the sample efficiency and accuracy of the search agent.
CONTROLS: Compare to the baseline Policy Optimization method without active learning, and to the Hierarchical Attention Mechanism for Intermediate Turn Selection.
COST: 10800
PREDICTION: We expect the active learning framework to effectively reduce the labeling burden, improve the accuracy and sample efficiency of the search agent, and demonstrate robust performance on complex search tasks.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE:  Knowledge Graph-Augmented Process Reward Learning
PROPOSAL: Integrate a knowledge graph into the process reward learning framework to leverage external knowledge and relationships between entities to improve the accuracy and efficiency of the search agent. We propose to use a graph neural network to aggregate and reason about the knowledge graph, and use the output as a guidance signal for the search agent. By incorporating external knowledge, we aim to enable the search agent to better understand the relationships between entities and make more informed decisions.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the performance of the knowledge graph-augmented process reward learning approach on complex search tasks, and compare it to the baseline process reward learning approach.
COST: 12600
PREDICTION: We expect the knowledge graph-augmented process reward learning approach to improve the accuracy and efficiency of the search agent, and demonstrate robust performance on complex search tasks.

ACTION: ADD 7
TITLE:  Ensemble-Based Process Reward Learning for Robust Search Agents
PROPOSAL: Combine the outputs of multiple process reward learning approaches using an ensemble method to improve the robustness and accuracy of the search agent. We propose to use a weight-sharing framework to combine the predictions of multiple reward learning models, and use a self-supervised learning objective to adaptively update the model weights. By ensembling multiple process reward learning approaches, we aim to mitigate the effects of overfitting and improve the search agent's ability to generalize to new tasks.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the performance of the ensemble-based process reward learning approach on complex search tasks, and compare it to the baseline process reward learning approach and the individual process reward learning approaches.
COST: 16200
PREDICTION: We expect the ensemble-based process reward learning approach to improve the accuracy and robustness of the search agent, and demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on complex search tasks.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: REVISED: Learning Turn-Level Rewards for Agentic Search
PROPOSAL: Instead of using a sequence-to-sequence model to predict additional value contributed by each answer, use a neural network that predicts a relevance score for each intermediate sub-answer, conditioned on the current question and the agent's knowledge from previous turns. This relevance score represents how relevant each intermediate sub-answer is to the final answer. Then, use a variant of the subgroup Gumble-Nelder Optimization objective to aggregate these relevance scores into a single process reward for each intermediate turn.

CONTROLS: Compare the revised approach to the original sequence-to-sequence model, and evaluate its performance in standard agentic search benchmarks, such as WebSearch2019. Also, investigate the impact of different ways to aggregate the relevance scores, such as summing or averaging them.

COST: 432

PREDICTION: The revised approach will perform similarly to or better than the original sequence-to-sequence model, and will provide a more interpretable and versatile measure of process rewards. However, it may require more computational resources to train and integrate with the agentic search algorithm.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Optimal Turn Pruning
PROPOSAL: Incorporate an algorithm that dynamically prunes unproductive turns from the search trajectory, based on their predicted relevance scores and the agent's current knowledge. The goal is to keep only the most informative and relevant turns, reducing unnecessary computations and speeding up the search process. To do this, use a threshold-based policy that removes turns with low relevance scores or identifies breaking points in the search trajectory where a change in direction is warranted.

CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the agent with and without turn pruning, and evaluate the impact of different pruning thresholds and policies on the agent's performance and computational efficiency. Also, investigate the interplay between turn pruning and reward masking to identify potential synergies.

PREDICTION: The agent with turn pruning will achieve significantly faster search times and better performance on complex search tasks, but may require careful tuning of the pruning threshold and policy to avoid removing crucial information.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE:  Turn-Level Value Estimation through Rollout Clustering
PROPOSAL: We extend GRPO by clustering rollouts based on their intermediate reasoning steps, estimating the expected influence of each turn on the final outcome using the clusters' relative outcomes. This provides a dense reward signal for each interaction turn, aligned with the final objective.
CONTROLS: We compare our approach with the original GRPO, GRPO with our inverse reward design, and two ablations: (1) without clustering, using the average outcome of all rollouts, and (2) without estimating turn-level influence.
COST: 2160
PREDICTION: Our approach may improve sample efficiency and provide valuable feedback for intermediate turns, but may suffer from high variance due to the clustering process or incorrect estimation of turn-level influence.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE:  Contribution-based Reward Shaping
PROPOSAL: We propose a mechanism to shape the process reward signal by tracking the contribution of each turn to the final answer at the level of individual words or entities. This is achieved by calculating the mutual information between each turn's text and the final answer's text. Only contributions exceeding a certain threshold receive the reward.
CONTROLS: We compare our approach to the original GRPO and the revised turn-level value estimation method, as well as two ablations: (1) without contribution tracking, and (2) without the threshold.
COST: 3000
PREDICTION: Our method may effectively focus the learning signal on productive turns and improve performance, but may require careful tuning of the thresholds to avoid overlooking crucial information.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE:  Target-Domain Evidence Retrieval as Process Reward Proxy
PROPOSAL: We explore using a separate, domain-specific retriever to fetch relevant evidence from the web that is aligned with the target domain (e.g., a specific named entity or topic). Then, we use the retriever's relevance scores as a process reward for each intermediate turn, primarily targeting the turns where new evidence is introduced.
CONTROLS: We compare our approach with the previous methods and two baselines: (1) a state-of-the-art, task-agnostic retriever, and (2) a simple, domain-agnostic evidence retrieval baseline.
COST: 3421.9
PREDICTION: Our method may accurately identify informative turns and provide valuable supervision, but may struggle with generalizability to unseen domains or tasks. 

And, considering scalability and wide applicability, experimentation with this method against more diverse domains (e.g.: scientific writing Kundu et al., 2020; question-answering tasks over diverse entity-classification problems in Envision Hatum et al., 2019) will help quantify performance.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE:  Multi-Agent Reward Systems for Agentic Search
PROPOSAL: In agentic search environments where multiple tools and resources are involved, we propose a framework for reward shaping that integrates process rewards from individual tool calls to inform the search agent's overall policy. This involves representing the agent's environment as a multi-agent system where tools are seen as agents interacting with the search engine, and policy gradients are passed through the multi-agent system to determine the agent's final actions.
CONTROLS: We evaluate our multi-agent reward system against several ablations: (1) single-agent reward shaping, (2) ignoring reward signals from tool calls, and (3) without the multi-agent framework, incorporating only outcome-based rewards.
COST: 4339.21942
PREDICTION: By integrating rewards from multiple tool calls, our method may provide a more nuanced understanding of which turns in the search process contribute to the final answer, and thus could improve search agent performance. However, its applicability might be limited by complexity and the potential for increased training requirements.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE:  Addressing Advantage Collapse with Noise Regularization
PROPOSAL: We investigate the use of noise regularization to address the issue of advantage collapse in agentic search. By intentionally adding noise to the reward signals, we can provide a more robust gradient signal and encourage the model to explore the search space more effectively, especially in cases where the group relative rewards are zero.
CONTROLS: We compare our method with the original GRPO, GRPO with inverse reward design, and two ablations: (1) without noise regularization, and (2) with a fixed noise level.
COST: 5332.8
PREDICTION: By regulating the reward signals, our method should be able to mitigate the problem of advantage collapse and improve the model's exploration capabilities. However, the optimal noise level needs to be carefully tuned to avoid overly disrupting the learning process.

ACTION: ADD 7
TITLE:  Hierarchical Process Reward Shaping for Agentic Search
PROPOSAL: We propose a hierarchical reward shaping framework that combines the strengths of multi-level reinforcement learning and task-agnostic process reward estimation. This involves training a high-level policy to select sub-policies for specific search tasks, with each sub-policy being trained using task-agnostic process rewards and behavior cloning.
CONTROLS: We compare our method with the original GRPO, GRPO with inverse reward design, and two ablations: (1) without hierarchical policy, and (2) without behavior cloning.
COST: 6900
PREDICTION: Our hierarchical framework may provide a more flexible and adaptive approach to agentic search, allowing the model to select appropriate sub-policies for specific tasks and environments. However, it may require significant computational resources and careful tuning of hyperparameters.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Reward Augmentation through Pragmatic Recovery of Validity (RAPRV)
PROPOSAL: We propose a reinforcement learning approach that generates two types of intermediate supervision signals for each turn in a multi-turn search agent: a validity signal indicating whether the tool's retrieved content is relevant, and a productivity signal gauged from the sequential alignment of retrieved content with the target query. This twofold signal is distilled from the agent's probability estimates over content relevance and query alignment. These intermediate signals guide policy updates throughout the trajectory, complementing the terminal outcome reward.
CONTROLS: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) without additional supervision signals
COST: 269.2 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: RAPRV should exhibit better sample efficiency, especially in scenarios where agent estates are dominated by many garbage turns, such as those receiving meaningless or irrelevant retrieval responses. Difficulty in cold-start settings could emerge, where the relevance signal relies heavily on learned\x relevance estimates.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Search Flow Distillation as Turn-Level Process Reward
PROPOSAL: We design a Process Reward (PR) mechanism anchored to the learned latent representation of the search flow. By iterative pooling over turn embeddings in a temporal convolutional network, we distill process information that highlights productive turns. Then, a supervised learning module assigns turn-level scores from the product of relevance, engagement, and contextual coherence metrics, trained on human-annotated data. Only a fraction of the aggregated turn embedding representations are utilized to compute the reward. PR enables better feature exploitation while adding relatively minimal computational overhead.
CONTROLS: Reward Augmentation through Pragmatic Recovery of Validity (RAPRV), Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), using outcome rewards only
COST: 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Search Flow Distillation has a potential to augment turn-by-turn the process reward, as anticipated from its strong signal integration from supplementary input data to help an LLM distinguish good versus failing runs of controlled situations better, but transitioning variance might increase progressively, forming many incorrect aggregate signals from terrible sub-scoresCLUD

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: (Modification to Search Flow Distillation as Turn-Level Process Reward)
PROPOSAL: We modify the turn-level score assignment module of Search Flow Distillation to leverage a duel-encoder system, comprising a retrieval dua-encoder for tool interaction logs and a query dua-encoder for current search queries, with contrastive loss minimization over encoded query-key pair hard negatives. This enhancement refines contextual understanding of productive turns by leveraging cues in search logs, thereby alleviating potential inconsistencies in learning process outcomes when initialized in distant contexts far from the query.
CONTROLS: Original Search Flow Distillation, Reward Augmentation through Pragmatic Recovery of Validity (RAPRV), Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) using outcome rewards only
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The enhancement should improve contextual understanding of productive turns and guide more accurate policy updates by better capturing log-related cues, but potential over-reliance on distant cues could still render the approach noisy.

TITLE: Hierarchical Process Rewards via Temporal Graph Embeddings
PROPOSAL: We propose encoding turn sequences as temporal graphs, leveraging graph neural networks (GNNs) to extract hierarchical process representations. Each node represents an interaction turn, with edges capturing temporal dependencies and content relationships. By computing node embeddings at multiple scales, we obtain a hierarchy of informative process features that facilitate turn-level reward computation via a learned scoring function. This hierarchical approach allows for more nuanced understanding of productive turns and their dependencies across multi-turn trajectories.
CONTROLS: Original Search Flow Distillation, Reward Augmentation through Pragmatic Recovery of Validity (RAPRV), Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) using outcome rewards only
COST: 840 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Hierarchical Process Rewards via Temporal Graph Embeddings should significantly improve turn-level credit assignment and exploit intermediate process features, potentially yielding substantial gains in search agent performance and sample efficiency. However, complexity may introduce increased computational overhead, necessitating careful model selection and tuning.

TITLE: Real-Time Self-Modifying Reward Schedules for Exploration-Exploitation Balancing
PROPOSAL: We propose self-modifying reward schedules that adapt in real-time to balance exploration and exploitation in agentic search. Inspired by model-based reinforcement learning, we maintain a probabilistic model of the agent's trajectory and use it to compute a time-dependent reward schedule. As the agent explores the state-action space, the schedule self-modifies to encourage more or less exploration based on the observed transition dynamics and outcome rewards. This adaptive strategy promotes balanced long-term planning and short-term decision-making.
CONTROLS: Original Search Flow Distillation, Reward Augmentation through Pragmatic Recovery of Validity (RAPRV), Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with outcome rewards, Hierarchical Process Rewards via Temporal Graph Embeddings
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Real-Time Self-Modifying Reward Schedules should improve exploration-exploitation trade-offs and facilitate efficient adaptation to complex search environments, potentially leading to better convergence and sample efficiency. However, the added complexity may require significant tuning and monitoring to avoid divergence or reward hacking.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: (Modification to Hierarchical Process Rewards via Temporal Graph Embeddings)
PROPOSAL: We modify the Hierarchical Process Rewards approach to incorporate domain-specific structure via multi-modal fusion of graph and semantic embeddings. By integrating both object and relation-aware representations, we enhance the expressiveness of turn-level features and reduce overfitting to specific domains. Specifically, we leverage multi-modal pre-training and transfer learning techniques to fine-tune the GNNs on downstream tasks, ensuring that the extracted hierarchical process features are generic yet informed by domain-specific context.
CONTROLS: Original Hierarchical Process Rewards via Temporal Graph Embeddings, along with additional pre-trained multi-modal embeddings, auxiliary metrics for semantic and relational accuracy, and a domain-specific training schedule
COST: 1345.678925 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Multi-modal fusion should improve the robustness and generalizability of Hierarchical Process Rewards, enabling it to excel in a wider range of domains with increased semantic and relational understanding. However, the added complexity may necessitate more extensive hyperparameter tuning and model selection.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Contrastive Multi-Task Learning for Process Awareness
PROPOSAL: We propose a contrastive multi-task learning framework that jointly optimizes multiple tasks: process awareness, relevance evaluation, and downstream search performance. By formulating process awareness as a masked self-supervised learning task and leveraging the redundancy across tasks, we encourage the model to develop a robust understanding of productive turns and intermediate process features. The framework exploits the shared feature space and auxiliary tasks to improve process awareness without additional supervision, thereby reducing the burden of designing bespoke reward engines.
CONTROLS: Original Search Flow Distillation, Reward Augmentation through Pragmatic Recovery of Validity (RAPRV), (Modification to Hierarchical Process Rewards via Temporal Graph Embeddings), Real-Time Self-Modifying Reward Schedules for Exploration-Exploitation Balancing
COST: 1500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Contrastive Multi-Task Learning should enhance process awareness by encouraging the model to develop complementary, robust features over different tasks and views. By leveraging multi-task learning, this approach may improve the scalability and adaptability of process-aware RL agents without requiring additional supervision or bespoke reward design.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Transfer Learning for Domain-Adaptable Process-Aware Search Agents
PROPOSAL: We propose leveraging transfer learning techniques to adapt process-aware search agents to new domains. By fine-tuning the pre-trained process awareness weights on downstream tasks and adapting the model architecture to domain-specific requirements, we achieve efficient knowledge transfer across tasks and domains. The approach is facilitated by the jointly optimized shared feature space in Contrastive Multi-Task Learning, allowing the process-aware model to adapt to diverse domains with minimal retraining. By effectively exploiting shared knowledge across related tasks, we bridge the gap between process-aware learning and real-world deployment scenarios.
CONTROLS: Original Search Flow Distillation, Reward Augmentation through Pragmatic Recovery of Validity (RAPRV), (Modification to Hierarchical Process Rewards via Temporal Graph Embeddings), Real-Time Self-Modifying Reward Schedules for Exploration-Exploitation Balancing, Contrastive Multi-Task Learning for Process Awareness
COST: 1665.1 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Transfer Learning for Domain-Adaptable Process-Aware Search Agents should improve the scalability of process-aware RL agents by facilitating efficient adaptation to diverse domains with minimal retraining, ultimately enhancing the applicability of these search agents in real-world deployment scenarios.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Reward Augmentation through Pragmatic Recovery of Validity (RAPRV)
PROPOSAL: We propose a reinforcement learning approach that generates two types of intermediate supervision signals for each turn in a multi-turn search agent: a validity signal indicating whether the tool's retrieved content is relevant, and a productivity signal gauged from the sequential alignment of retrieved content with the target query. This twofold signal is distilled from the agent's probability estimates over content relevance and query alignment. These intermediate signals guide policy updates throughout the trajectory, complementing the terminal outcome reward.
CONTROLS: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) without additional supervision signals
COST: 800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: RAPRV should exhibit better sample efficiency, especially in scenarios where agent estates are dominated by many garbage turns, such as those receiving meaningless or irrelevant retrieval responses. Difficulty in cold-start settings could emerge, where the relevance signal relies heavily on learned\x relevance estimates.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Search Flow Distillation as Turn-Level Process Reward
PROPOSAL: We design a Process Reward (PR) mechanism anchored to the learned latent representation of the search flow. By iterative pooling over turn embeddings in a temporal convolutional network, we distill process information that highlights productive turns. Then, a supervised learning module assigns turn-level scores from the product of relevance, engagement, and contextual coherence metrics, trained on human-annotated data. Only a fraction of the aggregated turn embedding representations are utilized to compute the reward. PR enables better feature exploitation while adding relatively minimal computational overhead.
CONTROLS: Reward Augmentation through Pragmatic Recovery of Validity (RAPRV), Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), using outcome rewards only
COST: 1200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Search Flow Distillation has a potential to augment turn-by-turn the process reward, as anticipated from its strong signal integration from supplementary input data to help an LLM distinguish good versus failing runs of controlled situations better, but transitioning variance might increase progressively, forming many incorrect aggregate signals from terrible sub-scoresCLUD

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Exploring Sequence-Level Masking for Dense Process Rewards
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the effect of sequence-level masking on dense process rewards, a procedure where for each rollout and intermediate turn, a mask is computed to highlight relevant turns based on the LLM's attention weights, along with a control that leaves the input sequence unchanged. The mask influences the inherent value of each turn through a learnable embedding fed into the reward head. This encourages the RL policy to value productive turns more, while ignoring those without relevant context.
CONTROLS: Unmasked input sequence, a masking-based baseline relying solely on the relative position of turns.
COST: 1200
PREDICTION: This approach may provide a denser learning signal at moderate computational overhead and help recognize productive turns, but will likely lead to a bias toward shorter trajectories and overreliance on the mask predictions, hindering scalability and sample efficiency.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Hierarchical Reward Abstraction through Intermediate Subgoals
PROPOSAL: Building on the problem of advantage collapse, we will propose a hierarchical reward abstraction method that decomposes the final objective into subgoals at the intermediate turn level. By multiplying a rollout's reward value by a term that represents the degree of subgoal accomplishment, the signal becomes denser and accumulates during each turn rather than at the final state. This makes the training process more sample-efficient and allows the policy to differentiate between turns.
CONTROLS: Standard outcome-based GRPO and a baseline extended with basic subgoal formulation that fails to regularize the accomplishment degree.
COST: 10800
PREDICTION: Hierarchical reward abstraction can reduce sample inefficiency and, with proper regularization of the subgoal accomplishment degree, balance reward exploration-exploitation. However, overemphasizing subgoal accomplishment might compromise policy generalizability to new, unseen states.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Using Meta-Gradients for Scalable Process Reward Updates
PROPOSAL: We'll explore incorporating meta-gradients into the process reward update to efficiently adapt the reward function to distinct distributional characteristics of returned tool results. This involves computing meta-gradients on both the rollout's value and the policy's parameters to update the reward network's weights along with the policy's. We'll update these gradients using Adam updates tailored for rewards. This aims to counterbalance the curse of sparsity while covering unseen scenarios.
CONTROLS: Updates based solely on regular evaluation metrics, such as accuracy, and no meta-learning integration.
COST: 6900
PREDICTION: Combining meta-learning for process rewards may not improve policy performance over standard process rewards alone unless matching the quality of the ground truth answer is achieved, yet could bring more generalization and efficiency due to reduced sparsity.

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Transfer Learning from Pre-Trained Relevance Models for Intrinsic Motivation
PROPOSAL: We design a transfer-learning-based method for leveraging pre-trained relevance models to inject dense, informative, and application-agnostic signals into our process reward. By projecting pre-trained representation onto our task-specific reward network, we'll be able to achieve more general, universally applicable training objectives. This scheme can significantly reduce the need for domain-specific annotations.
CONTROLS: Baselines relying directly on intrinsic curiosity or self-supervision from intermediate steps, ignoring pre-existing relevance models, hand-designed relevance or pseudo-labels.
COST: 12750
PREDICTION: Applying transfer learning from pre-trained relevance models might have negative transfer or misalignment in cases where relevance and Final Answer relevance diverge, but their general-purpose nature can result in faster convergence.

TITLE: Exploring Sequence-Level Masking for Dense Process Rewards
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the effect of sequence-level masking on dense process rewards, a procedure where for each rollout and intermediate turn, a mask is computed to highlight relevant turns based on the LLM's attention weights, along with a control that leaves the input sequence unchanged. The mask influences the inherent value of each turn through a learnable embedding fed into the reward head. This encourages the RL policy to value productive turns more, while ignoring those without relevant context.
CONTROLS: Unmasked input sequence, a masking-based baseline relying solely on the relative position of turns.

PREDICTION: This approach may provide a denser learning signal at moderate computational overhead and help recognize productive turns, but will likely lead to a bias toward shorter trajectories and overreliance on the mask predictions, hindering scalability and sample efficiency.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Hierarchical Reward Abstraction through Intermediate Subgoals
PROPOSAL: Building on the problem of advantage collapse, we will propose a hierarchical reward abstraction method that decomposes the final objective into subgoals at the intermediate turn level. By multiplying a rollout's reward value by a term that represents the degree of subgoal accomplishment, the signal becomes denser and accumulates during each turn rather than at the final state. This makes the training process more sample-efficient and allows the policy to differentiate between turns.
CONTROLS: Standard outcome-based GRPO and a baseline extended with basic subgoal formulation that fails to regularize the accomplishment degree.
COST: 32400
PREDICTION: Hierarchical reward abstraction can reduce sample inefficiency and, with proper regularization of the subgoal accomplishment degree, balance reward exploration-exploitation. However, overemphasizing subgoal accomplishment might compromise policy generalizability to new, unseen states.

PROPOSAL: We'll explore incorporating meta-gradients into the process reward update to efficiently adapt the reward function to distinct distributional characteristics of returned tool results. This involves computing meta-gradients on both the rollout's value and the policy's parameters to update the reward network's weights along with the policy's. We'll update these gradients using Adam updates tailored for rewards. This aims to counterbalance the curse of sparsity while covering unseen scenarios.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Query-Space Distillation for Self-Supervised Pre-Training of Sparse Perception Models
PROPOSAL: This experiment proposes a self-supervised pre-training method for SPMs, which aims to learn fine-grained 3D scene representations using unlabeled multi-view driving data. We leverage an attention-based encoder-decoder architecture and propose Query-Space Distillation (QSD), a novel self-distillation mechanism that distills the knowledge from the target Sparse Queries into the input Query Priors. Specifically, the model generates a sparse set of implicit queries, which are projected onto a coarse BEV grid to obtain the target sparse queries. We then compute the similarity between the input query priors and the target sparse queries using a contrastive loss. By minimizing this loss, the model learns to concentrate on the most relevant features and distill the spatial-temporal information into the query priors, thus enhancing the interpretability and representational power of the sparse queries. During pre-training, we adopt a weak supervision strategy, where we only provide a weak depth map derived from the video frame. We evaluate our method on the KITTI dataset and compare it with existing self-supervised methods, such as UniPAD and ViDAR.
CONTROLS: Comparison with UniPAD and ViDAR; ablations with and without QSD; controls for varying numbers of queries and weak supervision levels.
COST: 14400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our method outperforms existing self-supervised methods, achieving high accuracy on 3D object detection and semantic segmentation tasks; however, it may suffer from increased computational costs due to the additional contrastive loss.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: SPM-Embodied Navigation for Self-Supervised 3D Representation Learning
PROPOSAL: This experiment proposes an embodied navigation task to enhance the self-supervised pre-training of SPMs on unlabeled multi-view driving data. We equip a virtual agent with a SPM and have it navigate through diverse scenarios in a synthetic Carla environment. The goal is to encourage the agent to observe and understand the 3D structure of the environment by itself, without human intervention. We design a novel control mechanism that utilizes the sparse queries to reason about the environment and make decisions. Specifically, we use the top-k queries with the highest attention scores to guide the agent's actions and encourage exploration. During pre-training, we adopt a multi-task setting, where the agent needs to predict the future poses, detect objects, and segment the environment. We evaluate our method on the Carla environment and compare it with existing self-supervised methods, such as Query-Space Distillation from experiment 1.
CONTROLS: Comparison with Query-Space Distillation; ablations with and without the embodied navigation task; controls for varying numbers of queries, agent actions, and multi-task settings.
COST: 21600 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our method improves the robustness and generalizability of the SPMs to various scenarios, and allows them to better reason about the 3D structure of the environment; however, the navigation task may increase the computational costs and make the model more prone to overfitting.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Unsupervised Sparse Query Refinement through Graph-Based Spatial Reasoning
PROPOSAL: This experiment proposes an unsupervised refinement method for sparse queries in SPMs, aiming to improve their spatial reasoning and representation capabilities on unlabeled multi-view driving data. We present a novel graph-based framework that models the spatial relationships between sparse queries through a Markov Random Field (MRF). Each node in the graph represents a query, and the edges capture the spatial coherence between queries. We design an energy-based minimization process that refines the sparse queries based on the node-edge constraints. The resulting refined queries are more spatially consistent, facilitating better spatial reasoning and representation learning. During pre-training, we combine our refinement method with Query-Space Distillation (exp 1) and SPM-Embodied Navigation (exp 2) for a more comprehensive self-supervised pre-training process. We evaluate our method on the KITTI dataset and compare it with existing self-supervised methods.
CONTROLS: Comparison with Query-Space Distillation and SPM-Embodied Navigation; ablations with and without the graph-based refinement; controls for varying numbers of queries and graph sizes.
COST: 43200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our method significantly improves the spatial reasoning and representation capabilities of SPMs, leading to enhanced performance on object detection and segmentation tasks; however, the refinement process may be computationally expensive due to the energy-based minimization process.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Self-Supervised Sparse Perception Model Pre-Training through Adversarial Multi-Task Learning
PROPOSAL: This experiment proposes a self-supervised pre-training method for SPMs, which leverages adversarial multi-task learning to improve the representation and reasoning capabilities of SPMs on unlabeled multi-view driving data. We design a framework with two types of tasks: prediction tasks, which are the standard 3D object detection, segmentation, and motion prediction tasks, and adversarial task, which is a task that encourages the model to learn a latent representation that is difficult to distinguish from the actual 3D scene. We then use a adversarial training process to train the model. This process involves an adversary that tries to distinguish between the predicted 3D scene and the actual 3D scene. The overall goal is to encourage the model to learn a more informative and robust representation. During pre-training, we combine our adversarial multi-task learning framework with Query-Space Distillation (exp 1), SPM-Embodied Navigation (exp 2), and Unsupervised Sparse Query Refinement (exp 3) for a more comprehensive self-supervised pre-training process. We evaluate our method on the KITTI dataset and compare it with existing self-supervised methods.
CONTROLS: Comparison with Query-Space Distillation, SPM-Embodied Navigation, and Unsupervised Sparse Query Refinement; ablations with and without the adversarial task; controls for varying numbers of tasks and pre-training iterations.
COST: 86400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our method significantly improves the representation and reasoning capabilities of SPMs, leading to enhanced performance on object detection, segmentation, and motion prediction tasks; however, the adversarial training process may be computationally expensive and slow down the pre-training process.

TITLE: Transferring Self-Supervised Knowledge to Task-Specific Sparse Perception Models
PROPOSAL: This experiment investigates the possibility of transferring self-supervised knowledge learned from unlabeled driving data to task-specific SPMs, which are trained on labeled data. We leverage the pre-trained SPMs (exp 1-4) and fine-tune them on labeled datasets, such as the KITTI or Waymo annotations. We also explore the idea of using a domain adaptation approach to transfer the knowledge from pre-trained SPMs to task-specific models, which are trained on different datasets. We evaluate our method using various transfer learning scenarios and compare the results with finetuning-from-scratch and domain adaptation techniques. We also analyze the effects of different pre-training methods, model architectures, and task-specific architectures on the transferability of knowledge.
CONTROLS: Transfer learning scenarios with and without pre-training; ablations with and without domain adaptation; control experiments with finetuning-from-scratch and domain adaptation.
COST: 162000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our method improves the transferability of self-supervised knowledge to task-specific SPMs, leading to faster adaptation and better performance on various driving tasks; however, the effectiveness of transfer may be affected by the task-specific architectures, pre-training methods, and datasets.

TITLE: An Efficient Framework for Scalable Self-Supervised Training of Sparse Perception Models
PROPOSAL: This experiment proposes an efficient framework for scalable self-supervised training of SPMs, which addresses the computational and memory limitations of large-scale self-supervised training. We develop a modular framework that decomposes the training process into smaller, parallelizable tasks, and leverages various optimization techniques, such as mixed-precision training and knowledge distillation, to accelerate the training process. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Query-Space Distillation for Self-Supervised Pre-Training of Sparse Perception Models
PROPOSAL: This experiment proposes a self-supervised pre-training method for SPMs, which aims to learn fine-grained 3D scene representations using unlabeled multi-view driving data. We leverage an attention-based encoder-decoder architecture and propose Query-Space Distillation (QSD), a novel self-distillation mechanism that distills the knowledge from the target Sparse Queries into the input Query Priors. Specifically, the model generates a sparse set of implicit queries, which are projected onto a coarse BEV grid to obtain the target sparse queries. We then compute the similarity between the input query priors and the target sparse queries using a contrastive loss. By minimizing this loss, the model learns to concentrate on the most relevant features and distill the spatial-temporal information into the query priors, thus enhancing the interpretability and representational power of the sparse queries. During pre-training, we adopt a weak supervision strategy, where we only provide a weak depth map derived from the video frame. We evaluate our method on the KITTI dataset and compare it with existing self-supervised methods, such as UniPAD and ViDAR.
CONTROLS: Comparison with UniPAD and ViDAR; ablations with and without QSD; controls for varying numbers of queries and weak supervision levels.
COST: 43200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our method outperforms existing self-supervised methods, achieving high accuracy on 3D object detection and semantic segmentation tasks; however, it may suffer from increased computational costs due to the additional contrastive loss.

TITLE: SPM-Embodied Navigation for Self-Supervised 3D Representation Learning
PROPOSAL: This experiment proposes an embodied navigation task to enhance the self-supervised pre-training of SPMs on unlabeled multi-view driving data. We equip a virtual agent with a SPM and have it navigate through diverse scenarios in a synthetic Carla environment. The goal is to encourage the agent to observe and understand the 3D structure of the environment by itself, without human intervention. We design a novel control mechanism that utilizes the sparse queries to reason about the environment and make decisions. Specifically, we use the top-k queries with the highest attention scores to guide the agent's actions and encourage exploration. During pre-training, we adopt a multi-task setting, where the agent needs to predict the future poses, detect objects, and segment the environment. We evaluate our method on the Carla environment and compare it with existing self-supervised methods, such as Query-Space Distillation from experiment 1.
CONTROLS: Comparison with Query-Space Distillation; ablations with and without the embodied navigation task; controls for varying numbers of queries, agent actions, and multi-task settings.

PREDICTION: Our method improves the robustness and generalizability of the SPMs to various scenarios, and allows them to better reason about the 3D structure of the environment; however, the navigation task may increase the computational costs and make the model more prone to overfitting.

TITLE: Unsupervised Sparse Query Refinement through Graph-Based Spatial Reasoning
PROPOSAL: This experiment proposes an unsupervised refinement method for sparse queries in SPMs, aiming to improve their spatial reasoning and representation capabilities on unlabeled multi-view driving data. We present a novel graph-based framework that models the spatial relationships between sparse queries through a Markov Random Field (MRF). Each node in the graph represents a query, and the edges capture the spatial coherence between queries. We design an energy-based minimization process that refines the sparse queries based on the node-edge constraints. The resulting refined queries are more spatially consistent, facilitating better spatial reasoning and representation learning. During pre-training, we combine our refinement method with Query-Space Distillation (exp 1) and SPM-Embodied Navigation (exp 2) for a more comprehensive self-supervised pre-training process. We evaluate our method on the KITTI dataset and compare it with existing self-supervised methods.
CONTROLS: Comparison with Query-Space Distillation and SPM-Embodied Navigation; ablations with and without the graph-based refinement; controls for varying numbers of queries and graph sizes.
COST: 129600 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our method significantly improves the spatial reasoning and representation capabilities of SPMs, leading to enhanced performance on object detection and segmentation tasks; however, the refinement process may be computationally expensive due to the energy-based minimization process.

TITLE: Self-Supervised Sparse Perception Model Pre-Training through Adversarial Multi-Task Learning
PROPOSAL: This experiment proposes a self-supervised pre-training method for SPMs, which leverages adversarial multi-task learning to improve the representation and reasoning capabilities of SPMs on unlabeled multi-view driving data. We design a framework with two types of tasks: prediction tasks, which are the standard 3D object detection, segmentation, and motion prediction tasks, and adversarial task, which is a task that encourages the model to learn a latent representation that is difficult to distinguish from the actual 3D scene. We then use a adversarial training process to train the model. This process involves an adversary that tries to distinguish between the predicted 3D scene and the actual 3D scene. The overall goal is to encourage the model to learn a more informative and robust representation. During pre-training, we combine our adversarial multi-task learning framework with Query-Space Distillation (exp 1), SPM-Embodied Navigation (exp 2), and Unsupervised Sparse Query Refinement (exp 3) for a more comprehensive self-supervised pre-training process. We evaluate our method on the KITTI dataset and compare it with existing self-supervised methods.
CONTROLS: Comparison with Query-Space Distillation, SPM-Embodied Navigation, and Unsupervised Sparse Query Refinement; ablations with and without the adversarial task; controls for varying numbers of tasks and pre-training iterations.
COST: 259200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our method significantly improves the representation and reasoning capabilities of SPMs, leading to enhanced performance on object detection, segmentation, and motion prediction tasks; however, the adversarial training process may be computationally expensive and slow down the pre-training process.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Temporal Graph Attention Network for Modeling Dynamics in Autonomous Driving
PROPOSAL: We propose a Temporal Graph Attention Network (TGAT) to model the dynamics of the environment and the vehicle's motion in autonomous driving scenarios. The TGAT learns to represent the scene as a graph, where nodes represent objects and edges represent spatial and temporal relationships. By applying graph attention mechanisms, the network captures the complex interactions between objects and the vehicle, enabling the prediction of future scene configurations.
CONTROLS: We compare our approach to standard temporal modeling techniques and evaluate its performance on tasks such as future scene prediction and motion forecasting.
COST: 89730
PREDICTION: Our TGAT-based model improves the accuracy of scene prediction and motion forecasting tasks, and demonstrates a strong ability to handle complex scenarios with multiple interacting objects and vehicles.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Self-Supervised Pre-Training for Sparse Perception Models via Multi-Branch Rendering
PROPOSAL: Develop a self-supervised pre-training framework for SPMs that employs multi-branch rendering to learn fine-grained 3D scene representations. Utilize a combination of 2D RGB and depth images as input to multiple rendering branches, each responsible for predicting different aspects of the scene, such as occupancy, depth, and semantic information. Leverage robust loss functions and ensemble techniques to aggregate predictions from all branches, effectively capturing the spatiotemporal geometry of the scene without relying on dense BEV or volumetric features.
CONTROLS: Compare with existing rendering-based pre-training methods (e.g., UniPAD, ViDAR) and query-based methods (e.g., Frozen-DETR, GLID), as well as ablate individual rendering branches to understand their contributions.
COST: 3240
PREDICTION: Expected to improve SPMs' performance on downstream tasks by at least 5% compared to supervised pre-training, particularly for 3D object detection and occupancy prediction. May struggle with 2D object detection tasks due to the limited spatial resolution of the rendered depth maps.

TITLE: Query-Space 3D Masked Autoencoder for Pre-training Sparse Perception Models
PROPOSAL: We propose a query-space 3D masked autoencoder, Q3D-MAE, that takes a sparse set of image queries as input and learns to reconstruct the corresponding 3D scene occupancy. This approach employs a novel 3D attention mechanism to focus on relevant regions of the scene, allowing the model to capture fine-grained 3D geometry and semantics. During pre-training, Q3D-MAE will use a self-paced masking strategy to gradually reveal the 3D scene structure, leading to improved robustness and generalizability to downstream sparse perception tasks.
CONTROLS: A baseline of pre-training with random maskings, as well as an ablation study with and without the 3D attention mechanism.
COST: 180
PREDICTION: Expected improved performance on downstream tasks, such as object detection and semantic segmentation, with a potential marginal decrease in reconstruction quality due to the lack of explicit supervisions for dense features.
