ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Transferring Pre-trained Q3D-MAE to Heterogeneous Sparse Perception Models via Query-Based Multi-Task Learning
PROPOSAL: To tackle the challenge of transferring pre-trained Q3D-MAE to diverse sparse perception models, we introduce a query-based multi-task learning framework, QBMTL. QBMTL adaptively selects and fine-tunes the pre-trained Q3D-MAE on downstream tasks by learning task-specific query weights. This approach allows QBMTL to leverage the knowledge of Q3D-MAE while adapting to the unique query structures and decoding mechanisms of downstream models. By combining QBMTL with Q3D-MAE, we demonstrate improved performance on a variety of downstream tasks, such as object detection and semantic segmentation, for a range of heterogeneous sparse perception models.
CONTROLS: A baseline of fine-tuning the pre-trained Q3D-MAE on individual tasks without QBMTL, as well as an ablation study with and without task-specific query weights.
COST: 270
PREDICTION: Expected improved performance and better adaptability to diverse downstream tasks, with a potential increase in computational cost due to the increased number of learnable parameters.

TITLE: Evaluating Q3D-MAE and QBMTL on Real-World Driving Data: A Comparison with State-of-the-Art Pre-training Methods
PROPOSAL: We evaluate Q3D-MAE and QBMTL on a range of real-world driving datasets, including KITTI, nuScenes, and Waymo Open Dataset, and compare their performance with state-of-the-art pre-training methods, such as UniPAD, ViDAR, and GaussianPretrain. This comparison assesses the effectiveness of Q3D-MAE and QBMTL in capturing fine-grained 3D scene representations and transferring knowledge to downstream sparse perception tasks. We also investigate the impact of different pre-training datasets, such as synthetic data, image collections, and unlabeled driving footage, on the performance of Q3D-MAE and QBMTL.

COST: 720
PREDICTION: Expected Q3D-MAE and QBMTL to outperform state-of-the-art pre-training methods on downstream tasks, such as object detection and semantic segmentation, with a potential decrease in performance when pre-trained on synthetic data.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Understanding the Effect of Query Sampling on Q3D-MAE and QBMTL: A Theoretical Analysis
PROPOSAL: We provide a theoretical analysis of the effect of query sampling on the performance of Q3D-MAE and QBMTL. We prove that the convergence of Q3D-MAE depends on the quality and diversity of the sampled queries, and that a uniform sampling strategy may not be optimal. We also derive an upper bound on the error of QBMTL when using a bucketing-based query sampling strategy, and show that it outperforms the uniform sampling strategy by a factor of log(n), where n is the number of tasks.
CONTROLS: A control group with uniform query sampling, as well as an ablation study with and without the bucketing-based query sampling strategy.
COST: 360
PREDICTION: Expected the theoretical analysis to provide insights into the design and optimization of Q3D-MAE and QBMTL, with a potential decrease in performance if the query sampling strategy is not well-designed.

TITLE: Weakly Supervised Pre-training of Sparse Perception Models using Unsupervised Depth Prediction
PROPOSAL: We propose a weakly supervised pre-training approach for sparse perception models, which utilizes unsupervised depth prediction as a self-supervisory signal. Our approach, dubbed WSPD, leverages a depth estimation network to predict disparity maps from RGB images. We then use these disparity maps as a weak supervisory signal to train sparse perception models, such as Q3D-MAE and QBMTL. By pre-training on unsupervised depth predictions, we demonstrate improved performance on downstream tasks, such as object detection and semantic segmentation.

textes:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Query-Space 3D Masked Autoencoder for Pre-training Sparse Perception Models
PROPOSAL: We propose a query-space 3D masked autoencoder, Q3D-MAE, that takes a sparse set of image queries as input and learns to reconstruct the corresponding 3D scene occupancy. This approach employs a novel 3D attention mechanism to focus on relevant regions of the scene, allowing the model to capture fine-grained 3D geometry and semantics. During pre-training, Q3D-MAE will use a self-paced masking strategy to gradually reveal the 3D scene structure, leading to improved robustness and generalizability to downstream sparse perception tasks.
CONTROLS: A baseline of pre-training with random maskings, as well as an ablation study with and without the 3D attention mechanism.
COST: 540
PREDICTION: Expected improved performance on downstream tasks, such as object detection and semantic segmentation, with a potential marginal decrease in reconstruction quality due to the lack of explicit supervisions for dense features.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Transferring Pre-trained Q3D-MAE to Heterogeneous Sparse Perception Models via Query-Based Multi-Task Learning
PROPOSAL: To tackle the challenge of transferring pre-trained Q3D-MAE to diverse sparse perception models, we introduce a query-based multi-task learning framework, QBMTL. QBMTL adaptively selects and fine-tunes the pre-trained Q3D-MAE on downstream tasks by learning task-specific query weights. This approach allows QBMTL to leverage the knowledge of Q3D-MAE while adapting to the unique query structures and decoding mechanisms of downstream models. By combining QBMTL with Q3D-MAE, we demonstrate improved performance on a variety of downstream tasks, such as object detection and semantic segmentation, for a range of heterogeneous sparse perception models.
CONTROLS: A baseline of fine-tuning the pre-trained Q3D-MAE on individual tasks without QBMTL, as well as an ablation study with and without task-specific query weights.
COST: 810
PREDICTION: Expected improved performance and better adaptability to diverse downstream tasks, with a potential increase in computational cost due to the increased number of learnable parameters.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Evaluating Q3D-MAE and QBMTL on Real-World Driving Data: A Comparison with State-of-the-Art Pre-training Methods
PROPOSAL: We evaluate Q3D-MAE and QBMTL on a range of real-world driving datasets, including KITTI, nuScenes, and Waymo Open Dataset, and compare their performance with state-of-the-art pre-training methods, such as UniPAD, ViDAR, and GaussianPretrain. This comparison assesses the effectiveness of Q3D-MAE and QBMTL in capturing fine-grained 3D scene representations and transferring knowledge to downstream sparse perception tasks. We also investigate the impact of different pre-training datasets, such as synthetic data, image collections, and unlabeled driving footage, on the performance of Q3D-MAE and QBMTL.
CONTROLS: Baseline pre-training methods, UniPAD, ViDAR, and GaussianPretrain, as well as a control group where Q3D-MAE is pre-trained using synthetic data.
COST: 2160
PREDICTION: Expected Q3D-MAE and QBMTL to outperform state-of-the-art pre-training methods on downstream tasks, such as object detection and semantic segmentation, with a potential decrease in performance when pre-trained on synthetic data.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Understanding the Effect of Query Sampling on Q3D-MAE and QBMTL: A Theoretical Analysis
PROPOSAL: We provide a theoretical analysis of the effect of query sampling on the performance of Q3D-MAE and QBMTL. We prove that the convergence of Q3D-MAE depends on the quality and diversity of the sampled queries, and that a uniform sampling strategy may not be optimal. We also derive an upper bound on the error of QBMTL when using a bucketing-based query sampling strategy, and show that it outperforms the uniform sampling strategy by a factor of log(n), where n is the number of tasks.
CONTROLS: A control group with uniform query sampling, as well as an ablation study with and without the bucketing-based query sampling strategy.
COST: 1080
PREDICTION: Expected the theoretical analysis to provide insights into the design and optimization of Q3D-MAE and QBMTL, with a potential decrease in performance if the query sampling strategy is not well-designed.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: REVISED Query-Space 3D Masked Autoencoder for Pre-training Sparse Perception Models
PROPOSAL: We revise Q3D-MAE to incorporate a hierarchical attention mechanism, which enables the model to focus on both local and global structures of the scene. Additionally, we introduce a new reconstructor head, which is jointly learned with the autoencoder. This allows Q3D-MAE to learn a more complex and hierarchical representation of the scene, leading to improved performance on downstream tasks.
CONTROLS: The original Q3D-MAE model, as well as a control group without the hierarchical attention mechanism.
COST: 1620
PREDICTION: Expected the revised Q3D-MAE to outperform the original model on downstream tasks, such as object detection and semantic segmentation, with a potential increase in complexity and computational cost due to the added hierarchical attention mechanism.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Weakly Supervised Pre-training of Sparse Perception Models using Unsupervised Depth Prediction
PROPOSAL: We propose a weakly supervised pre-training approach for sparse perception models, which utilizes unsupervised depth prediction as a self-supervisory signal. Our approach, dubbed WSPD, leverages a depth estimation network to predict disparity maps from RGB images. We then use these disparity maps as a weak supervisory signal to train sparse perception models, such as Q3D-MAE and QBMTL. By pre-training on unsupervised depth predictions, we demonstrate improved performance on downstream tasks, such as object detection and semantic segmentation.
CONTROLS: A baseline of pre-training on random labels, as well as an ablation study with and without the weak supervisory signal from depth prediction.
COST: 2700
PREDICTION: Expected WSPD to improve performance on downstream tasks, with a potential decrease in performance if the quality of the depth predictions is low.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: Information-Theoretic Analysis of Query-Based Pre-training for Sparse Perception Models
PROPOSAL: We perform an information-theoretic analysis of query-based pre-training for sparse perception models, focusing on the information-theoretic bounds of Q3D-MAE and QBMTL. Our analysis reveals the relationship between the mutual information between the input queries and the output labels, and the mutual information between the input queries and the encoder's internal representations. We derive a theoretical upper bound on the performance of Q3D-MAE and QBMTL, and demonstrate that this bound is tight under certain conditions.
CONTROLS: A control group with a random encoding mechanism, as well as an ablation study with and without the information-theoretic analysis.
COST: 1980
PREDICTION: Expected the information-theoretic analysis to provide insights into the design and optimization of Q3D-MAE and QBMTL, with a potential decrease in performance if the mutual information between the input queries and the output labels is low.

ACTION: ADD 7
TITLE: Query-Specific Attention for Improving Pre-training of Sparse Perception Models
PROPOSAL: We propose a query-specific attention mechanism for Q3D-MAE and QBMTL, which enables the models to focus on the most important queries for each task. Our approach, dubbed QSA, uses a query-specific attention weight to combine the features from different queries, and demonstrated improved performance on downstream tasks. We also investigate the effect of QSA on the robustness and generalizability of Q3D-MAE and QBMTL.
CONTROLS: A baseline of using a fixed attention weight, as well as an ablation study with and without the query-specific attention mechanism.
COST: 2400
PREDICTION: Expected QSA to improve performance on downstream tasks, with a potential decrease in performance if the query-specific attention weights are not well learned.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Investigating the Impact of Pseudo-label Quality on Test-time Adaptive Object Detection
PROPOSAL: We will conduct a controlled experiment on the popular COCO dataset to compare different strategies of pseudo-label filtering thresholds (e.g., 0.5, 0.7, 0.9) and analyze their impact on the detection performance of a test-time adaptive object detector (TTAOD) that uses self-training with pseudo-labeled objects.
CONTROLS: Baseline: standard Faster R-CNN model without any form of test-time adaptation; Ablated baseline: TTAOD with no pseudo-label filtering; Ablated baseline: different pseudo-label generation methods (e.g., simple thresholding, confidence-based filtering, and refinement via agreement among models).
COST: 20
PREDICTION: Increasing pseudo-label quality would improve detection performance, but setting the threshold too high might lead to under-estimation of available pseudo-labels on certain images (potentially causing stability issues).

textes.jumeau:
ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Investigation on Plug-and-play Vision-Language Detectors for Test-time Adaptive Detection
PROPOSAL: We will compare the performance of popular pre-trained vision-language models (e.g., GLIP and Grounding DINO) directly applied to test-time adaptive object detection on various real-world benchmarks (e.g., COCO, LVIS, and OpenImages). These models would not be fine-tuned on the specific test domain but still be expected to adapt due to their pre-trained knowledge and capacity to generalize.
CONTROLS: Baseline: standard Faster R-CNN model without any form of test-time adaptation; Ablated baseline: different pre-trained vision-language models; Evaluation chamber: adaptation performance under different levels of label scarcity, noise, and shift.
COST: 26.92
PREDICTION: While strong pre-trained vision-language models would adapt decently well on their own with little to no fine-tuning, their performance will nevertheless degrade as the domain shift and complexity increase, necessitating some form of adaptation mechanism to be incorporated prevent collapse to weak initial knowledge.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Investigation on Plug-and-play Vision-Language Detectors for Test-time Adaptive Detection
PROPOSAL: We will extend the previous proposal by incorporating self-supervised methods to refine the pre-trained vision-language detector's adaptation to the target domain through online pseudo-label refinement and mix-up strategies. Additionally, we will examine the convergence and stability of this self-supervised adaptation process across different test batches and regression metrics (e.g., cross-entropy loss and detection accuracy).
CONTROLS: Baseline: standard Faster R-CNN model without any form of test-time adaptation; Ablated baseline: different pre-trained vision-language models; Ablated chamber: adaptation with and without pseudo-label refinement; Evaluation chamber: adaptation performance under different levels of label scarcity, noise, and shift.
COST: 40
PREDICTION: Self-supervised adaptation, particularly pseudo-label refinement and mix-up strategies, will allow plug-and-play vision-language detectors to achieve significant performance gains, remaining effective up to a moderate degree of domain shift and label scarcity, where pseudo-labeling stops working efficiently.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Adapting Vision-Language Detectors with Gaussian Mixture Model-based Pseudo-label Clustering
PROPOSAL: We will implement a clustering-based strategy using a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) to categorize pseudo-labels produced on test images into reliable and unreliable categories. A separate branch of the network will then be trained to iteratively enhance the pseudo-labels (with lower ambiguity) and correct the pseudo-labels (with higher ambiguity) simultaneously, thus reducing the overfitting risk and potential instability in the adaptation process.
CONTROLS: Baseline: standard Faster R-CNN model without any form of test-time adaptation; Ablated baseline: different pseudo-label generation methods (e.g., simple thresholding, confidence-based filtering); Evaluation chamber: adaptation performance under different levels of label scarcity, noise, and shift.
COST: 33.22
PREDICTION: Employing a GMM-based clustering will help adapt vision-language detectors effectively, especially under scenarios where pseudo-labels are sparse or have varying degrees of confidence and quality, as the network can iteratively focus on particular pseudo-labels for enhancement or correction. Still, abrupt changes in feature distributions could cause the GMM to misestimate the target category means, leading to inconsistencies between pseudo-labeling orientations.

PREDICTION: While fine-grained variance analysis might predict lower adaptation accuracy in test images with aberrant pseudo-label statistics, the strengths in regenerated pseudo-label quality across varied complexity datasets may empirically outweigh the provisional performance decrease, depending on how distribution disorderness is reflected in pseudo-label theoretic sensitivity analysis.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Augmenting Test-time Adaptive Object Detection with Adversarial Training and Expectation Maximization
PROPOSAL: We will incorporate adversarial training and Expectation Maximization (EM) to enhance test-time adaptive object detection across various target domains. Adversarial training will be designed to help the network robustly adapt to potential perturbations in unlabeled data. Meanwhile, EM-based pseudo-label update strategy will be employed to iteratively refine pseudo-labels generated at each test time step while progressively reducing estimation uncertainty.
CONTROLS: Baseline: standard Faster R-CNN model without any form of test-time adaptation; Ablated baseline: different adaptation components (e.g., pseudo-label generation, adversarial training); Ablated chamber: adaptation using specific intermediate pseudo-label metrics (e.g., overlap ratio); Evaluation chamber: adaptation performance under different levels of label scarcity, noise, and shift.
COST: 60
PREDICTION: Successful deployment of the proposed combination of robustness-enhancing adversarial training and uncertainty-aware Expectation Maximization would bring a considerable boost in test-time adaptation stability and robustness; However, since EM-based refiner tends to refine from less confident probability distributions, growth pace of initially generated pseudo-labels may slow down depending on its initial support.

TITLE: Investigating the Impact of Pseudo-label Quality on Test-time Adaptive Object Detection
PROPOSAL: We will conduct a controlled experiment on the popular COCO dataset to compare different strategies of pseudo-label filtering thresholds (e.g., 0.5, 0.7, 0.9) and analyze their impact on the detection performance of a test-time adaptive object detector (TTAOD) that uses self-training with pseudo-labeled objects.
CONTROLS: Baseline: standard Faster R-CNN model without any form of test-time adaptation; Ablated baseline: TTAOD with no pseudo-label filtering; Ablated baseline: different pseudo-label generation methods (e.g., simple thresholding, confidence-based filtering, and refinement via agreement among models).
COST: 60
PREDICTION: Increasing pseudo-label quality would improve detection performance, but setting the threshold too high might lead to under-estimation of available pseudo-labels on certain images (potentially causing stability issues).

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Investigation on Plug-and-play Vision-Language Detectors for Test-time Adaptive Detection
PROPOSAL: We will compare the performance of popular pre-trained vision-language models (e.g., GLIP and Grounding DINO) directly applied to test-time adaptive object detection on various real-world benchmarks (e.g., COCO, LVIS, and OpenImages). These models would not be fine-tuned on the specific test domain but still be expected to adapt due to their pre-trained knowledge and capacity to generalize.
CONTROLS: Baseline: standard Faster R-CNN model without any form of test-time adaptation; Ablated baseline: different pre-trained vision-language models; Evaluation chamber: adaptation performance under different levels of label scarcity, noise, and shift.
COST: 80
PREDICTION: While strong pre-trained vision-language models would adapt decently well on their own with little to no fine-tuning, their performance will nevertheless degrade as the domain shift and complexity increase, necessitating some form of adaptation mechanism to be incorporated prevent collapse to weak initial knowledge.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Investigation on Plug-and-play Vision-Language Detectors for Test-time Adaptive Detection
PROPOSAL: We will extend the previous proposal by incorporating self-supervised methods to refine the pre-trained vision-language detector's adaptation to the target domain through online pseudo-label refinement and mix-up strategies. Additionally, we will examine the convergence and stability of this self-supervised adaptation process across different test batches and regression metrics (e.g., cross-entropy loss and detection accuracy).
CONTROLS: Baseline: standard Faster R-CNN model without any form of test-time adaptation; Ablated baseline: different pre-trained vision-language models; Ablated chamber: adaptation with and without pseudo-label refinement; Evaluation chamber: adaptation performance under different levels of label scarcity, noise, and shift.
COST: 120
PREDICTION: Self-supervised adaptation, particularly pseudo-label refinement and mix-up strategies, will allow plug-and-play vision-language detectors to achieve significant performance gains, remaining effective up to a moderate degree of domain shift and label scarcity, where pseudo-labeling stops working efficiently.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Adapting Vision-Language Detectors with Gaussian Mixture Model-based Pseudo-label Clustering
PROPOSAL: We will implement a clustering-based strategy using a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) to categorize pseudo-labels produced on test images into reliable and unreliable categories. A separate branch of the network will then be trained to iteratively enhance the pseudo-labels (with lower ambiguity) and correct the pseudo-labels (with higher ambiguity) simultaneously, thus reducing the overfitting risk and potential instability in the adaptation process.
CONTROLS: Baseline: standard Faster R-CNN model without any form of test-time adaptation; Ablated baseline: different pseudo-label generation methods (e.g., simple thresholding, confidence-based filtering); Evaluation chamber: adaptation performance under different levels of label scarcity, noise, and shift.
COST: 100
PREDICTION: Employing a GMM-based clustering will help adapt vision-language detectors effectively, especially under scenarios where pseudo-labels are sparse or have varying degrees of confidence and quality, as the network can iteratively focus on particular pseudo-labels for enhancement or correction. Still, abrupt changes in feature distributions could cause the GMM to misestimate the target category means, leading to inconsistencies between pseudo-labeling orientations.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Domain-Agnostic Vision-Language Detector with On-the-Fly Label Aggregation
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel test-time adaptive object detection (TTAOD) method, Domain-Agnostic Vision-Language Detector with On-the-Fly Label Aggregation (DAVLDA), leveraging the strengths of pre-trained vision-language foundation models. DAVLDA introduces a label aggregation module that dynamically fuses multi-source pseudo-labels from diverse target domains, even in the absence of high-quality pseudo-labels or source statistics. This approach limits overfitting and preserves pre-trained knowledge. During adaptation, DAVLDA's label aggregation scheme leverages both class-specific confidence indicators and instance-specific similarity metrics computed from cross-attention maps between the vision and language modalities. To handle scenarios where targets lack pseudo-labels, DAVLDA implements a ClassProposal Lane (CPL), tasked with probing the detector for previously unseen entities by coarse-graining pseudo-labels into potentially novel category instances. A weighted ensemble of these ideas, combined with a learned embedding predictor, enhances the method's adaptability under real-world distributions and nobbles transmission of valuable information across varied domains.
CONTROLS: Freeze-1—a standard pre-trained vision-language detector with no adaptation; Freeze-2—a pre-trained detector with self-training under standard pseudo-label filtering; Adaptive-3—a vanilla one-pass self-training over the adapted detector; Freeze-1+Adaptive-1—a fusion of above Freeze-1 with domain-adaptive inference at test time with output sampling from various distributions of pre-trained topology.
COST: 40
PREDICTION: DAVLDA displays significant improvement over existing adaptive detectors, notably outperforming Freeze-2 and comparable to Advanced-3 when tested on diverse cross-domain and cross-category benchmarks under specified adaptation conditions, but performance may degrade in scenarios with unrepresentative few-shot target domains.

TITLE: Localized-Certainty Weighted Ensemble for Reliable Pseudo-Label Adaptation
PROPOSAL: We propose the Localized-Certainty Weighted Ensemble (LCWE) framework to improve the reliability of pseudo-label adaptation in test-time adaptive object detection. LCWE combines the benefits of self-training, localization of pseudo-label uncertainty, and complexity regularization in pseudo-label weighting. TITLE: Self-Consistent Learning for Zero-Shot Adjustment of Test-Time Adaptive Object Detection
PROPOSAL: We propose a self-consistent learning framework that enables zero-shot adjustment of test-time adaptive object detection (TTAOD) models without manual label annotation. Our approach, dubbed Self-Consistent Learning (SCL), involves a novel dual-pathway architecture where the first pathway serves as a proxy teacher, providing self-generated pseudolabels for the second pathway to refine upon. By iteratively refining the pseudo-labels through self-supervised learning and optimization, the model adaptively adjusts its internal representation and learning configuration to align with the changing test data distribution. Moreover, we incorporate a conditional branch that tailors the learning behavior based on the uncertainty of the pseudo-labels and the dynamics of the test data, securing the model's consistency and robustness.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Meta-Learned Visual-Linguistic Calibration for Adaptable Test-Time Object Detection
PROPOSAL: We introduce meta-learned visual-linguistic calibration (MLVC) to enhance the adaptability of test-time object detection (TTOD) models in diverse and dynamic environments. Our approach employs a meta-learning framework to learn a meta-model that can adapt to various domains and distributions. By leveraging a meta-representation learning mechanism, MLVC learns to calibrate the visual-linguistic alignment in a task-agnostic manner, allowing for more effective knowledge transfer and adaptation to unseen domains. Furthermore, we propose a transformer-based visual-linguistic collaborator that pairs the pre-trained visual backbone with a learnable linguistic module, enabling more efficient and robust fusion of visual and linguistic cues.

CONTROLS: MLVC compared against DAVLDA, ITAZLM, our revised LCWE approach, and SCL.
COST: 240
PREDICTION: MLVC exhibits excellent adaptability and outperforms current state-of-the-art TTAOD methods on a variety of complex test data distributions, showcasing its value in scenarios with limited prior knowledge and dynamic environments. However, the increased computational overhead may lead to performance imbalances in memory-constrained settings or when prioritizing high-priority adaptability.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Asymmetric Entropy Regularization for Pseudo-Label Quality Refinement
PROPOSAL: We propose an asymmetric entropy regularization (AER) scheme to refine pseudo-label quality in test-time adaptive object detection (TTAOD) tasks. AER exploits the asymmetry between the meta-training and meta-adaptation phases to regularize pseudo-labels and mitigate the effects of noisy or unreliable pseudo-labels. By introducing a meta-learning based hyperparameter adjustment mechanism, AER dynamically adjusts the regularization strength according to the changing data distribution, leading to more robust and transferable pseudo-labels. Our approach outperforms existing methods in scenarios with diverse test data distributions and varying pseudo-label quality, demonstrating its potential as a plug-and-play refining module for TTAOD methods.

CONTROLS: AER in conjunction with MLVC, ITAZLM, and SCL.
COST: 300
PREDICTION: AER significantly improves pseudo-label quality, leading to enhanced adaptation performance and reduced overfitting, but may face difficulties in terms of stability when dealing with highly imbalanced test datasets or categories with very few associated pseudo-labels.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Branch Test-Time Adaptation Network with Hierarchical Pseudo-Label Refining
PROPOSAL: We introduce a multi-branch test-time adaptation network (MB-TAN) with a hierarchical pseudo-label refining (HPLR) module to tackle challenging TTAOD tasks with diverse and dynamic test data distributions. MB-TAN employs a hybrid architecture that combines multiple adaptative branches with a common backbone, each learning to adapt to a specific aspect of the test data. HPLR refines the pseudo-labels generated by each branch in a hierarchical manner, leveraging local visual-linguistic cues and more global semantic features to mitigate the effects of noisy or unreliable pseudo-labels. Our approach outperforms existing methods on a range of TTAOD benchmarks, showcasing its capability to learn robust and transferable representations adapt to various test data distributions.

CONTROLS: MB-TAN + HPLR in conjunction with AER, MLVC, ITAZLM, and SCL.
COST: 480
PREDICTION: MB-TAN + HPLR exhibits excellent adaptability, robustness, and transferability, but its high computational overhead may pose limitations in terms of real-time adaptability or resource-constrained scenarios; a more efficient implementation or approximations may be necessary to make it scalable.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Deliberation-Aware Test-Time Adaptation for Object Detection with Partial Supervision
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel approach for test-time adaptation (TTA) of object detection models, dubbed Deliberation-Aware TTA (DA-TTA). DA-TTA incorporates a deliberation module, which evaluates the reliability of pseudo-labels generated by the model during TTA, allowing the model to prioritize more reliable pseudo-labels and adapt more effectively to the test data distribution. Our method is especially effective when faced with partial supervision, where only some of the target classes are labeled. We demonstrate that DA-TTA outperforms existing TTA methods on a range of benchmarks, including those with partial supervision.

CONTROLS: DA-TTA in conjunction with all previous approaches (1-7).
COST: 720
PREDICTION: DA-TTA showcases enhanced adaptability and robustness under partial supervision, but its integration with previous approaches (1-7) might lead to increased computational complexity; efficient approximations or abstractions of the deliberation module could help mitigate this issue.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISED Localized-Certainty Weighted Ensemble for Reliable Pseudo-Label Adaptation
PROPOSAL: We refine our previous Localized-Certainty Weighted Ensemble (LCWE) approach by incorporating an uncertainty-aware patch-based weighting strategy to linearize the learning complexity and improve the robustness of pseudo-label weighting. LCWE combines the benefits of self-training, localization of pseudo-label uncertainty, and complexity regularization in pseudo-label weighting. Our approach also leverages a patch-based weighting scheme to reduce the impact of noisy pseudo-labels and effectively aggregate both class-agnostic and class-conditional real-value pseudo-labels. We further extend LCWE by introducing a novel label-aware context-agnostic pseudo-label diffusion strategy, allowing the model to propagate reliable pseudo-labels even in the absence of high-quality pseudo-labels. This is achieved by conditioning the pseudo-label diffusion process on the model's confidence estimates, thus improving the overall robustness and reliability of the pseudo-label adaptation process.

CONTROLS: LCWE with and without the label-aware context-agnostic pseudo-label diffusion strategy, compared to Freeze-1, Freeze-2, DAVLDA, and ITAZLM.
COST: 360
PREDICTION: The refined LCWE approach significantly improves the reliability and robustness of pseudo-label adaptation, yielding performance comparable to or better than state-of-the-art TTAOD methods. However, the added computational complexity may impact performance in scenarios with extremely limited computational resources or high-priority adaptability requirements.

TITLE: Meta-Learned Visual-Linguistic Calibration for Adaptable Test-Time Object Detection
PROPOSAL: We introduce meta-learned visual-linguistic calibration (MLVC) to enhance the adaptability of test-time object detection (TTOD) models in diverse and dynamic environments. Our approach employs a meta-learning framework to learn a meta-model that can adapt to various domains and distributions. By leveraging a meta-representation learning mechanism, MLVC learns to calibrate the visual-linguistic alignment in a task-agnostic manner, allowing for more effective knowledge transfer and adaptation to unseen domains. Furthermore, we propose a transformer-based visual-linguistic collaborator that pairs the pre-trained visual backbone with a learnable linguistic module, enabling more efficient and robust fusion of visual and linguistic cues.

CONTROLS: MLVC compared against DAVLDA, ITAZLM, our revised LCWE approach, and SCL.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Asymmetric Entropy Regularization for Pseudo-Label Quality Refinement
PROPOSAL: We propose an asymmetric entropy regularization (AER) scheme to refine pseudo-label quality in test-time adaptive object detection (TTAOD) tasks. AER exploits the asymmetry between the meta-training and meta-adaptation phases to regularize pseudo-labels and mitigate the effects of noisy or unreliable pseudo-labels. By introducing a meta-learning based hyperparameter adjustment mechanism, AER dynamically adjusts the regularization strength according to the changing data distribution, leading to more robust and transferable pseudo-labels. Our approach outperforms existing methods in scenarios with diverse test data distributions and varying pseudo-label quality, demonstrating its potential as a plug-and-play refining module for TTAOD methods.

CONTROLS: AER in conjunction with MLVC, ITAZLM, and SCL.
COST: 900
PREDICTION: AER significantly improves pseudo-label quality, leading to enhanced adaptation performance and reduced overfitting, but may face difficulties in terms of stability when dealing with highly imbalanced test datasets or categories with very few associated pseudo-labels.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Branch Test-Time Adaptation Network with Hierarchical Pseudo-Label Refining
PROPOSAL: We introduce a multi-branch test-time adaptation network (MB-TAN) with a hierarchical pseudo-label refining (HPLR) module to tackle challenging TTAOD tasks with diverse and dynamic test data distributions. MB-TAN employs a hybrid architecture that combines multiple adaptative branches with a common backbone, each learning to adapt to a specific aspect of the test data. HPLR refines the pseudo-labels generated by each branch in a hierarchical manner, leveraging local visual-linguistic cues and more global semantic features to mitigate the effects of noisy or unreliable pseudo-labels. Our approach outperforms existing methods on a range of TTAOD benchmarks, showcasing its capability to learn robust and transferable representations adapt to various test data distributions.

CONTROLS: MB-TAN + HPLR in conjunction with AER, MLVC, ITAZLM, and SCL.
COST: 1440
PREDICTION: MB-TAN + HPLR exhibits excellent adaptability, robustness, and transferability, but its high computational overhead may pose limitations in terms of real-time adaptability or resource-constrained scenarios; a more efficient implementation or approximations may be necessary to make it scalable.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Deliberation-Aware Test-Time Adaptation for Object Detection with Partial Supervision
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel approach for test-time adaptation (TTA) of object detection models, dubbed Deliberation-Aware TTA (DA-TTA). DA-TTA incorporates a deliberation module, which evaluates the reliability of pseudo-labels generated by the model during TTA, allowing the model to prioritize more reliable pseudo-labels and adapt more effectively to the test data distribution. Our method is especially effective when faced with partial supervision, where only some of the target classes are labeled. We demonstrate that DA-TTA outperforms existing TTA methods on a range of benchmarks, including those with partial supervision.

CONTROLS: DA-TTA in conjunction with all previous approaches (1-7).
COST: 2160
PREDICTION: DA-TTA showcases enhanced adaptability and robustness under partial supervision, but its integration with previous approaches (1-7) might lead to increased computational complexity; efficient approximations or abstractions of the deliberation module could help mitigate this issue.

PROPOSAL: We experimentally compare the impact of filtering pseudo-labels based on confidence thresholds, with different threshold values and specific flags for images lacking pseudo-labels. COST: 15
PREDICTION: We expect to see significant degradation in adaptation performance when pseudo-label filtering is applied at low confidence thresholds, especially for noisy or occluded images, demonstrating the importance of reliable pseudo-label generation under realistic test-time conditions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Provable Divergence-Based Adaptation Bound
PROPOSAL: We derive a mathematical expression for the divergence between the pre-trained detector and the target domain distribution, in terms of the relative entropy and the KL-divergence. We prove an upper bound on the test-time adaptation error, guaranteed to be within a factor of the bound on the divergence between the pre-trained detector and the target domain. This provides a rigorous analysis of the trade-off between the quality of the pre-trained detector and the effectiveness of test-time adaptation under realistic distribution shifts.
CONTROLS: Baseline testing on a small fixed set of real-world target datasets without adaptation (absolute performance ceiling).
COST: 50
PREDICTION: We expect to show that using our divergence-based bound to monitor the adaptation process and optimize it achieves an average accuracy of 90% or better, thus validating the effectiveness of our theoretical analysis under substantial domain shifts.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Provable Divergence-Based Adaptation Bound
PROPOSAL: We revise our proposal to specifically consider the case where the vision-language detector's pre-training is on a large-scale image-text corpus and also includes knowledge distillation from a backbone detector, as in recent self-supervised vision-language learning architectures, e.g. DALL-E. We continue to analyze the rate of convergence to the target domain with our divergence-based bound, but now relate this convergence to the strength of the knowledge distillation mechanism and its transferability across domains.
CONTROLS: Baseline testing using the latest DALL-E architecture and its variants without our divergence-based adaptation.
COST: 60
PREDICTION: By showing how our bound can be used to adaptively control the knowledge distillation mechanism during test-time, we expect to demonstrate a 15% improvement in adaptation performance under domain shifts when leveraging pre-trained vision-language knowledge, compared to fixed distillation parameters.

TITLE: Label-Aware Cross-Modal Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: To generate high-quality pseudo-labels, we propose a cross-modal contrastive learning method, where the vision-language model is trained to distinguish target-domain features from source-domain features, jointly on the image and text modalities, under a label-aware region of interest (ROI) matching framework. We use a memory bank of pseudo-labeled target-domain features to contrastively sharpen the feature distributions, promoting better adaptation under dynamic domain shifts.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Source-Free Adaptive Confidence Calibration
PROPOSAL: We introduce a source-free adaptive confidence calibration method designed to improve the performance of pre-trained vision-language detectors under domain shifts. We use the pseudo-labels and confidence predictions on the target domain to adapt the detector's confidence calibration, without relying on any source-domain labels or data. Our approach involves fine-tuning a confidence threshold estimation model using pseudo-labels and confidence predictions from the target domain, allowing us to adjust the detector's confidence levels to better match its performance under the new domain.
CONTROLS: Baseline testing without confidence calibration, and with standard confidence calibration methods that rely on source-domain data.
COST: 100
PREDICTION: We expect that our source-free confidence calibration method will improve the detection accuracy on the target domain by an average of 8%, compared to baseline methods, and show robustness under different domain shifts and batch sizes.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Turn Online Test-Time Adaptation
PROPOSAL: We propose a multi-turn online test-time adaptation framework, which iteratively refines the pre-trained vision-language detector's performance on the target domain by adapting to the recent test samples and pseudo-labels. Our approach involves using a re-evaluation mechanism to reassess the quality of pseudo-labels and confidence predictions, and a re-training component to fine-tune the detector's performance based on the re-evaluated pseudo-labels. We adopt a set of intermediate-quality pseudo-labels as guidance for re-training to prevent overfitting to noisy samples.
CONTROLS: Baseline testing using single-turn online test-time adaptation, and a re-training component without pseudo-label re-evaluation.
COST: 140
PREDICTION: We expect that our multi-turn online test-time adaptation framework will improve the detection accuracy on the target domain by an average of 18%, and demonstrate improved robustness under noisy and dynamic test conditions, such as changing lighting conditions and occlusions.

TITLE: Multi-Turn Online Test-Time Adaptation
PROPOSAL: We refine the multi-turn online test-time adaptation framework to incorporate a reality checking module, which monitors the quality and consistency of the pseudo-labels and confidence predictions across multiple turns. ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Vision-Language PMF for Adaptation
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of pivotal-mixture-of-experts (PMF) adaptation for vision-language detector adaptation during test time, leveraging the pre-trained detector's open-vocabulary capabilities to build a modularized neural architecture containing domain-agnostic and domain-sensitive components. Unsupervised multi-task learning will be employed, leveraging a PMF of domain-sensitive layers trained on a pre-labelled dataset and updated during testing to counteract domain shifts in the target domain. Online fine-tuning will adapt parameters of both the domain-sensitive and domain-agnostic layers based on pseudo-labels from unlabeled target data, ensuring knowledge transfer from the source domain pre-trained detector.
CONTROLS: Compare against (i) a standard pre-trained vision-language detector and (ii) state-of-the-art test-time adaptation methods.
COST: 1500
PREDICTION: This approach should improve upon existing methods in terms of generalizability and test-time adaptation speed. However, domain adaptation challenges may remain in unseen domain distributions.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Adaptive Thresholding for Reliable Pseudo-Labeling
PROPOSAL: Introduce an adaptive thresholding mechanism for pseudo-label filtering during test-time adaptation, tailored to the specific test image and its embedded pseudolabels. The percentage of confidently pseudo-labeled objects will determine an adaptive confidence threshold for the rest of the pseudolabel set; for test images without pseudo-labels (undersampled domain areas), a scheme for chaining uncertainty with less confident pseudo-labels to its neighboring images can yield suppressed noise-amplification effects, and robust utilization of most confident pseudo-labels, thereby, reliable pseudo-label quality will be extended.
CONTROLS: Compare against a baseline where pseudo-label confidence threshold is fixed; compare against pseudo-label-based TTAOD methods with an in-grown confidence threshold selection.
COST: 2500
PREDICTION: This adaptive thresholding mechanism should enhance pseudo-label reliability and avoid oversegmentation effects, ultimately boosting overall test-time adaptation performance. Potential challenges include imperfect identification of triggered chaining areas.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Euclidean TSP Dataset Scale
PROPOSAL: Create a Euclidean traveling salesman problem (TSP) dataset of varying sizes by randomly sampling points in a 2D plane and uniformly increasing point counts from 100 to 10000. Train a fixed-size neural network with multiple learning algorithms on each dataset, and measure the network's average distance performance on a held-out test set.
CONTROLS: Compare to baselines with a random search and a simple genetic algorithm on each dataset, with models of fixed size and varying sizes to evaluate the effect of neural network parameter count on performance.
COST: 10800,0
PREDICTION: This proposal will uncover simple, predictable trends in average distance performance as dataset size increases, and will also reveal how different learning algorithms affect these trends. However, performance may degrade unpredictably between TSP datasets of certain sizes, or may not follow a smooth trend due to the problem's NP-hardness.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Monotonically Increasing Dataset Reconstruction
PROPOSAL: REVISED PROPOSAL FOR 1. Investigating Euclidean TSP Dataset Scale: Instead of measuring average distance performance, we will try to iteratively increase the dataset size by gradually adding a small number of points (e.g. 200 more) at a time, and comparing the model's reconstruction accuracy of the existing data points as new points are added. Monitor how the model's reconstruction error evolves during this process.
CONTROLS: Compare to a model that uses a meta-learning approach to adapt to the increasing dataset size by storing and retrieving specific knowledge about the previously seen points, and compare to a baseline that uses a pre-trained model on an identical dataset of the same size, but without iteratively increasing the size.
COST: 11000
PREDICTION: This revised proposal will provide insight into the progressive degradation of the model's performance as the dataset size increases, revealing whether the model's adaptation capabilities are sufficient to handle the changing number of points. However, if the model memorizes local minima rather than generalizing to the increasing dataset size, the results might not be entirely smooth.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Scaling Representation Space Complexity
PROPOSAL: REVISED PROPOSAL FOR 1. Investigating Euclidean TSP Dataset Scale: In addition to varying the number of points in the TSP dataset, we will add a noise component that scales with the Euclidean distance between points. This will introduce a representation space complexity as the number of points increases, which interacts with the solution space complexity in a physically-meaningful way.
CONTROLS: Investigate how the performance of the model changes under this scaling factor, especially in comparison to a baseline that trains on datasets without this increasing representation space complexity.
COST: 11000
PREDICTION: This revised proposal will reveal insights into how the size of the representation space affects the achievable performance of the model when scaling up the solution space complexity. However, introducing noise may lead to performance degradation rather than predictable improvement, or may require adaptations in hyperparameter tuning that are not obvious upfront.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Theory of Solution Space Complexity
PROPOSAL: Establish a theoretical framework for understanding solution space complexity in machine learning problems like the Euclidean TSP. Specifically, analyze how the increase in solution space complexity relates to the number of local minima and the volume of the optimal solution region in the space of all possible solutions.
CONTROLS: Derive theoretical bounds for the expected performance degradation as a function of solution space complexity, and examine whether these bounds match empirical results from the machine learning experiments in this and similar works.
COST: 13000,0
PREDICTION: This theoretical framework will provide deep insights into why performance might degrade or improve under increasing solution space complexity, and will help to understand the fundamental limits of solution space complexity. However, deriving tight theoretical bounds might require additional and more complex mathematical machinery, and may not cover all aspects of real-world machine learning problem classes.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Similarity-Based Neural Network Scaling
PROPOSAL: Investigate a neural network designed to scale under similarity-based objectives rather than the typical Euclidean distance metrics, which should be directly beneficial for handling representation space complexities with increasing dimensionality. Specifically, train a neural network using a similarity-based loss function that is invariant to rotation and translation transformations in the data space, and measure how this affects the achievable performance as the dataset size and representation space complexity increase.
CONTROLS: Compare to a baseline that uses a standard Euclidean distance loss, and examine whether the similarity-based approach leads to more predictable and advantageous scaling behavior.
COST: 12000,0
PREDICTION: This proposal will reveal whether similarity-based neural network scaling can provide insights into how to lift the curse of dimensionality and smoothly scale performance under increasing representation space complexity. However, translating this approach to more complex machine learning problems and adapting it to different domain-specific objectives might require significant additional research.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Asymptotic Solution Space Complexity Bounds
PROPOSAL: REVISED PROPOSAL FOR 2. Theory of Solution Space Complexity: Strengthen the theoretical frameworks by deriving asymptotic bounds on the expected solution space complexity as a function of the number of points, noise, and other problem parameters. This will provide a deeper understanding of the fundamental trade-offs and limits in scaling machine learning problems.
CONTROLS: Examine whether these asymptotic bounds hold for a range of different machine learning problems, including the Euclidean TSP and more complex problems with varying representation and solution space complexities.
COST: 14000
PREDICTION: This revised proposal will establish a more comprehensive theoretical foundation for understanding solution space complexity, and will provide tighter bounds on performance degradation and scaling limits. However, deriving and verifying these asymptotic bounds might require significant additional mathematical development and may not be entirely generalizable to all real-world machine learning problems.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Generalized Neural Scaling Laws
PROPOSAL: Develop a unified framework for understanding neural scaling laws across a wide range of machine learning problems, including those with varying solution and representation space complexities. Specifically, derive a set of generalized scaling laws that accommodate different problem parameters and complexities, and examine whether these laws are consistent with empirical results from multiple machine learning experiments.

PREDICTION: This proposal will lead to a more comprehensive understanding of neural scaling laws and their limitations, and will help to identify the key factors that drive scaling behavior in different machine learning problems. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Scaling Law Discovery in Euclidean TSP
PROPOSAL: We will simulate the Euclidean Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) on scaled instances using the NSGA-II genetic algorithm and the Christofides algorithm, training a neural network using a Euclidean distance metric to guide it. We will then analyze the performance of the neural network as a function of model size, generation size, and compute budget, in order to identify any emergent scaling laws.
CONTROLS: Christofides algorithm and NSGA-II genetic algorithm as baselines; Euclidean distance metric only, no reinforcement learning loss; same neural network architecture and simulation parameters across all experiments.
COST: 332.2
PREDICTION: We expect to find smooth scaling laws for performance as a function of model size and generation size, with diminishing returns in performance as compute budget is scaled. The neural network may perform comparably to the Christofides algorithm on small instances but will outperform it on larger ones. Performance may degrade for very high-compute-budget cases due to overfitting.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Investigating Model Capacity Limits in TSP
PROPOSAL: Building on the results of our initial experiment, we will run the refined setup (with NSGA-II and Christofides initialization, and exploration of neural network architectures) until the point at which the model's performance starts to degrade significantly due to overfitting. We will then apply techniques such as regularization and early stopping to the model to further increase its capacity and observe how it affects the emergent scaling laws.
CONTROLS: same setup as previous experiment, with added application of regularization and early stopping to models showing signs of overfitting; control experiments where models without regularization and early stopping are trained to comparable capacity.
COST: 1500
PREDICTION: The application of regularization and early stopping will allow the model to achieve higher performance on the largest TSP instances tested, but may also lead to an increase in the steepness of the overfitting region due to the reduction of noise in the objective function.

TITLE: Weakly-Supervised Multilingual Co-Training of Quality Filters
PROPOSAL:   We propose a weakly-supervised multilingual co-training method to develop multiple quality filters for different languages. Utilizing a pre-existing weakly-supervised multilingual pretraining corpus C4 that is pre-aligned and filtered (e.g. Mondial), we initialize multiple quality filters using this pre-sampled and filtered web-crawl, each of them trained on selected subsets of languages C4. Then, a distillation process is applied, where a small baseline quality filter trained on in-domain native data is used to "revise" the co-trained quality filters. Each of the final quality filters are then used to select Mondial over another akin precrawl dataset’s random filtered examples.
CONTROLS: (1) Contrastive learning framework (2) Isolated Quality Filters 
COST: 10240
PREDICTION: To evaluate the robustness of our proposed framework, we expect to see significant performance improvements using multiple co-trained model filters as well as improving the quality of documents by selecting based on multiple discount/bias mitigation criteria. Lacking low-quality content property overlook could lead the quality prediction filters to fail.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multilingual Data Selection with Meta-Learning
PROPOSAL: We propose a meta-learning approach to train a multilingual data quality rater that can adapt to various languages and domains. The rater is trained using a meta-learning framework that learns to learn a representation of language-agnostic data quality features from a set of meta-training tasks on a diverse set of languages and domains. We will use a transformer-based meta-learning model, where the encoder is a multilingual BERT model and the decoder is a meta-learner that learns to predict data quality scores. The model will be trained on a large-scale multilingual dataset, such as the MM_corpus.
CONTROLS: We will compare our approach with several baseline approaches, including DCLM, AskLLM, and FineWeb2-HQ, and evaluate its performance using standard metrics such as perplexity, ROUGE, and BLEU.
COST: 1000
PREDICTION: Our approach should outperform the baselines in terms of adaptability to new languages and domains, and lead to better downstream performance of LLMs in multilingual settings.

PROPOSAL: We propose a multitask learning approach to train a single multilingual data quality rater that can judge documents on their content rather than just their language. The rater will be trained on a multitask setup with two tasks: language translation and data quality scoring, both of which are trained simultaneously using a shared encoder-decoder architecture. We will use a transformer-based model with two decoders, one for translation and one for data quality scoring. The model will be trained on a multilingual dataset, such as the WMT dataset for translation and the MM_corpus for data quality scoring.

PREDICTION: Our approach should be able to learn language-agnostic data quality features that can be used across different languages, leading to better adaptability and robustness in multilingual settings. However, it may require more training data and computational resources compared to the meta-learning approach.

TITLE: Multilingual Data Selection with Meta-Learning and Online Monitoring
PROPOSAL: We revise the meta-learning approach (proposal 1) to include online monitoring of the data quality and adaptability. If the model's performance on the validation set drops below a certain threshold, the training data will be updated and the model will be retrained. This will allow the model to adapt to changes in the distribution of the data and to learn from its successes and failures.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multilingual Data Selection with Meta-Learning
PROPOSAL: We propose a meta-learning approach to train a multilingual data quality rater that can adapt to various languages and domains. The rater is trained using a meta-learning framework that learns to learn a representation of language-agnostic data quality features from a set of meta-training tasks on a diverse set of languages and domains. We will use a transformer-based meta-learning model, where the encoder is a multilingual BERT model and the decoder is a meta-learner that learns to predict data quality scores. The model will be trained on a large-scale multilingual dataset, such as the MM_corpus.
CONTROLS: We will compare our approach with several baseline approaches, including DCLM, AskLLM, and FineWeb2-HQ, and evaluate its performance using standard metrics such as perplexity, ROUGE, and BLEU.

We will use a transformer-based model with two decoders, one for translation and one for data quality scoring. The model will be trained on a multilingual dataset, such as the WMT dataset for translation and the MM_corpus for data quality scoring.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Transferability of FineWeb-Edu Classifier Across Languages
PROPOSAL: We will adapt the FineWeb-Edu classifier to six languages (Spanish, French, German, Italian, Portuguese, and Dutch) and evaluate its performance using multilingual benchmarks (WMT news articles, CCAligned, and ParaCrawl). We will analyze the ratings produced by each language-specific rater to determine whether the quality signal is transferred across languages, and whether it captures content quality rather than language-specific features.
CONTROLS: Compare to FineWeb2-HQ with benchmark-derived supervision, and to traditional heuristic filtering methods.
COST: 6000
PREDICTION: The FineWeb-Edu classifier will outperform FineWeb2-HQ in all languages, capturing content quality rather than language-specific features, and task-adaptation will be most effective for French and Spanish. Performance will degrade significantly in German, Italian, and Portuguese, but retain consistency across all six languages.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Developing a Large-Scale Multilingual Wasserstein Distance Metric for Data Selection
PROPOSAL: We will adapt the Optimal Transport (OT) framework to develop a multilingual Wasserstein distance metric for data selection. This will involve learning a domain transfer embedding space using a multimodal transformer and computing the OT distance between the pretraining corpus and a high-quality sample set. We will evaluate this metric using perplexity-based filtering, quality rating, and manual assessment of the selected corpora.
CONTROLS: Compare to existing model-based selection methods, such as DCLM, AskLLM, and QuRating, using pretraining corpora in six languages.
COST: 10680
PREDICTION: The multilingual Wasserstein distance metric will outperform existing model-based selection methods in all languages, providing more nuanced control over data selection and density in the selected corpus. However, manual assessment will reveal that it favors shorter texts, and robustness to significant perturbations of the high-quality sample set may be poor.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Comparison of Global and Local Model-Based Data Selection Methods for Multilingual Web Crawls
PROPOSAL: We will implement and compare global and local model-based data selection methods, including DCLM, AskLLM, and the FineWeb-Edu classifier, using global and local embeddings learned from the corpus and task-specific weights. We will evaluate their performance using web crawl datasets in six languages, considering selection metrics such as recall, precision, and quality rating.
CONTROLS: Compare global to local methods, and to heuristic filtering methods.
COST: 6650.42
PREDICTION: Global methods will outperform local methods in monolingual data selection but will degrade significantly in multilingual settings, where local methods show better performance, especially in languages where the global vocabulary is less familiar. We will also observe that local methods struggle to capture global quality trends, hampering recall.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Comparison of Global and Local Model-Based Data Selection Methods for Multilingual Web Crawls
PROPOSAL: We will implement and compare global and local model-based data selection methods, including DCLM, AskLLM, and the FineWeb-Edu classifier. For each method, we will experiment with using knowledge distillation to adapt the teacher model to the specific task and language, with or without fine-tuning on web-crawled data. We will evaluate their performance using web crawl datasets in six languages, considering selection metrics such as recall, precision, and quality rating.
CONTROLS: Compare global to local methods, with and without knowledge distillation, and to heuristic filtering methods.
COST: 10000
PREDICTION: Incorporating knowledge distillation will significantly improve performance of global methods and also enhance local methods in monolingual settings; however, its impact may be less pronounced in languages where the teacher model's knowledge is already well-represented in the local data. I expect that fine-tuning knowledge distilled local models will result in comparable or even better performance than analogous somewhat poorly defined adaptation mechanisms devised so far.

TITLE: Investigating the Impact of Lexical and Stylistic Variability on Multilingual Data Selection
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the factors that contribute to inconsistencies in model-based data selection across languages, focusing on lexical and stylistic variability in web-crawled datasets. We will experimentally manipulate text representations to better capture semantic meaning, coreference, and context-aware word embeddings, analyzing their impact on quality rating and selection consistency.
CONTROLS: Compare modified representations to standard contextualized embeddings and evaluate against baseline methods.

PREDICTION: Modifying representations to account for stylistic and lexical differences between languages will improve quality rating consistency across languages, and analysis will reveal that current models over-rely on specific linguistic structures and under-rely on contextual cues.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Developing a Large-Scale Multilingual Wasserstein Distance Metric for Data Selection
PROPOSAL: We will improve the Wasserstein distance metric by incorporating self-supervised contrastive learning to better capture semantic relationships between texts in different languages. This will involve pre-training a multilingual transformer with a domain adaptation loss to stabilize the metric's performance across diverse languages and adaptation tasks. We will then evaluate the performance of this enhanced metric using web crawl datasets in six languages.
CONTROLS: Compare to existing model-based selection methods, such as DCLM, AskLLM, and QuRating, using pretraining corpora in six languages.
COST: 14000
PREDICTION: The contrastive learning variant of the Wasserstein distance metric will surpass the performance of existing model-based selection methods in most languages, but its adaptation to informal writing styles will remain precarious, and sensitivity analysis will be required to detect changes in upstream supervision methods' systematic defects.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Transferability of FineWeb-Edu Classifier Across Languages
PROPOSAL: We will adapt the FineWeb-Edu classifier to six languages (Spanish, French, German, Italian, Portuguese, and Dutch) and evaluate its performance using multilingual benchmarks (WMT news articles, CCAligned, and ParaCrawl). We will analyze the ratings produced by each language-specific rater to determine whether the quality signal is transferred across languages, and whether it captures content quality rather than language-specific features.
CONTROLS: Compare to FineWeb2-HQ with benchmark-derived supervision, and to traditional heuristic filtering methods.
COST: 18000
PREDICTION: The FineWeb-Edu classifier will outperform FineWeb2-HQ in all languages, capturing content quality rather than language-specific features, and task-adaptation will be most effective for French and Spanish. Performance will degrade significantly in German, Italian, and Portuguese, but retain consistency across all six languages.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Developing a Large-Scale Multilingual Wasserstein Distance Metric for Data Selection
PROPOSAL: We will adapt the Optimal Transport (OT) framework to develop a multilingual Wasserstein distance metric for data selection. This will involve learning a domain transfer embedding space using a multimodal transformer and computing the OT distance between the pretraining corpus and a high-quality sample set. We will evaluate this metric using perplexity-based filtering, quality rating, and manual assessment of the selected corpora.
CONTROLS: Compare to existing model-based selection methods, such as DCLM, AskLLM, and QuRating, using pretraining corpora in six languages.
COST: 32000
PREDICTION: The multilingual Wasserstein distance metric will outperform existing model-based selection methods in all languages, providing more nuanced control over data selection and density in the selected corpus. However, manual assessment will reveal that it favors shorter texts, and robustness to significant perturbations of the high-quality sample set may be poor.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Comparison of Global and Local Model-Based Data Selection Methods for Multilingual Web Crawls
PROPOSAL: We will implement and compare global and local model-based data selection methods, including DCLM, AskLLM, and the FineWeb-Edu classifier, using global and local embeddings learned from the corpus and task-specific weights. We will evaluate their performance using web crawl datasets in six languages, considering selection metrics such as recall, precision, and quality rating.
CONTROLS: Compare global to local methods, and to heuristic filtering methods.
COST: 20000
PREDICTION: Global methods will outperform local methods in monolingual data selection but will degrade significantly in multilingual settings, where local methods show better performance, especially in languages where the global vocabulary is less familiar. We will also observe that local methods struggle to capture global quality trends, hampering recall.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Comparison of Global and Local Model-Based Data Selection Methods for Multilingual Web Crawls
PROPOSAL: We will implement and compare global and local model-based data selection methods, including DCLM, AskLLM, and the FineWeb-Edu classifier. For each method, we will experiment with using knowledge distillation to adapt the teacher model to the specific task and language, with or without fine-tuning on web-crawled data. We will evaluate their performance using web crawl datasets in six languages, considering selection metrics such as recall, precision, and quality rating.
CONTROLS: Compare global to local methods, with and without knowledge distillation, and to heuristic filtering methods.
COST: 30000
PREDICTION: Incorporating knowledge distillation will significantly improve performance of global methods and also enhance local methods in monolingual settings; however, its impact may be less pronounced in languages where the teacher model's knowledge is already well-represented in the local data. I expect that fine-tuning knowledge distilled local models will result in comparable or even better performance than analogous somewhat poorly defined adaptation mechanisms devised so far.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Impact of Lexical and Stylistic Variability on Multilingual Data Selection
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the factors that contribute to inconsistencies in model-based data selection across languages, focusing on lexical and stylistic variability in web-crawled datasets. CONTROLS: Compare modified representations to standard contextualized embeddings and evaluate against baseline methods.
COST: 40000
PREDICTION: Modifying representations to account for stylistic and lexical differences between languages will improve quality rating consistency across languages, and analysis will reveal that current models over-rely on specific linguistic structures and under-rely on contextual cues.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multilingual rater pretraining via auxiliary masked language modeling
PROPOSAL: Pretrain a masked language model as a multilingual rater on a large pool of web documents from multiple languages. Train the model to predict missing tokens (masked) in documents pairs that are (1) semantically similar, but one is in English and the other is not; (2) semantically dissimilar, and both are in the same language; and (3) semantically dissimilar, and both are in different languages. This multi-task setup aims to encourage the model to evaluate document quality based on content rather than language.
CONTROLS: Experiment with a control group that uses the same setup but with English-only supervised learning; and baseline models trained on standard masked language modeling without a data quality evaluation task.
COST: 12000
PREDICTION: The multilingual pretraining setup should yield a robust rater that can evaluate document quality across languages. However, the model might struggle with specific language characteristics, leading to reduced performance in certain languages.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the role of document length in multilingual quality assessment
PROPOSAL: Analyze the relationship between document length and quality judgments in multilingual settings, using the rater pretraining model from proposal 1 as a starting point. Create a subset of documents with varying lengths and train a new model to predict quality based solely on document length. Compare the performance of this model to the original rater on a range of tasks, including pretraining data selection and downstream LLM evaluation.
CONTROLS: Investigate how document length affects the performance of heuristic models currently used for data selection; and examine whether controlling for language has any impact on the results.
COST: 18000
PREDICTION: We expect to find that the rater model's performance degrades as document length increases, likely due to the model's reliance on context to make quality judgments. However, the extent of this degradation may vary across languages.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multilingual quality assessment with web documents and human relevance judgements
PROPOSAL: Collect a diverse set of web documents from multiple languages and obtain human relevance judgements (HRJs) for each document. Train and evaluate a sequence-to-sequence model (e.g., BART) on human relevance judgements as a gold standard for quality assessment. Compare the quality assessments from this approach to those from proposal 1 (multilingual rater) on pretraining data selection and downstream LLM evaluation.
CONTROLS: Ablate the use of HRJs and instead select a random set of documents or document similarity based solely on embedding similarities or heuristics to serve as an alternative evaluation strategy for quality data sets trained on.
COST: 27000
PREDICTION: The sequence-to-sequence model should outperform the multilingual rater on the quality assessment task, as it learns from human judgements of relevance. However, the multi-lingual rater model may show performance when paired with data augmentation or distillation techniques.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Large-Scale Volumetric Occupancy-Aware Representation
PROPOSAL: Experimentally evaluate the effectiveness of a volumetric occupancy-aware neural network, which directly integrates occupancy and appearance prediction in a single, end-to-end, differentiable architecture.
We will utilize DenseFusion [1] and DenseAxialReward [2] codebases to develop this parser model.
CONTROLS: Compare with baseline geometry-only networks such as MeshR-CNN [4] and Occupancy Networks (ON) [3] on challenging real-world benchmarks such as ShapeNet [5] and ModelNet [6], and appearance-only networks like appearance fields [7].
COST: 1500
PREDICTION: We expect this method to achieve state-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmarks for 3D reconstruction, moderate performance on appearance prediction, and outperform existing methods that attempt to fuse geometry and appearance in a single model due to the challenges inherent in this task. It might fail to accurately capture nuanced view-dependent effects due to the early combination of occupancy and appearance predictions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Occlusion-aware Latent 3D Representation for View-dependent Appearance
PROPOSAL: We'll implement a neural network architecture based on the NeRF model, that instead of predicting a density function solely from input rays, predicts a density function that accounts for view-dependent occlusion and appearance. This will be achieved by modifying the network to output an additional occlusion-aware term that can account for partial occlusions between objects. We'll train the network on a large dataset of real-world objects with associated multiview images.
CONTROLS: We'll compare our Occlusion-aware model to a NeRF model without the occlusion-aware term, as well as to a baseline occupancy grid representation that only accounts for geometry.
COST: 4000
PREDICTION: We expect the Occlusion-aware model to perform significantly better on tasks that require capturing view-dependent occlusion, such as latent 3D reconstruction and image-to-3D generation from views with partial occlusion. However, it may not outperform the baseline occupancy grid representation for tasks that focus solely on geometry.

This will allow us to learn a more detailed occlusion-aware representation with minimal increase in trainable parameters and computational cost. The hierarchical architecture will consist of multiple scales of voxel grids, each encoding increasingly detailed geometry and appearance information.
CONTROLS: We'll compare our Hierarchical Voxel Grid model to the Occlusion-aware model from proposal 1, as well as to a state-of-the-art dense voxel grid representation.
COST: 6000
PREDICTION: We expect the Hierarchical Voxel Grid model to significantly outperform the Occlusion-aware model by accurately capturing detailed geometry and occlusion patterns, while also surpassing the dense voxel grid baseline for its ability to represent view-dependent appearance effectively.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Bridge Between Geometry and Appearance: Multimodal Fusion for 3D Latents
PROPOSAL: To further address the challenge of jointly representing geometry and appearance, we'll investigate multimodal fusion techniques that allow for simultaneous learning of both modalities within a single 3D latent space. This will be achieved by introducing a novel fusion module that merges information from geometry and appearance streams within the hierarchical voxel grid structure. We'll utilize a shared latent code to couple the geometry and appearance information, enabling the model to learn representations that are consistent across different views and illumination conditions.
CONTROLS: We'll compare our Multimodal Fusion model to both the Occlusion-aware model and the Hierarchical Voxel Grid model from previous proposals, as well as to a baseline model that simply concatenates geometry and appearance features.
COST: 8000
PREDICTION: We expect the Multimodal Fusion model to improve over the existing proposals by robustly capturing both geometric and appearance information, and to generalize well to new viewpoints and lighting conditions. However, it may require more sophisticated regularization techniques to avoid mode collapse and ensure stable training.
